Every changed line is one that a decision named. The other lines of the draft are as they were, and nobody had to read them again. The new version sits with the others, ready for the queries of Documents, Parameters and the Context:

$ sxml xquery --method=adaptive --expression='collection("drafts") ! string(rfc/@docName)'
"draft-example-vane-protocol-00"
"draft-example-vane-protocol-01"
"draft-example-vane-protocol-02"
$ sxml xquery --param=today=2026-11-30 --param=drafts=drafts/vane-02.xml expiry.xq
draft-example-vane-protocol-02: published 2026-11-30, expires 2027-06-03

What we built

The three tools are short because the module does the work, and they agree with each other because the rules are written once: what a requirement is, how it is numbered and what its text is live in spec.xqm, and the edits, the check and the list of changes all use them. Along the way, the project used most of this chapter:

  • library modules that import each other, with record types, enumeration types, typed functions, a private helper and an error code of their own;
  • updating functions that insert, delete and replace exactly the nodes of one decision, and transform with inside one of them;
  • FLWOR expressions with where, joins of two versions by anchor, and switch on the kind of change;
  • external variables with a type and a default, and an enumeration that limits them;
  • fn:message and error for a check that a script can rely on;
  • serialization as text and as JSON, and --output for each step.

Project: Publishing the Specification takes the draft the rest of the way, to HTML and RFC-style text, with XSLT, and runs this chapter's check before it publishes.

Summary

XQuery adds to XPath what you need to write programs:

  • FLWOR expressions iterate, filter, sort, group, number and join;
  • constructors build XML, and output declarations write it as XML, XHTML, HTML, text, JSON or CSV;
  • switch, typeswitch, sequence types and try/catch deal with untidy data;
  • functions, which can be recursive, and library modules organize a program, and external variables make it a tool;
  • updates change documents, or copies of them, one named node at a time.

Next, a different way to think about turning documents into other documents: XSLT.

Transforming with XSLT

XQuery describes a result by computing it: for each requirement, make this element. XSLT describes it by rules: when you meet a requirement, make this element. A stylesheet is a set of template rules, each with a pattern that says which nodes it applies to. The processor walks the input, finds the best rule for each node, and the rules decide whether and how to go on to the children.

That way of working fits documents well, and the Vane draft is a document: paragraphs hold text, cross references, key words and notes in any order, and sections nest as deep as the authors like. Rules say what to do with each part without knowing the whole structure in advance. It is also what makes XSLT easy to extend: a new stylesheet can import an old one and override only the rules it wants to change.

A stylesheet is itself an XML document, with its instructions in the XSLT namespace, http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform, usually with the prefix xsl. This chapter turns the draft, vane.xml in docs/book/examples/spec, into the things a specification needs: a copy for publication, an HTML page, a plain-text version in the style of an RFC, and indexes. Run the commands in that directory.

The built-in rules

The smallest stylesheet has no rules at all:

empty.xsl:

<xsl:stylesheet version="4.0" xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform">
</xsl:stylesheet>

Even so, it does something:

$ sxml transform empty.xsl vane.xml | grep -v '^ *$' | head -12
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
    The Vane Protocol for Feature Flag Rollouts
      Example Software
      ada@example.com
      Example Software
      alan@example.com
    Applications
    feature flag
    progressive delivery
      This document specifies Vane, the protocol between the SDKs that
      evaluate feature flags in applications and the Vane service that
      holds the flags. It defines the states of a flag, the messages of the

When no rule matches a node, a built-in rule applies. For elements and the document node, it processes the children. For text, it copies the text. So an empty stylesheet writes all the text of a document, without the tags: the title, the authors' organizations and email addresses, the keywords, the abstract and then the rest of the draft. (grep leaves out the lines that hold only the spaces between elements; they are text too, and the empty stylesheet copies them.) The attributes are gone, docName and every anchor, because the built-in rules don't process attributes, and so is the comment at the top of the file: the built-in rule for comments and processing instructions makes nothing.

Copying with changes

The built-in behaviour can be changed for a whole mode, the set of rules that are used together. With on-no-match="shallow-copy", a node that no rule matches is copied, and its children are processed. Now the stylesheet copies the document as it is, and you only write rules for what should change. This is the most useful pattern in XSLT.

Before an Internet-Draft is published, the editorial notes (cref) come out, and an IANA section that only says there is nothing to do is removed:

publication.xsl:

<xsl:stylesheet version="4.0"
    xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform">
  <!-- Copy every node that no template matches. -->
  <xsl:mode on-no-match="shallow-copy"/>

  <!-- Editorial notes and the comment at the top are for the authors. -->
  <xsl:template match="cref | /comment()"/>

  <!-- An IANA section without actions is removed before publication. -->
  <xsl:template match="section[@anchor = 'iana']
                              [normalize-space(t) = 'This document has no IANA actions.']"/>
</xsl:stylesheet>

$ sxml transform publication.xsl vane.xml | head -4
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?><rfc version="3" category="std" ipr="trust200902" submissionType="IETF" docName="draft-example-vane-protocol-01">
  <front>
    <title abbrev="Vane">The Vane Protocol for Feature Flag Rollouts</title>
    <seriesInfo name="Internet-Draft" value="draft-example-vane-protocol-01"/>

The rules with an empty body make nothing, so the notes, the comment and the IANA section are gone; everything else is copied with its attributes. A pattern is not limited to a name: /comment() is a comment whose parent is the document node, and the predicates on section say which section. Save the result and compare:

$ sxml transform --output=public.xml publication.xsl vane.xml
$ sxml xpath --context-item=vane.xml 'count(//cref), count(//section)'
2
9
$ sxml xpath --context-item=public.xml 'count(//cref), count(//section)'
0
8
$ sxml xpath --context-item=public.xml '//t[@anchor = "req-8"]'
<t anchor="req-8">A pause <bcp14>SHOULD</bcp14> last five minutes.
      </t>

The space before the note is still there: it is a text node of its own, and only the note's element was left out. A rule's body could just as well write a new element in the old one's place, as the next sections do for every element of the draft.

The rest of this chapter goes through the parts of XSLT you'll use the most:

  • Templates and Modes: rules, patterns, priorities, parameters and modes, for an HTML page and a plain-text draft;
  • Keys, Numbers and Grouping: looking up the targets of cross references, numbering sections and requirements, an index of terms and the references;
  • Many Outputs, Functions and Packages: a page for each section, and the stylesheets organized as modules and a package;
  • Project: Publishing the Specification: one script that checks the draft and writes HTML, text, JSON and a page of changes.

XSLT also draws: Drawing with XSLT writes SVG with template rules, and Transforming SVG changes drawings it did not make. Printing the Tree with XSLT prints a tree of TypeScript code as text with one rule for each kind of element, and A Pipeline, a Second Target and a Changing Schema writes an OpenAPI document from an XSD schema with template rules.

Templates and Modes

Template rules

A template rule has a match pattern and a body. The body is a sequence constructor: literal result elements (any element that is not in the XSLT namespace, such as <p>), text, and instructions. This stylesheet makes an HTML page of the draft, with one rule for each kind of element:

draft.xsl:

<xsl:stylesheet version="4.0" expand-text="yes"
    xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform"
    xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"
    exclude-result-prefixes="xs">
  <xsl:output method="html" indent="yes"/>

  <!-- "show" writes the editorial notes into the page. -->
  <xsl:param name="notes" select="'hide'"/>

  <xsl:template match="/">
    <html>
      <head>
        <title>{rfc/front/title}</title>
      </head>
      <body>
        <h1>{rfc/front/title}</h1>
        <!-- The same sections, processed twice in two modes. -->
        <xsl:apply-templates select="." mode="toc"/>
        <xsl:apply-templates select="rfc/middle/section"/>
      </body>
    </html>
  </xsl:template>

  <!-- The page: one rule for each kind of element. -->
  <xsl:template match="section">
    <section id="{@anchor}">
      <h2>{name}</h2>
      <xsl:apply-templates select="* except name"/>
    </section>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="t">
    <p><xsl:apply-templates/></p>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="t[@anchor]" priority="1">
    <p id="{@anchor}" class="requirement"><xsl:apply-templates/></p>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="xref">
    <a href="#{@target}">{if (node()) then . else @target}</a>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="bcp14">
    <span>
      <xsl:attribute name="class">
        <xsl:call-template name="strength">
          <xsl:with-param name="keyword" select="normalize-space()"/>
        </xsl:call-template>
      </xsl:attribute>
      <xsl:value-of select="."/>
    </span>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="cref">
    <xsl:if test="$notes = 'show'">
      <span class="note">[{@source}: {normalize-space()}]</span>
    </xsl:if>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="dl | dd">
    <xsl:copy><xsl:apply-templates/></xsl:copy>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="dt">
    <dt id="{@anchor}"><xsl:apply-templates/></dt>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="sourcecode">
    <pre>{.}</pre>
  </xsl:template>

  <!-- A named template, called with a typed parameter. -->
  <xsl:template name="strength">
    <xsl:param name="keyword" as="xs:string"/>
    <xsl:choose>
      <xsl:when test="$keyword = ('MUST', 'MUST NOT', 'REQUIRED', 'SHALL', 'SHALL NOT')">bcp14 absolute</xsl:when>
      <xsl:when test="starts-with($keyword, 'SHOULD') or contains($keyword, 'RECOMMENDED')">bcp14 recommended</xsl:when>
      <xsl:otherwise>bcp14 optional</xsl:otherwise>
    </xsl:choose>
  </xsl:template>

  <!-- The table of contents: the mode "toc". -->
  <xsl:template match="/" mode="toc">
    <ol class="toc">
      <xsl:apply-templates select="rfc/middle/section" mode="toc"/>
    </ol>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="section" mode="toc">
    <li>
      <a href="#{@anchor}">{name}</a>
      <xsl:if test="section">
        <ol>
          <xsl:apply-templates select="section" mode="toc"/>
        </ol>
      </xsl:if>
    </li>
  </xsl:template>

(The file goes on with the rules of a second mode, shown later in this chapter.) Run it, and look at the first part of the page:

$ sxml transform draft.xsl vane.xml | head -31
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>The Vane Protocol for Feature Flag Rollouts</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>The Vane Protocol for Feature Flag Rollouts</h1>
    <ol class="toc">
      <li><a href="#intro">Introduction</a><ol><li><a href="#terminology">Terminology</a></li></ol></li>
      <li><a href="#states">Flag States</a></li>
      <li><a href="#messages">Messages</a><ol><li><a href="#rollout">Rollout</a></li><li><a href="#status">Status</a></li></ol></li>
      <li><a href="#pause">Pause</a></li>
      <li><a href="#security">Security Considerations</a></li>
      <li><a href="#iana">IANA Considerations</a></li>
    </ol>
    <section id="intro">
      <h2>Introduction</h2>
      <p>An application has many features, and each feature has a flag. An
      <a href="#term-sdk">SDK</a> in the application keeps the flags
      in a cache and evaluates them for each user. It holds an update stream
      open to the Vane service, which sends a message on it whenever a flag
      changes, and it asks the service for the status of a flag.</p>
      <section id="terminology">
        <h2>Terminology</h2>
        <p>The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL
        NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED",
        "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as
        described in BCP 14 <a href="#RFC2119">RFC2119</a> <a href="#RFC8174">RFC8174</a>
        when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.</p>
        <dl>

Let's read it rule by rule:

  • match="/" matches the document node, where every transformation starts. It writes the page, and xsl:apply-templates processes the draft's sections where the page's body goes.
  • match="section" writes a section with a heading, and processes the section's children except its name. A nested section matches the same rule, so sections nest in the page as deep as in the draft.
  • match="t" writes a paragraph, and match="xref" a link. An xref with no content shows its target's anchor for now; Keys, Numbers and Grouping makes "Section 4" of it.
  • match="dl | dd" uses xsl:copy, which copies the element without its attributes or children: the content comes from the rules again. A pattern with | matches either kind of node.
  • The text in between is copied by the built-in rule, so the words of a paragraph pass through with the elements inside them turned into HTML.

xsl:apply-templates is the engine of XSLT. It selects nodes (with select, or the children by default), and for each one it finds the best matching rule. The xsl:output element says how to write the result: here as HTML, indented. The html method writes the <!DOCTYPE html> and the meta element for the encoding itself.

Text value templates

With expand-text="yes" on the stylesheet, curly braces in text work as they do in XQuery: {name} is replaced by the value of the expression name, the section's title. In attributes of literal result elements, curly braces always work; they are attribute value templates: id="{@anchor}" gives the HTML element the draft's anchor, so the links work. Without expand-text, you write <xsl:value-of select="name"/> instead, as older stylesheets do and as the bcp14 rule does once.

Priorities

Two rules match a requirement: t and t[@anchor]. When several rules match, the one with the highest priority wins. A rule can state its priority, as the second one does. Otherwise, the priority comes from the pattern: a pattern with a predicate or several steps is more specific than a plain name, and gets a higher default priority (0.5 against 0). So the priority="1" above isn't even needed; it just makes the intent clear. The requirements get an id and a class:

$ sxml transform draft.xsl vane.xml | grep -A2 'id="req-1"'
      <p id="req-1" class="requirement">A <a href="#term-flag">flag</a>
      <span class="bcp14 absolute">MUST</span> be in exactly one of the states "stable",
      "rolling-out" and "paused".</p>

Patterns are not expressions that are evaluated from the top: a pattern tests a node. t matches any t element anywhere, section/t a paragraph whose parent is a section (not one in the abstract), and section[1] a section that is the first section child of its parent.

Named templates and parameters

The bcp14 rule shows several more things:

  • A template with a name instead of a match is a named template. xsl:call-template calls it, and xsl:with-param passes its parameters, which can have types: strength takes an xs:string.
  • xsl:attribute makes an attribute from a sequence constructor, here the text the named template writes.
  • xsl:choose picks the first xsl:when whose test is true, or xsl:otherwise. There is also xsl:if for a single test, as in the cref rule.
  • A stylesheet declares every prefix it uses, xs too: here xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema" on xsl:stylesheet makes xs:string a type, and exclude-result-prefixes="xs" keeps the declaration out of the result. Unlike XPath and XQuery, XSLT predeclares no prefix but xml; an undeclared one is an error (XPST0081 in an expression or a type such as as, XTSE0280 in a name such as mode).

xsl:param at the top level declares a stylesheet parameter, with a default. notes decides whether the editorial notes show, and --param sets it from the command line:

$ sxml transform --param=notes=show draft.xsl vane.xml | grep 'class="note"'
      <span class="note">[AM: Should an owner be able to change the duration?]</span></p>
      <span class="note">[AB: This needs a requirement anchor of its own.]</span></p>

Modes

The page processes the same sections twice: once for the table of contents and once for the content. A mode is a named set of rules. xsl:apply-templates mode="toc" uses only the rules of the toc mode, so a section there makes a list item with a link, not a section element. Each mode has its own built-in rules, too, which is why the toc mode has a rule for the document node: without it, the built-in rule would copy all the text of the draft into the table of contents.

A mode can do more than a part of the page. The rest of draft.xsl is a second rendering of the whole draft, as plain text in the style of an RFC: section numbers, paragraphs indented by three spaces and wrapped at 72 columns, and a reference written as [RFC2119]:

  <!-- Plain text in the style of an RFC: the mode "text". -->
  <xsl:template match="/" mode="text">
    <xsl:apply-templates select="rfc/front/title, rfc/middle/section" mode="text"/>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="title" mode="text">
    <xsl:text>{.}&#10;&#10;</xsl:text>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="section" mode="text">
    <xsl:variable name="number" select="
        string-join(ancestor-or-self::section ! (count(preceding-sibling::section) + 1), '.')"/>
    <xsl:text>{$number}.  {name}&#10;&#10;</xsl:text>
    <xsl:apply-templates select="* except name" mode="text"/>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="t | dd" mode="text">
    <xsl:variable name="text">
      <xsl:apply-templates mode="text"/>
    </xsl:variable>
    <xsl:variable name="indent" select="if (self::dd) then '      ' else '   '"/>
    <!-- Lines of at most 72 characters, indented. -->
    <xsl:value-of select="replace(normalize-space($text),
                                  '(.{1,' || 72 - string-length($indent) || '})( |$)',
                                  $indent || '$1&#10;')"/>
    <xsl:text>&#10;</xsl:text>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="dl" mode="text">
    <xsl:apply-templates select="*" mode="text"/>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="dt" mode="text">
    <xsl:text>   {.}&#10;</xsl:text>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="sourcecode" mode="text">
    <xsl:value-of select="tokenize(., '&#10;')[normalize-space()] ! ('     ' || . || '&#10;')"
                  separator=""/>
    <xsl:text>&#10;</xsl:text>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="xref[empty(node())]" mode="text">[{@target}]</xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="cref" mode="text"/>

The t rule applies the rules of the mode to the paragraph's children inside an xsl:variable, so the variable holds the paragraph's text with every xref and bcp14 already turned into text. normalize-space joins its lines, and one replace breaks it again into lines of at most 69 characters plus the indent: (.{1,69})( |$) takes as many characters as fit before a space or the end. The section number is the position of each enclosing section among its siblings, joined with dots.

xsl:value-of with separator="" joins the lines of the ABNF without a space between them, and xsl:text writes text exactly, which keeps the whitespace of the stylesheet out of the result: &#10; is a line feed.

Starting somewhere else

A transformation normally starts by applying templates to the document node in the default mode. --initial-mode starts in another mode. The toc mode alone is a table of contents:

$ sxml transform --initial-mode=toc draft.xsl vane.xml
<ol class="toc">
  <li><a href="#intro">Introduction</a><ol><li><a href="#terminology">Terminology</a></li></ol></li>
  <li><a href="#states">Flag States</a></li>
  <li><a href="#messages">Messages</a><ol><li><a href="#rollout">Rollout</a></li><li><a href="#status">Status</a></li></ol></li>
  <li><a href="#pause">Pause</a></li>
  <li><a href="#security">Security Considerations</a></li>
  <li><a href="#iana">IANA Considerations</a></li>
</ol>

And the text mode is the plain-text draft. Its result is text, not HTML, so --method=text replaces the stylesheet's output method:

$ sxml transform --initial-mode=text --method=text draft.xsl vane.xml | head -30
The Vane Protocol for Feature Flag Rollouts

1.  Introduction

   An application has many features, and each feature has a flag. An SDK
   in the application keeps the flags in a cache and evaluates them for
   each user. It holds an update stream open to the Vane service, which
   sends a message on it whenever a flag changes, and it asks the
   service for the status of a flag.

1.1.  Terminology

   The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT",
   "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and
   "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP
   14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they appear in all
   capitals, as shown here.

   Flag
      A named switch in an application that turns a feature on for a
      share of its users.

   SDK
      The library in an application that evaluates flags from its cache
      and keeps the cache current with Vane messages.

   Percentage
      A whole number from 0 to 100 that an owner gives to roll a flag
      out to that share of users. An SDK puts a user in the share by a
      hash of the flag and the user, so the user stays in it while the
$ sxml transform --initial-mode=text --method=text draft.xsl vane.xml | grep 'in a pause ('
   A service MUST NOT roll out a flag while it is in a pause ([pause]).

The reference to Section 4 still shows as [pause]: an xref without text needs a lookup of its target, the subject of the next section.

--initial-template calls a named template instead of applying templates. A stylesheet that needs no input names its starting template xsl:initial-template, and runs without a document:

bcp14.xsl:

<xsl:stylesheet version="4.0" expand-text="yes"
    xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform">
  <xsl:output method="text"/>

  <!-- The key words of BCP 14, from strongest to weakest. -->
  <xsl:variable name="keywords" select="'MUST', 'MUST NOT', 'REQUIRED', 'SHALL',
      'SHALL NOT', 'SHOULD', 'SHOULD NOT', 'RECOMMENDED', 'NOT RECOMMENDED',
      'MAY', 'OPTIONAL'"/>

  <xsl:template name="xsl:initial-template">
    <xsl:text>BCP 14 has {count($keywords)} key words: {string-join($keywords, ', ')}.&#10;</xsl:text>
  </xsl:template>
</xsl:stylesheet>

$ sxml transform bcp14.xsl
BCP 14 has 11 key words: MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, NOT RECOMMENDED, MAY, OPTIONAL.

Keys, Numbers and Grouping

Keys

An xref without text, such as <xref target="pause"/>, asks the renderer for the text: "Section 4" when it points to a section, "[RFC5234]" when it points to a reference. To write it, a stylesheet must find the element whose anchor is the target. A key is an index that the processor builds for that. You declare what to index and by which value, and the key function looks nodes up:

xrefs.xsl:

<xsl:stylesheet version="4.0" expand-text="yes"
    xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform">
  <xsl:output method="text"/>

  <!-- Every element with an anchor, found by its anchor. -->
  <xsl:key name="anchor" match="*[@anchor]" use="@anchor"/>

  <xsl:template match="/">
    <xsl:apply-templates select="//xref"/>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="xref">
    <xsl:text>{@target} -> </xsl:text>
    <xsl:apply-templates select="key('anchor', @target)" mode="xref-text"/>
    <xsl:text>&#10;</xsl:text>
  </xsl:template>

  <!-- The text of an xref depends on what it points to. -->
  <xsl:template match="section" mode="xref-text">
    <xsl:text>Section </xsl:text>
    <xsl:number level="multiple" count="section" format="1.1"/>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="reference" mode="xref-text">[{@anchor}]</xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="dt" mode="xref-text">the term "{.}"</xsl:template>
</xsl:stylesheet>

$ sxml transform xrefs.xsl vane.xml
term-sdk -> the term "SDK"
RFC2119 -> [RFC2119]
RFC8174 -> [RFC8174]
term-flag -> the term "Flag"
term-flag -> the term "Flag"
RFC5234 -> [RFC5234]
term-percentage -> the term "Percentage"
term-pause -> the term "Pause"
pause -> Section 4
RFC6238 -> [RFC6238]
term-pause -> the term "Pause"

key('anchor', @target) finds the elements whose @anchor equals the xref's target, in the document of the context node; a third argument names another document. A predicate such as //*[@anchor = current()/@target] would give the same result, but the key is built once and each lookup is fast, however large the draft is. The rules of the mode xref-text then decide the text by the kind of element the key found: one rule for a section, one for a reference, one for a term.

Numbers

The draft has no section numbers in it, and it should not: when the authors insert a section, every number after it changes, and every "Section 4" in the text with it. The renderer numbers by position, and xsl:number is the instruction that does it:

numbers.xsl:

<xsl:stylesheet version="4.0" expand-text="yes"
    xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform">
  <xsl:output method="text"/>

  <xsl:template match="/">
    <xsl:apply-templates select="//middle//(section | t[@anchor])"/>
  </xsl:template>

  <!-- 1, 1.1, 2, ...: the position among the sections at each level. -->
  <xsl:template match="section">
    <xsl:number level="multiple" count="section" format="1.1"/>
    <xsl:text>  {name}&#10;</xsl:text>
  </xsl:template>

  <!-- R1, R2, ...: the position among all requirements of the draft. -->
  <xsl:template match="t">
    <xsl:text>    R</xsl:text>
    <xsl:number level="any" count="t[@anchor]" format="1"/>
    <xsl:text> {@anchor}: {bcp14}&#10;</xsl:text>
  </xsl:template>
</xsl:stylesheet>

$ sxml transform numbers.xsl vane.xml
1  Introduction
1.1  Terminology
2  Flag States
    R1 req-1: MUST
    R2 req-2: MUST
    R3 req-3: SHOULD
3  Messages
3.1  Rollout
    R4 req-4: MUST
    R5 req-5: MUST NOT
    R6 req-9: MAY
3.2  Status
    R7 req-6: MUST
    R8 req-10: SHOULD NOT
4  Pause
    R9 req-7: MUST
    R10 req-8: SHOULD
    R11 req-11: MAY
5  Security Considerations
6  IANA Considerations

level="multiple" counts the node and each of its ancestors that match count among their siblings, and format="1.1" writes the numbers with dots between them. level="any" counts every matching node before it in the document, at any depth: that numbers the requirements from R1 to R11 in reading order, while their anchors keep the order in which they were written (req-9 was added in the second draft and is the sixth requirement). Other formats give a, A, i, I or 01, as in format="a)" or format="i.". A format token that xsl:number does not know falls back to decimal digits, so R1 as a format would write 1; the R is written as text before the number.

Grouping

xsl:for-each-group puts the selected items into groups and processes each group once. Inside it, current-grouping-key() is the key of the group, and current-group() its items.

group-by groups by a computed value. An index of the draft's terms is grouped by first letter, and lists the sections that use each term, found with a second key:

term-index.xsl:

<xsl:stylesheet version="4.0" expand-text="yes"
    xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform">
  <xsl:output method="text"/>

  <!-- The xrefs, found by the anchor they point to. -->
  <xsl:key name="uses" match="xref" use="@target"/>

  <xsl:template match="/">
    <xsl:for-each-group select="//dt" group-by="substring(., 1, 1)">
      <xsl:sort select="current-grouping-key()"/>
      <xsl:text>{current-grouping-key()}&#10;</xsl:text>
      <xsl:for-each select="current-group()">
        <xsl:sort select="."/>
        <xsl:text>  {.}: </xsl:text>
        <!-- The sections that use the term, each once. -->
        <xsl:for-each select="key('uses', @anchor)/ancestor::section[1]">
          <xsl:if test="position() > 1">, </xsl:if>
          <xsl:number level="multiple" count="section" format="1.1"/>
        </xsl:for-each>
        <xsl:text>&#10;</xsl:text>
      </xsl:for-each>
    </xsl:for-each-group>
  </xsl:template>
</xsl:stylesheet>

$ sxml transform term-index.xsl vane.xml
F
  Flag: 1.1, 2
P
  Pause: 3.1, 4
  Percentage: 3.1
S
  SDK: 1

key('uses', @anchor) gives every xref to the term, and /ancestor::section[1] the section around each one. A path removes duplicates and returns nodes in document order, so a section that uses a term twice would still be listed once, and the sections come in the order of the draft.

The references are grouped by the references element they are in, normative or informative:

references.xsl:

<xsl:stylesheet version="4.0" expand-text="yes"
    xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform">
  <xsl:output method="text"/>

  <xsl:template match="/">
    <xsl:for-each-group select="//reference" group-by="../name">
      <xsl:text>{current-grouping-key()}&#10;</xsl:text>
      <xsl:for-each select="current-group()">
        <!-- The newest first; references of the same year by anchor. -->
        <xsl:sort select="front/date/@year" data-type="number" order="descending"/>
        <xsl:sort select="@anchor"/>
        <xsl:text>  [{@anchor}] {front/date/@year} {front/title}&#10;</xsl:text>
      </xsl:for-each>
    </xsl:for-each-group>
  </xsl:template>
</xsl:stylesheet>

$ sxml transform references.xsl vane.xml
Normative References
  [RFC8174] 2017 Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words
  [RFC5234] 2008 Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF
  [RFC2119] 1997 Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels
Informative References
  [RFC6238] 2011 TOTP: Time-Based One-Time Password Algorithm

Grouping by position

Grouping is not only for values. Documents often have structure that is only implied by the order of elements. The terms of the draft are a dl, a flat list in which each dt is followed by its dd. group-starting-with starts a new group at each item that matches a pattern, which turns the flat list into entries:

glossary.xsl:

<xsl:stylesheet version="4.0" expand-text="yes"
    xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform">
  <xsl:output indent="yes"/>

  <!-- A dl is a flat list: dt, dd, dt, dd. Each dt starts an entry. -->
  <xsl:template match="/">
    <glossary>
      <xsl:for-each-group select="//dl/*" group-starting-with="dt">
        <entry term="{current-group()[1]}">
          <xsl:value-of select="normalize-space(current-group()[2])"/>
        </entry>
      </xsl:for-each-group>
    </glossary>
  </xsl:template>
</xsl:stylesheet>

$ sxml transform glossary.xsl vane.xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<glossary>
  <entry term="Flag">A named switch in an application that turns a feature on for a share of its users.</entry>
  <entry term="SDK">The library in an application that evaluates flags from its cache and keeps the cache current with Vane messages.</entry>
  <entry term="Percentage">A whole number from 0 to 100 that an owner gives to roll a flag out to that share of users. An SDK puts a user in the share by a hash of the flag and the user, so the user stays in it while the percentage grows.</entry>
  <entry term="Pause">A state in which a flag refuses every rollout for a time.</entry>
</glossary>

There are two more ways to form groups. group-adjacent puts neighbouring items with the same key together, such as runs of paragraphs of the same kind, and group-ending-with ends a group at each item that matches a pattern.

Sorting

xsl:sort sorts the items of xsl:apply-templates, xsl:for-each and xsl:for-each-group. In term-index.xsl it sorts the groups by their key and the terms in each group by name. In references.xsl, two sorts make two sort keys: the year, newest first, as a number (data-type="number", order="descending"), and the anchor for references of the same year.

Strings sort by their Unicode code points unless a sort names a collation, with collation or lang: lang="de" sorts by the rules of German. Working with Text sorts the authors of the references, M'Raihi among them, and the anchors req-1 to req-11 in the order people expect.

Many Outputs, Functions and Packages

Writing many files

A transformation has one principal result, the one that goes to standard output, and can make any number of result documents with xsl:result-document. This stylesheet makes a page for each top-level section of the draft and an index that links to them:

pages.xsl:

<xsl:stylesheet version="4.0" expand-text="yes"
    xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform">
  <xsl:output method="html" indent="yes"/>

  <xsl:template match="/">
    <ul>
      <xsl:for-each select="rfc/middle/section">
        <xsl:variable name="page" select="'sections/' || @anchor || '.html'"/>
        <!-- One page for each top-level section... -->
        <xsl:result-document href="{$page}">
          <h1>{name}</h1>
          <p>{count(.//t[@anchor])} requirements, {count(section)} subsections</p>
        </xsl:result-document>
        <!-- ...and a link to it in the index. -->
        <li><a href="{$page}">{name}</a></li>
      </xsl:for-each>
    </ul>
  </xsl:template>
</xsl:stylesheet>

sxml writes files only where you allow it. Without --result-directory, it writes the principal result and tells you about each result document it did not write:

$ sxml transform pages.xsl vane.xml
sxml transform: result document 'sections/intro.html' not written; give --result-directory
sxml transform: result document 'sections/states.html' not written; give --result-directory
sxml transform: result document 'sections/messages.html' not written; give --result-directory
sxml transform: result document 'sections/pause.html' not written; give --result-directory
sxml transform: result document 'sections/security.html' not written; give --result-directory
sxml transform: result document 'sections/iana.html' not written; give --result-directory
<ul>
  <li><a href="sections/intro.html">Introduction</a></li>
  <li><a href="sections/states.html">Flag States</a></li>
  <li><a href="sections/messages.html">Messages</a></li>
  <li><a href="sections/pause.html">Pause</a></li>
  <li><a href="sections/security.html">Security Considerations</a></li>
  <li><a href="sections/iana.html">IANA Considerations</a></li>
</ul>

With --result-directory, the result documents are written below that directory, and --output puts the principal result into a file too:

$ mkdir site
$ sxml transform --result-directory=site --output=site/index.html pages.xsl vane.xml
$ find site -type f | sort
site/index.html
site/sections/iana.html
site/sections/intro.html
site/sections/messages.html
site/sections/pause.html
site/sections/security.html
site/sections/states.html
$ cat site/sections/messages.html
<h1>Messages</h1>
<p>5 requirements, 2 subsections</p>

All the files are written only when the whole transformation succeeds, and a result document that would land outside the directory is an error. Run the same command again, and sxml refuses to replace the files without --force:

$ sxml transform --result-directory=site --output=site/index.html pages.xsl vane.xml; echo $?
sxml transform: 'site/index.html' exists; give --force to replace it
3

Functions and packages

The HTML page and the plain text of Templates and Modes need the same things: the number of a section or a requirement, and the text of an xref. Written once, they belong in functions that every stylesheet of the draft can call.

xsl:function declares a function that XPath expressions in the stylesheet can call, with typed parameters and result. Its name must have a namespace prefix of your own; here spec, for urn:example:spec.

A package is a stylesheet module with a name and a version, whose components (functions, templates, variables, keys, modes) are private unless it says otherwise. Other stylesheets use a package and see only what it makes public. Packages let a team share a library of functions without the risk of names clashing or of rules leaking into each other. This one holds the draft's functions:

spec.xsl:

<xsl:package name="spec.xsl" package-version="1.0" version="4.0" expand-text="yes"
    xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform"
    xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"
    xmlns:spec="urn:example:spec">

  <!-- Private: every element with an anchor, found by its anchor. -->
  <xsl:key name="anchor" match="*[@anchor]" use="@anchor"/>

  <!-- Private: the strength of each BCP 14 key word. -->
  <xsl:variable name="spec:strengths" as="map(xs:string, xs:string)" select="{
      'MUST': 'absolute', 'MUST NOT': 'absolute', 'REQUIRED': 'absolute',
      'SHALL': 'absolute', 'SHALL NOT': 'absolute',
      'SHOULD': 'recommended', 'SHOULD NOT': 'recommended',
      'RECOMMENDED': 'recommended', 'NOT RECOMMENDED': 'recommended',
      'MAY': 'optional', 'OPTIONAL': 'optional' }"/>

  <xsl:function name="spec:strength" as="xs:string" visibility="public">
    <xsl:param name="keyword" as="element(bcp14)"/>
    <xsl:sequence select="$spec:strengths(normalize-space($keyword))"/>
  </xsl:function>

  <!-- "3.1" for a section, "R6" for a requirement: numbers by position. -->
  <xsl:function name="spec:number" as="xs:string" visibility="public">
    <xsl:param name="node" as="element()"/>
    <!-- One text node, whose string is the result. -->
    <xsl:value-of>
      <xsl:choose>
        <xsl:when test="$node/self::section">
          <xsl:number select="$node" level="multiple" count="section" format="1.1"/>
        </xsl:when>
        <xsl:otherwise>
          <xsl:text>R</xsl:text>
          <xsl:number select="$node" level="any" count="t[@anchor]"/>
        </xsl:otherwise>
      </xsl:choose>
    </xsl:value-of>
  </xsl:function>

  <!-- The text of an xref: its own, or one made from what it points to. -->
  <xsl:function name="spec:xref-text" as="xs:string" visibility="public">
    <xsl:param name="xref" as="element(xref)"/>
    <xsl:variable name="target" select="key('anchor', $xref/@target, root($xref))"/>
    <xsl:sequence select="
        if ($xref/node()) then string($xref)
        else if ($target/self::section) then 'Section ' || spec:number($target)
        else if ($target/self::t) then 'Requirement ' || spec:number($target)
        else '[' || $xref/@target || ']'"/>
  </xsl:function>
</xsl:package>

The three functions are public. The key anchor and the variable spec:strengths are private: only the package's own functions can see them. spec:number puts its xsl:choose inside xsl:value-of, which makes one text node of what xsl:text and xsl:number write, and the function's as="xs:string" turns that node into its string. Without the xsl:value-of, a requirement's number would be two text nodes, "R" and "6", and two strings are not the one string the function promises (XTTE0780).

A stylesheet uses the package with xsl:use-package. It can call the public functions, and nothing else:

private.xsl:

<xsl:stylesheet version="4.0" expand-text="yes"
    xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform"
    xmlns:spec="urn:example:spec">
  <xsl:use-package name="spec.xsl" package-version="1.0"/>
  <xsl:output method="text"/>

  <xsl:template match="/">{$spec:strengths?MUST}</xsl:template>
</xsl:stylesheet>

$ sxml transform private.xsl vane.xml
private.xsl:7:29: err:XPST0008: the variable is not declared

The sxml command finds a package by reading its name as a file name, relative to the stylesheet. A program that embeds sxml can find packages any way it likes: by name and version, in a database, or built in (Embedding sxml in C).

Importing stylesheets

Some template rules are shared too: an xref becomes the text that spec:xref-text makes, and a cref becomes nothing, in every output. They go in a module of their own, with a function that gives the text of a paragraph as a reader sees it:

common.xsl:

<xsl:stylesheet version="4.0" expand-text="yes"
    xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform"
    xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"
    xmlns:spec="urn:example:spec"
    exclude-result-prefixes="xs spec">
  <!-- What the HTML, the text and the JSON output share. Each stylesheet
       that imports this module uses the package spec.xsl. -->

  <xsl:template match="xref">{spec:xref-text(.)}</xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="cref"/>

  <!-- The text of a paragraph as a reader sees it. -->
  <xsl:function name="spec:text" as="xs:string">
    <xsl:param name="paragraph" as="element()"/>
    <xsl:variable name="text">
      <xsl:apply-templates select="$paragraph/node()"/>
    </xsl:variable>
    <xsl:sequence select="normalize-space($text)"/>
  </xsl:function>
</xsl:stylesheet>

xsl:import brings in the rules of another stylesheet, with a lower import precedence: a rule in the importing stylesheet beats any rule it imports, whatever their priorities. That is how you extend a stylesheet without changing it. The HTML stylesheet imports common.xsl, uses the package, and replaces the xref rule with one that puts a link around the imported rule's text, which xsl:apply-imports calls:

html.xsl:

<xsl:stylesheet version="4.0" expand-text="yes"
    xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform"
    xmlns:spec="urn:example:spec"
    exclude-result-prefixes="spec">
  <!-- The shared rules, with a lower import precedence than these. -->
  <xsl:import href="common.xsl"/>
  <xsl:use-package name="spec.xsl" package-version="1.0"/>
  <xsl:output method="html" indent="yes"/>

  <xsl:template match="/">
    <html>
      <head>
        <title>{rfc/front/title}</title>
      </head>
      <body>
        <h1>{rfc/front/title}</h1>
        <p class="draft">{rfc/@docName}</p>
        <nav>
          <ol class="toc">
            <xsl:apply-templates select="rfc/middle/section" mode="toc"/>
          </ol>
        </nav>
        <xsl:apply-templates select="rfc/middle/section, rfc/back/references"/>
        <section id="requirements">
          <h2>Index of Requirements</h2>
          <table>
            <xsl:apply-templates select="//t[@anchor]" mode="index"/>
          </table>
        </section>
      </body>
    </html>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="section">
    <section id="{@anchor}">
      <h2>{spec:number(.)}. {name}</h2>
      <xsl:apply-templates select="* except name"/>
    </section>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="t">
    <p><xsl:apply-templates/></p>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="t[@anchor]">
    <p id="{@anchor}" class="requirement">
      <span class="number">{spec:number(.)}</span>
      <xsl:text> </xsl:text>
      <xsl:apply-templates/>
    </p>
  </xsl:template>

  <!-- A link around the text that common.xsl makes. -->
  <xsl:template match="xref">
    <a href="#{@target}"><xsl:apply-imports/></a>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="bcp14">
    <span class="bcp14 {spec:strength(.)}">{.}</span>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="dl | dd">
    <xsl:copy><xsl:apply-templates/></xsl:copy>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="dt">
    <dt id="{@anchor}"><xsl:apply-templates/></dt>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="sourcecode">
    <pre>{.}</pre>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="references">
    <section id="{@anchor}">
      <h2>{name}</h2>
      <xsl:apply-templates select="references"/>
      <xsl:if test="reference">
        <dl>
          <xsl:apply-templates select="reference"/>
        </dl>
      </xsl:if>
    </section>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="reference">
    <dt id="{@anchor}">[{@anchor}]</dt>
    <dd>{string-join(front/author/@fullname, ', ')}, "{front/title}",
      {front/date/@month} {front/date/@year}.</dd>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="section" mode="toc">
    <li>
      <a href="#{@anchor}">{spec:number(.)}. {name}</a>
      <xsl:if test="section">
        <ol>
          <xsl:apply-templates select="section" mode="toc"/>
        </ol>
      </xsl:if>
    </li>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="t" mode="index">
    <tr>
      <td><a href="#{@anchor}">{spec:number(.)}</a></td>
      <td>{bcp14}</td>
      <td>{ancestor::section[1] ! (spec:number(.) || '. ' || name)}</td>
    </tr>
  </xsl:template>
</xsl:stylesheet>

$ sxml transform html.xsl vane.xml | grep -B1 -A1 'Section 4'

        (<a href="#pause">Section 4</a>).</p>

An xsl:use-package must be in the principal stylesheet module, not in a module it imports (XTSE3008), so each stylesheet that imports common.xsl uses the package itself. xsl:include is the other way to combine modules: the included rules count as if they were written in the including stylesheet, with the same precedence.

The plain-text stylesheet imports the same module and keeps its xref rule. Its rules are those of the text mode of draft.xsl, now in the default mode of a stylesheet of their own, with an RFC's first line and the references at the end:

text.xsl:

<xsl:stylesheet version="4.0" expand-text="yes"
    xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform"
    xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"
    xmlns:spec="urn:example:spec"
    exclude-result-prefixes="xs spec">
  <xsl:import href="common.xsl"/>
  <xsl:use-package name="spec.xsl" package-version="1.0"/>
  <xsl:output method="text"/>

  <xsl:template match="/">
    <!-- The first line: the series on the left, the date on the right. -->
    <xsl:variable name="date" select="rfc/front/date ! (@month || ' ' || @year)"/>
    <xsl:text>Internet-Draft{spec:spaces(72 - 14 - string-length($date))}{$date}&#10;</xsl:text>
    <xsl:apply-templates select="rfc/front/title, rfc/middle/section, rfc/back/references"/>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="title">
    <xsl:text>&#10;{.}&#10;&#10;</xsl:text>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="section">
    <xsl:text>{spec:number(.)}.  {name}&#10;&#10;</xsl:text>
    <xsl:apply-templates select="* except name"/>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="references">
    <xsl:text>{name}&#10;&#10;</xsl:text>
    <xsl:apply-templates select="* except name"/>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="t | dd">
    <xsl:call-template name="paragraph">
      <xsl:with-param name="indent" select="if (self::dd) then 6 else 3"/>
      <xsl:with-param name="text">
        <xsl:apply-templates/>
      </xsl:with-param>
    </xsl:call-template>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="reference">
    <xsl:text>   [{@anchor}]&#10;</xsl:text>
    <xsl:call-template name="paragraph">
      <xsl:with-param name="indent" select="6"/>
      <xsl:with-param name="text">{string-join(front/author/@fullname, ', ')}, "{front/title}", {front/date/@month} {front/date/@year}, &lt;{@target}&gt;.</xsl:with-param>
    </xsl:call-template>
  </xsl:template>

  <!-- Lines of at most 72 characters, indented. -->
  <xsl:template name="paragraph">
    <xsl:param name="indent" as="xs:integer"/>
    <xsl:param name="text" as="xs:string"/>
    <xsl:variable name="spaces" select="spec:spaces($indent)"/>
    <xsl:value-of select="replace(normalize-space($text),
                                  '(.{1,' || 72 - $indent || '})( |$)',
                                  $spaces || '$1&#10;')"/>
    <xsl:text>&#10;</xsl:text>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:function name="spec:spaces" as="xs:string">
    <xsl:param name="count" as="xs:integer"/>
    <xsl:sequence select="string-join(replicate(' ', $count))"/>
  </xsl:function>

  <xsl:template match="dl">
    <xsl:apply-templates select="*"/>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="dt">
    <xsl:text>   {.}&#10;</xsl:text>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="sourcecode">
    <xsl:value-of select="tokenize(., '&#10;')[normalize-space()] ! ('     ' || . || '&#10;')"
                  separator=""/>
    <xsl:text>&#10;</xsl:text>
  </xsl:template>
</xsl:stylesheet>

      <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc6238>.

spec:spaces is a function of the stylesheet itself, not of the package: a function that only one stylesheet needs stays there. It has no visibility, and in a stylesheet that is not a package that makes no difference.

Transformations from queries

fn:transform runs a stylesheet from XPath or XQuery and returns its results in a map; ?output is the principal result. With the sxml command, it reads the stylesheet as fn:doc reads files. A query can check what a stylesheet makes, such as the line lengths of the plain-text draft:

$ sxml xpath --context-item=vane.xml 'let $lines := transform({ "stylesheet-location": "text.xsl", "source-node": . })?output => tokenize("\n") return (count($lines), max($lines ! string-length()))'
122
72

The plain text has 122 lines, counting the empty ones, and none is longer than 72 characters.

Large inputs are a subject of their own: a stylesheet whose mode is streamable reads its input once, without building a tree of it. Streaming Large Trace Files shows how, on files of traces.

Project: Publishing the Specification

An Internet-Draft is written once and read in several forms: as a web page with a table of contents, as plain text in the style of an RFC, and by tools that want the requirements as data. Each new version also needs a page that says what changed since the last one. This project makes all of them from vane.xml with one script, and stops before it writes anything when the draft has a mistake that would make the published text wrong.

The pieces come from the earlier sections of this chapter. The HTML page is html.xsl and the plain text is text.xsl, both with the package spec.xsl and the module common.xsl from Many Outputs, Functions and Packages. New are a check, a JSON output and the page of changes.

The script

publish.sh:

#!/bin/sh
# Publishes a draft into the directory site/: checks it, then writes the
# HTML page, the plain text, the requirements as JSON and a page of the
# changes since the earlier draft. Stops at the first step that fails.
#
# Usage: sh publish.sh [DRAFT [EARLIER-DRAFT]]
set -e
draft=${1:-vane.xml}
earlier=${2:-vane-00.xml}

sxml validate --schema=vane.xsd "$draft"
sxml xquery --param=draft="$draft" publish-check.xq

mkdir -p site
sxml transform --force --output=site/vane.html html.xsl "$draft"
sxml transform --force --output=site/vane.txt text.xsl "$draft"
sxml transform --force --output=site/requirements.json requirements.xsl "$draft"
sxml transform --force --output=site/changes.html --param=old="$earlier" changes.xsl "$draft"
echo "published $draft into site/"

The steps run in order, and set -e stops the script at the first one that fails: every sxml command exits with a status other than 0 when it fails. The validation against vane.xsd comes first, because a stylesheet that meets an element it doesn't expect makes wrong output, not an error. Every transformation writes its own file with --output, and --force replaces the file of the last run.

The check

The schema says what the draft may contain. It cannot say that every reference is cited, or that a key word is marked as one. A query can:

publish-check.xq:

(: Checks a draft before it is published. Problems that make the
   published text wrong are errors and stop publication; open editorial
   matters are warnings. :)
declare namespace spec = "urn:example:spec";
declare option output:method "text";
declare option output:item-separator "&#10;";

declare variable $draft external := "vane.xml";
declare variable $rfc := doc($draft)/rfc;

(: The key words of BCP 14, as a regular expression of whole words. :)
declare variable $keywords :=
  "(^|\W)(MUST|SHALL|REQUIRED|SHOULD|RECOMMENDED|MAY|OPTIONAL)(\W|$)";

let $anchors := $rfc//@anchor
let $errors := (
  for $xref in $rfc//xref[not(@target = $anchors)]
  return `{$xref/ancestor::section[1]/@anchor}: xref to a missing anchor "{$xref/@target}"`,
  for $reference in $rfc//reference[not(@anchor = $rfc//xref/@target)]
  return `references: [{$reference/@anchor}] is never cited`,
  for $text in $rfc/middle//t//text()[not(ancestor::bcp14)]
  where not($text/ancestor::section/@anchor = "terminology")
  where matches($text, $keywords)
  return `{$text/ancestor::section[1]/@anchor}: a key word without bcp14: "{normalize-space($text)}"`
)
let $warnings := (
  for $t in $rfc//t[bcp14][not(@anchor)]
  return `{$t/ancestor::section[1]/@anchor}: a requirement without an anchor`,
  for $cref in $rfc//cref
  return `{$cref/ancestor::section[1]/@anchor}: open note {$cref/@anchor} ({$cref/@source})`
)
return if (exists($errors))
  then error(xs:QName("spec:check"), string-join($errors, "; "))
  else $warnings ! `warning: {.}`

The query makes two lists. An error is a problem that makes the published text wrong: an xref to an anchor that doesn't exist, a reference that no xref cites, a key word written in capitals but without bcp14, which a reader cannot tell from a requirement. (The key words of the Terminology section are quoted on purpose, so the check skips that section.) A warning is open editorial work: a paragraph with a key word but no anchor, which other documents cannot refer to, and a note. When there are errors, fn:error stops the query with all of them in its description, and sxml xquery exits with status 1; otherwise the query writes the warnings, one on each line.

Project: Editing a Specification Without Rewriting It builds a stricter check, which counts the unanchored SHOULD as an error, and the edits that fix what it finds.

The requirements as JSON

Tools that test an SDK, or a tracker of open requirements, want the requirements as data. With the json output method, a stylesheet's result can be a map, written as a JSON object:

requirements.xsl:

<xsl:stylesheet version="4.0" expand-text="yes"
    xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform"
    xmlns:spec="urn:example:spec"
    exclude-result-prefixes="spec">
  <xsl:import href="common.xsl"/>
  <xsl:use-package name="spec.xsl" package-version="1.0"/>
  <xsl:output method="json" indent="yes"/>

  <!-- The requirements as JSON, for tools: an array of objects. -->
  <xsl:template match="/">
    <xsl:sequence select="{
        'draft': string(rfc/@docName),
        'requirements': array { //t[@anchor] ! spec:requirement(.) }
      }"/>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:function name="spec:requirement" as="map(*)">
    <xsl:param name="t" as="element(t)"/>
    <xsl:sequence select="{
        'anchor': string($t/@anchor),
        'number': spec:number($t),
        'keyword': string($t/bcp14),
        'section': spec:number($t/ancestor::section[1]),
        'text': spec:text($t)
      }"/>
  </xsl:function>
</xsl:stylesheet>

The text of each requirement is the text a reader sees, with the xrefs made by the rules of common.xsl: spec:text applies the templates of the stylesheet that imports it.

The changes

The page of changes compares the draft with the earlier one, which the parameter old names. Requirements are matched by anchor: an anchor is given once and never changes, so the same anchor in both drafts is the same requirement, however its text and its number changed. A key finds a requirement by anchor in either document:

changes.xsl:

<xsl:stylesheet version="4.0" expand-text="yes"
    xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform"
    xmlns:spec="urn:example:spec"
    exclude-result-prefixes="spec">
  <xsl:import href="common.xsl"/>
  <xsl:use-package name="spec.xsl" package-version="1.0"/>
  <xsl:output method="html" indent="yes"/>

  <!-- The earlier draft, compared by requirement anchor. -->
  <xsl:param name="old" select="'vane-00.xml'"/>
  <xsl:variable name="old-draft" select="doc($old)"/>

  <xsl:key name="requirement" match="t[@anchor]" use="@anchor"/>

  <xsl:template match="/">
    <html>
      <head>
        <title>Changes in {rfc/@docName}</title>
      </head>
      <body>
        <h1>Changes from {$old-draft/rfc/@docName} to {rfc/@docName}</h1>
        <table>
          <xsl:apply-templates select="//t[@anchor]" mode="change"/>
          <xsl:apply-templates mode="removed" select="
              $old-draft//t[@anchor][empty(key('requirement', @anchor, current()))]"/>
        </table>
      </body>
    </html>
  </xsl:template>

  <xsl:template match="t" mode="change">
    <xsl:variable name="before" select="key('requirement', @anchor, $old-draft)"/>
    <xsl:variable name="status" select="
        if (empty($before)) then 'added'
        else if (spec:text($before) = spec:text(.)) then 'unchanged'
        else 'changed'"/>
    <xsl:if test="$status != 'unchanged'">
      <tr class="{$status}">
        <td><a href="vane.html#{@anchor}">{spec:number(.)}</a></td>
        <td>{$status}</td>
        <td>
          <xsl:if test="$status = 'changed'">
            <del>{spec:text($before)}</del>
            <br/>
          </xsl:if>
          <ins>{spec:text(.)}</ins>
        </td>
      </tr>
    </xsl:if>
  </xsl:template>

  <!-- A requirement that only the old draft has. -->
  <xsl:template match="t" mode="removed">
    <tr class="removed">
      <td>{@anchor}</td>
      <td>removed</td>
      <td><del>{spec:text(.)}</del></td>
    </tr>
  </xsl:template>
</xsl:stylesheet>

Each requirement of the new draft is added, changed or the same; a requirement whose anchor only the old draft has was removed, and gets a row of its own in the mode removed. The texts are compared as spec:text makes them, so a line broken in another place is not a change. The links point into the HTML page, vane.html, which the script writes next to this one.

The plain text is the draft as text.xsl writes it:

$ sed -n '/^4\./,/^5\./p' site/vane.txt
4.  Pause

   After three failed checks in a row, a service MUST put the flag in a

5.  Security Considerations

The JSON file is for programs, and a query reads it back as one:

$ head -10 site/requirements.json
{

Swap the drafts, and the same stylesheet shows the way back: the three new requirements are removed rows.

$ sxml transform --param=old=vane.xml changes.xsl vane-00.xml | grep -c 'class="removed"'
3

When the draft is wrong

Two broken copies show the two guards. In the first, an xref points to RFC6239, which the draft does not have. The schema's key reference from xref/@target to the anchors finds it, and nothing is written:

$ sed 's/target="RFC6238"/target="RFC6239"/' vane.xml > broken.xml
$ sh publish.sh broken.xml; echo $?
broken.xml:98:38: cvc-identity-constraint.4.3: element 'xref': its key sequence is no key sequence of the referenced key (keyref 'xref-target')
1

In the second, the citation of RFC 6238 is gone and a SHOULD has lost its markup. The copy is valid, and the check stops it:

$ sed -e 's| <xref target="RFC6238"/>||' -e 's|<bcp14>SHOULD</bcp14> last|SHOULD last|' vane.xml > unmarked.xml
$ sh publish.sh unmarked.xml; echo $?
publish-check.xq:33:8: spec:check: references: [RFC6238] is never cited; pause: a key word without bcp14: "A pause SHOULD last five minutes."
1

The files in site/ are still those of the last good run. Each step adds one guarantee, and the stylesheets can assume what the steps before them checked: that every target exists, that every key word is marked, that the draft has the structure the schema describes.

Summary

XSLT transforms documents by rules:

  • template rules match nodes with patterns, and xsl:apply-templates moves the processing on; the best rule wins by import precedence and priority;
  • modes process the same nodes in different ways, and a mode with on-no-match="shallow-copy" copies everything you don't change;
  • keys index documents, xsl:number numbers sections and requirements by their position, and xsl:for-each-group groups by value or by position;
  • result documents write many files, and imports, functions and packages organize large stylesheets that share their rules;
  • a script of small checked steps turns one source into every form a document is read in.

XSLT can also transform files too large for memory, as they stream past; Streaming Large Trace Files teaches it on the trace archives of the last project. Next, the diagram tool of Project: Drawing Diagrams with SVG puts XQuery and XSLT together on a different kind of XML: pictures.

Project: Drawing Diagrams with SVG

Many teams draw their architecture with a text description and a tool that turns it into a picture: Graphviz reads a -> b, Mermaid reads graph TD. The description is small, it can be reviewed in a diff, and nobody moves boxes by hand. In this project we'll build a small tool of that kind from the parts of this book. The description is XML, the layout is computed by XQuery, and the picture is SVG, which is XML too, so the same tools can write it, check it and change it afterwards.

The diagram we'll draw is the Vane system and who calls whom in it: the two SDKs, the modules of the Vane service, and the stores the service keeps its data in. Later projects draw other things with the same code: the flag's state machine, a diff of call chains, and a diff of traces.

The files are in docs/book/examples/svg.

SVG in one page

SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) is an XML vocabulary for drawings. Its elements are in the namespace http://www.w3.org/2000/svg; without that namespace, a browser shows an SVG file as unknown XML instead of a picture. Here is one box with a label and an arrow:

box.svg:

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="200" height="140" viewBox="0 0 200 140">
  <style>
    rect { fill: #eef3fb; stroke: #3b5b92 }
  </style>
  <defs>
    <marker id="arrow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="10" refY="5"
            markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto">
      <path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <rect x="30" y="20" width="140" height="40" rx="6"/>
  <text x="100" y="45" text-anchor="middle">vane/flags</text>
  <line x1="100" y1="60" x2="100" y2="120" stroke="black" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>
</svg>

The root svg element gives the size of the picture (width, height) and its coordinate system (viewBox: the left, top, width and height of the area drawn). Coordinates grow to the right and down: (0, 0) is the top left corner. The other elements draw in document order, later ones on top of earlier ones:

  • rect is a box at x, y of size width by height; rx rounds its corners.
  • text writes text with its baseline at y; text-anchor="middle" centres it on x.
  • line goes from (x1, y1) to (x2, y2). marker-end puts a marker on its end: here the triangle that marker defines inside defs, which holds things that are used rather than drawn, and is referred to by its id as url(#arrow).
  • style holds CSS rules, as in HTML. Presentation can also be written as attributes (stroke="black"); a rule in style applies to every element it matches.
  • g (not used here) groups elements; a class or an id on the group applies to everything inside.

Open the file in a browser to see it. For the tools in this book it is just a document:

$ sxml check box.svg
$ sxml xpath --context-item=box.svg '/*/* ! local-name()'
"style"
"defs"
"rect"
"text"
"line"

The description and the drawing

A diagram is described by a small vocabulary of our own, without a namespace: a diagram with a title, a node for each box (an id, a label, and kind="store" for a data store), and an edge for each arrow, from the caller to what it calls:

diagram.xml:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- The Vane system and who calls whom: the two SDKs, the modules of the
     Vane service (one program; a module is a box named vane/MODULE), and
     the stores it keeps its data in. A node is a box; kind="store" draws
     a data store. An edge goes from the caller to what it calls. The
     layout is computed: diagram.svg is the drawing. -->
<diagram title="Vane">
  <node id="browser" label="@vane/browser"/>
  <node id="node" label="@vane/node"/>
  <node id="api" label="vane/api"/>
  <node id="flags" label="vane/flags"/>
  <node id="registry" label="vane/registry"/>
  <node id="cache" label="vane/cache"/>
  <node id="postgresql" label="postgresql" kind="store"/>
  <node id="redis" label="redis" kind="store"/>
  <edge from="browser" to="api" label="HTTP"/>
  <edge from="node" to="api" label="HTTP"/>
  <edge from="api" to="flags"/>
  <edge from="flags" to="registry"/>
  <edge from="flags" to="cache"/>
  <edge from="registry" to="postgresql" label="SQL"/>
  <edge from="cache" to="redis" label="Redis"/>
</diagram>

The Vane service is one program, so its parts are modules, not services; each module is a box of its own, labelled vane/MODULE. The prefix says that the boxes are parts of one program. A box drawn around them would say it too, but it would need a second kind of node and a layout that nests boxes inside boxes, new machinery for one picture; the labels do the job with what the vocabulary already has. The two SDKs call the service over HTTP, the modules call each other directly (those edges have no label), and two modules talk to the stores.

Nothing in the description says where a box goes. That is the tool's job, and its result is this drawing:

diagram.svg:

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="299" height="416" viewBox="0 0 299 416">
  <title>Vane</title>
  <style>
    .node rect { fill: #eef3fb; stroke: #3b5b92; stroke-width: 1.5 }

  <g class="edge" id="edge-browser-api">

The boxes are in five layers: the two SDKs at the top, the api module they call below them, and so on down to PostgreSQL and Redis. Each node is a group g with a rect and a text; each edge is a group with a path, lines at right angles from box to box, and, when the edge has one, its label beside it. The groups have ids made from the description (node-registry, edge-flags-cache) and classes (node, service, store, edge) that the five style rules use: service is the class of every box that is not a store, an SDK or a module alike. Stores have rounder corners.

Both files are ordinary XML:

$ sxml check diagram.xml diagram.svg
$ sxml xpath --context-item=diagram.xml 'count(//node), count(//edge), //node[@kind = "store"]/@label/string()'
8
7
"postgresql"
"redis"

An XPath expression over the drawing has to say the namespace. A name test without a prefix, such as //rect, looks for elements in no namespace and finds none. *:rect matches rect in any namespace, and Q{http://www.w3.org/2000/svg}g names the namespace in the expression itself:

$ sxml xpath --context-item=diagram.svg 'count(//rect), count(//*:rect)'
0
8
$ sxml xpath --context-item=diagram.svg '//Q{http://www.w3.org/2000/svg}g/@id/string()'
"edge-browser-api"
"edge-node-api"
"edge-api-flags"
"edge-flags-registry"
"edge-flags-cache"
"edge-registry-postgresql"
"edge-cache-redis"
"node-browser"
"node-node"
"node-api"
"node-flags"
"node-registry"
"node-cache"
"node-postgresql"
"node-redis"

The plan

The tool has two halves, and the next sections build them one at a time:

  • Computing a Layout decides where each box goes and how each edge runs, with the layered method that Graphviz and the Eclipse Layout Kernel use: layers so that edges point down, an order in each layer so that few edges cross, then coordinates and lines at right angles. It is written with maps, arrays, records and functions as values.
  • Writing SVG with XQuery turns the layout into diagram.svg with constructors in the SVG namespace, and packs both halves into a library module, draw.xqm, that the later projects import.
  • Drawing with XSLT draws the same diagram with template rules, from a description the layout query has given coordinates.
  • Transforming SVG changes drawings that already exist, ours or anyone's: a dark theme, one node highlighted, ids and editor metadata removed, the text listed, the size changed.

Computing a Layout

A layout says where each box goes and which way each line runs. The method of this chapter is the one most tools for such diagrams follow: the layered method of Sugiyama, Tagawa and Toda, which Graphviz's dot and the layered algorithm of the Eclipse Layout Kernel (ELK) are built on. It puts the nodes in layers, one under the other, so that the edges point down; it orders each layer so that few edges cross; and only then does it work out coordinates. ELK adds an idea this chapter uses throughout: the order of the description, its model order, is information. Wherever two choices are equally good, the one that keeps the order the author wrote wins, so the author steers the drawing by the order of the nodes and edges and never moves a box by hand (Sören Domrös, Max Riepe and Reinhard von Hanxleden, Model Order in Sugiyama Layouts, IVAPP 2023).

The method has five phases:

  1. Break the cycles. Turn some edges round, so that no path leads in a circle.
  2. Assign layers. Give every node a layer, so that every edge points down.
  3. Order the layers. Sort each layer, so that few edges cross.
  4. Place. Work out the x of every box.
  5. Route. Draw the path of every edge.

Each phase is a function of the library module draw.xqm, namespace urn:example:draw. We'll read the module a part at a time and run each part as we go; Writing SVG with XQuery shows how it draws.

Breaking cycles

Layers only work if every edge can point down, and an edge that closes a circle cannot: some edge of the circle has to point up. A state machine has circles everywhere. states.xml has four states of a feature flag, and two transitions lead back to stable:

states.xml:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- Three states of a feature flag and a fourth that nothing leads to.
     Every state has an incoming edge except archived. -->
<diagram title="Flag states">
  <node id="stable" label="stable"/>
  <node id="checking" label="checking"/>
  <node id="rolling-out" label="rolling-out"/>
  <node id="archived" label="archived"/>
  <edge from="stable" to="checking" label="rollout.request"/>
  <edge from="checking" to="rolling-out" label="check.passed"/>
  <edge from="checking" to="stable" label="check.failed"/>
  <edge from="rolling-out" to="stable" label="step.done"/>
  <edge from="archived" to="stable" label="kill.request"/>
</diagram>

The first phase picks the edges to turn round. Drawn upward, they still point where they go, but for the layout they point down like the others. Finding the fewest such edges is a hard problem, so layout tools use a heuristic. Ours is a depth-first search, the one Graphviz uses: start at a node, follow its first edge, and the first edge of the node that leads to, and so on, and come back to try the next edge only when a node has no edges left to follow. The nodes on the way from the start to where the search is now are its path. An edge to a node on the path closes a circle; that edge is turned round.

(:~ One step of the depth-first search of draw:reversed: visit a node,
    then follow its edges in their order, and note each edge that leads
    back to a node the search is still inside. :)
declare %private function draw:visit(
  $diagram as element(diagram),
  $id as xs:string,
  $search as map(*)
) as map(*) {
  let $inside := map:put($search, "path", ($search?path, $id))
  let $done := fold-left(
    for $edge at $position in $diagram/edge
    where $edge/@from = $id and $edge/@to != $id
    return [ $position, $edge/@to/string() ],
    map:put($inside, "seen", ($inside?seen, $id)),
    fn($search, $edge) {
      if ($edge(2) = $search?path) then map:put($search, "back", ($search?back, $edge(1)))
      else if ($edge(2) = $search?seen) then $search
      else draw:visit($diagram, $edge(2), $search)
    }
  )
  return map:put($done, "path", $search?path)
};

(:~ Phase 1. The positions of the edges to reverse so that no path leads
    in a circle. A depth-first search starts from each node not yet seen,
    in the order of the description, and follows the edges in their
    order; an edge back to a node on the way it came closes a circle,
    and is reversed. A diagram without circles keeps all its edges as
    they are, and in one with circles the order of the description
    decides which edge turns: the first node is on top. :)
declare function draw:reversed($diagram as element(diagram)) as xs:integer* {
  sort(fold-left($diagram/node/@id/string(),
    { "seen": (), "path": (), "back": () },
    fn($search, $id) {
      if ($id = $search?seen) then $search else draw:visit($diagram, $id, $search)
    }
  )?back)
};

draw:visit calls itself: an XQuery function may be recursive, and the search is easiest to say that way. The state of the search is a map with three entries, passed from one step to the next: the nodes seen, the path, and the positions of the edges found to turn. map:put returns a new map with one entry changed; maps are values, and the old one is still there, which is why draw:visit can give back the path as it found it, $search?path, when it is done with a node. fold-left carries the map through the edges of a node and, in draw:reversed, through the nodes of the description. In a module, draw: is the module's prefix, and %private keeps draw:visit out of the module's interface.

The search starts at the first node of the description and follows the edges in their order, and that is where the model order comes in. Here, the search starts at stable and goes down to checking and rolling-out; the edges from them back to stable close circles. An import module declaration in the query names the module's namespace and file:

$ sxml xquery --method=adaptive --context-item=states.xml --expression='import module namespace draw = "urn:example:draw" at "draw.xqm"; for $position in draw:reversed(/diagram) return /diagram/edge[$position] ! `{@from} -> {@to}`'
"checking -> stable"
"rolling-out -> stable"

The Vane diagram has no circles, and the search turns nothing round:

$ sxml xquery --context-item=diagram.xml --expression='import module namespace draw = "urn:example:draw" at "draw.xqm"; count(draw:reversed(/diagram))'
0

The graph to lay out

The phases after the first work on a graph of their own: the nodes, the edges with the reversed ones turned round, and one more thing. An edge label needs room, and a label drawn halfway along a line lands on whatever happens to be there. ELK gives every label a label vertex: a small node of its own, put in the middle of its edge, that the layers, the order and the places treat like any other. A labelled edge becomes two links, one to its label vertex and one from it.

A vertex and a link are maps with fixed entries, and a record type says which entries those are and what they hold. declare record names the type and also declares a function of the same name that makes one. The module starts with the sizes of the drawing and its records:

(: The sizes of the drawing, in SVG user units. :)
declare variable $draw:box-height := 40;
declare variable $draw:box-min-width := 100;
declare variable $draw:gap-across := 30;
declare variable $draw:gap-down := 24;
declare variable $draw:track-gap := 10;
declare variable $draw:loop-width := 26;
declare variable $draw:padding := 20;

(:~ The width of a text in a sans-serif font of the given size: an
    estimate, from the average width of a letter. :)
declare function draw:text-width($text as xs:string?, $size as xs:integer) as xs:integer {
  xs:integer(ceiling(string-length($text) * $size * 0.56))
};

(: A vertex of the layered graph: a node of the diagram, the label of an
   edge, or a bend where an edge crosses a layer. Edges run along its x;
   left and right are how far it reaches on either side of that line. :)
declare record draw:vertex(
  id as xs:string,
  kind as xs:string,
  key as xs:decimal,
  left as xs:integer,
  right as xs:integer,
  height as xs:integer
);

(: A link of the layered graph: one step of the edge at that position
   in the description, from an upper vertex to a lower one. :)
declare record draw:link(from as xs:string, to as xs:string, edge as xs:integer);

(: A point, and a box: the top left corner and the size. :)
declare record draw:place(x as xs:integer, y as xs:integer);
declare record draw:box(x as xs:integer, y as xs:integer, width as xs:integer, height as xs:integer);

(: The route of an edge: an SVG path, and where its label goes. :)
declare record draw:route(path as xs:string, label as draw:place?);

(: A computed layout: the size of the drawing, a box per node id, and a
   route per edge, by the edge's position in the description. :)
declare record draw:layout(
  width as xs:integer,
  height as xs:integer,
  boxes as map(xs:string, draw:box),
  routes as map(xs:integer, draw:route)
);

A record is a map, so ?x reads an entry. The type checks what goes in:

$ sxml xquery --method=adaptive --expression='import module namespace draw = "urn:example:draw" at "draw.xqm"; draw:place(110, 20), draw:place(110, 20)?x'
{"x":110,"y":20}
110
$ sxml xquery --method=adaptive --expression='import module namespace draw = "urn:example:draw" at "draw.xqm"; draw:place(1.5, 20)'
expression:1:66: err:XPTY0004: The value does not match the required type (XPath 4.0, section 3.4, coercion rules)

A box is as wide as its label needs. The width of a text depends on the font, which the layout doesn't have, so draw:text-width estimates it from the average width of a letter. Here is the graph:

(:~ The graph to lay out: a vertex per node, sized for its label (and its
    loops, drawn to its right), a vertex for the label of every edge
    between two nodes, and the edges as links, the reversed ones turned
    round. A label is a vertex of its own so that it gets a place of its
    own, as ELK's label dummies do. A vertex's key is its place in the
    description; a label sits just after the node its edge leaves. :)
declare function draw:graph($diagram as element(diagram)) as map(*) {
  let $reversed := draw:reversed($diagram)
  let $order := map:merge(for $node at $n in $diagram/node return { $node/@id: $n })
  let $nodes := (
    for $node at $n in $diagram/node
    let $ends := max((count($diagram/edge[@from = $node/@id and @to != $node/@id]),
                      count($diagram/edge[@to = $node/@id and @from != $node/@id])))
    let $width := max(($draw:box-min-width, draw:text-width($node/@label, 14) + 24,
                       ($ends + 1) * 16))
    let $loops := $diagram/edge[@from = $node/@id and @to = $node/@id]
    let $loop-width := if (empty($loops)) then 0 else
      $draw:loop-width + max((0, $loops/@label ! (draw:text-width(., 12) + 4)))
    return draw:vertex($node/@id, "node", $n, $width idiv 2,
                       $width - $width idiv 2 + $loop-width, $draw:box-height)
  )
  let $steps := (
    for $edge at $e in $diagram/edge
    where $edge/@from != $edge/@to
    let $ends := if ($e = $reversed) then ($edge/@to, $edge/@from) else ($edge/@from, $edge/@to)
    let $label := $edge/@label ! draw:vertex(`label-{ $e }`, "label",
      $order($edge/@from) + 0.5, 1, draw:text-width(., 12) + 6, 16)
    return {
      "labels": $label,
      "links": if (exists($label)) then (
        draw:link($ends[1], $label?id, $e), draw:link($label?id, $ends[2], $e)
