  • rfc contains a front, a middle of one or more sections, and maybe a back, in that order. type="front" and type="section" name types that are declared earlier in the schema.
  • Its attributes each have a type: version is an integer and must be 3, category is one of five words, and docName has the type draft-name, a string that must look like the name of an Internet-Draft.
  • xs:assert is a rule in XPath that a valid rfc must meet. It is explained below.
  • xs:unique and xs:keyref are rules about values across the whole document: no two anchors are the same, and every xref names one.

The rest of the schema, from the top, declares the types the draft uses. Simple Types and Facets and Complex Types and Content Models read it part by part.

Validating

sxml validate checks documents against the schema. Both drafts are valid, so it prints nothing, and its exit status is 0:

$ sxml validate --schema=vane.xsd vane.xml vane-00.xml; echo "exit status $?"
exit status 0

To see what an invalid draft looks like, change a copy of the draft with sed and validate it from standard input, which - names. This copy has a requirement that says "MIGHT", an xref to a term that doesn't exist, and a two-digit year:

$ sed -e 's/<bcp14>MUST NOT/<bcp14>MIGHT/' \
      -e 's/target="term-percentage"/target="term-percentages"/' \
      -e 's/<date year="2026"/<date year="26"/' vane.xml \
  | sxml validate --schema=vane.xsd -
-:20:11: cvc-datatype-valid.1.2.1: attribute 'year' has the value '26', which is not valid for type 'xs:gYear'
-:94:37: cvc-enumeration-valid: element 'bcp14' has the value 'MIGHT', which is not valid for type 'keyword': the value is not one of the enumeration facets (XSD 1.1 Part 2, 4.3.5.4); the enumeration facets are 'MUST', 'MUST NOT', 'REQUIRED', 'SHALL', 'SHALL NOT', 'SHOULD', 'SHOULD NOT', 'RECOMMENDED', ...
-:92:9: cvc-identity-constraint.4.3: element 'xref': its key sequence is no key sequence of the referenced key (keyref 'xref-target')

sxml reports every error, not only the first. Each one has the line and column, the name of the rule in the XSD specification that failed (such as cvc-enumeration-valid), the value, and what was expected. The xref comes last although it is on line 92: rules across the document, such as the keyref, are checked at the end of the element they belong to, here rfc, when every anchor is known. Reading Validation Errors goes through the messages in detail.

For programs, --format=json writes the same report as JSON:

$ sxml validate --schema=vane.xsd --format=json vane.xml
{"schema":{"documents":["vane.xsd"],"status":"valid"},"files":[{"file":"vane.xml","status":"valid"}]}

Rules across values

The draft's name is written twice: in the docName attribute of rfc, and in the seriesInfo of the front matter, which is what the rendered draft shows. Nothing about the structure of the document says that the two must agree, but XSD 1.1 can say it with an assertion: an XPath condition on the element, here

<xs:assert test="not(@docName) or
                 @docName = front/seriesInfo[@name = 'Internet-Draft']/@value"/>

A draft whose docName was updated for -02 while its seriesInfo was not breaks it:

$ sed 's/docName="draft-example-vane-protocol-01"/docName="draft-example-vane-protocol-02"/' vane.xml \
  | sxml validate --schema=vane.xsd -
-:7:1: cvc-assertion: element 'rfc' breaks the assertion 'not(@docName) or                        @docName = front/ser...' of an anonymous type derived from 'xs:anyType'

The message shows the start of the assertion, so you can find it in the schema. Inside the test, the context item is the rfc element, with its attributes and children already validated, so the test can rely on their types. XSD 1.1 Features has more assertions.

Strict and lax

A reviewer sends notes about a short draft, with the draft inside them:

xsd-review.xml:

<!-- A review: a reviewer's notes around a short draft. The review
     vocabulary has no schema; the draft inside it has one. -->
<review by="Grace Hopper">
  <note>Is "MIGHT" one of the key words?</note>
  <rfc docName="draft-example-vane-brief-00">
    <front>
      <title>Vane in Brief</title>
      <seriesInfo name="Internet-Draft" value="draft-example-vane-brief-00"/>
      <author fullname="Ada Byron" surname="Byron"/>
      <date year="2026"/>
    </front>
    <middle>
      <section anchor="intro">
        <name>Introduction</name>
        <t>A service <bcp14>MIGHT</bcp14> refuse a rollout.</t>
      </section>
    </middle>
  </rfc>
</review>

vane.xsd declares no review element. By default, validation is strict: the document element must have a declaration in the schema, so the review is invalid. sxml still looks inside it, and validates the elements it does know:

$ sxml validate --schema=vane.xsd xsd-review.xml
xsd-review.xml:3:1: cvc-elt.1: no global declaration governs element 'review'
xsd-review.xml:15:22: cvc-enumeration-valid: element 'bcp14' has the value 'MIGHT', which is not valid for type 'keyword': the value is not one of the enumeration facets (XSD 1.1 Part 2, 4.3.5.4); the enumeration facets are 'MUST', 'MUST NOT', 'REQUIRED', 'SHALL', 'SHALL NOT', 'SHOULD', 'SHOULD NOT', 'RECOMMENDED', ...

With --mode=lax, elements without a declaration are let through, and the ones with a declaration are validated wherever they are. The review itself is no longer an error, but the draft inside it still is:

$ sxml validate --mode=lax --schema=vane.xsd xsd-review.xml; echo "exit status $?"
xsd-review.xml:15:22: cvc-enumeration-valid: element 'bcp14' has the value 'MIGHT', which is not valid for type 'keyword': the value is not one of the enumeration facets (XSD 1.1 Part 2, 4.3.5.4); the enumeration facets are 'MUST', 'MUST NOT', 'REQUIRED', 'SHALL', 'SHALL NOT', 'SHOULD', 'SHOULD NOT', 'RECOMMENDED', ...
exit status 1

Only the global declarations, the ones directly inside xs:schema, can be found this way. In vane.xsd that is only rfc: a section on its own is not validated even in lax mode, because the schema declares sections only inside other types.

DTDs

Older documents often carry a DTD, the schema language built into XML itself, in a document type declaration at the top. xml2rfc has one too, for authors who prefer it. A DTD can be part of the document, in its internal subset:

xsd-dtd.xml:

<!DOCTYPE cref [
  <!ELEMENT cref (#PCDATA)>
  <!ATTLIST cref anchor ID #REQUIRED source CDATA #IMPLIED>
]>
<cref source="AM">Should an owner be able to change the duration?</cref>

sxml check --validate-dtd validates a document against its DTD. This editorial note has no anchor, which its DTD requires:

$ sxml check --validate-dtd xsd-dtd.xml
xsd-dtd.xml:5:1: cvc-complex-type.4: element 'cref' lacks the required attribute 'anchor'

A DTD knows no types beyond names and IDs, and nothing about namespaces; that is why vocabularies with namespaces and typed values use XSD. Files and the Outside World shows external DTDs and entities, and Appendix A has the details of sxml check.

What's in this chapter

The rest of the chapter teaches XSD step by step:

  • Simple Types and Facets: built-in types, restrictions, lists and unions;
  • Complex Types and Content Models: sequences, choices, all, attributes, mixed, simple and empty content, groups;
  • Deriving Types: extension, restriction, xsi:type, substitution groups and xsi:nil;
  • Namespaces and Larger Schemas: target namespaces, import, wildcards and schema hints, on the flag's state machine;
  • Keys and References: xs:unique, xs:key and xs:keyref;
  • XSD 1.1 Features: assertions, conditional types, open content, default attributes and overrides;
  • Reading Validation Errors: what the messages mean, and how to fix what they report;
  • Typed Data and Schema-Aware Queries: using the types in XQuery and XSLT.

A schema is also a good source for code: Project: Generating Vane's SDKs from a Schema turns one into TypeScript types and runtime checks.

Simple Types and Facets

A simple type describes text: the value of an attribute, or the content of an element that has no children and no attributes. XSD has many simple types built in, and you make your own by restricting them, by making lists of them, and by joining them in unions.

Built-in types

These are the built-in types you'll use most. All of them are in the namespace http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema, usually with the prefix xs. The examples come from the draft where it has them:

TypeValuesExamples
xs:stringany textFlag States
xs:tokentext without leading, trailing or double spaces; these are removedtrust200902
xs:booleantrue, false, 1, 0true
xs:decimalexact decimal numbers1.0
xs:integerwhole numbers3, -3
xs:positiveInteger, xs:nonNegativeIntegerwhole numbers above zero, or from zero21
xs:doublefloating-point numbers1.5E3, INF
xs:date, xs:time, xs:dateTimedates and times of ISO 86012026-10-21, 09:30:00
xs:gYear, xs:gYearMontha year, a month of a year1997, 2026-10
xs:durationa length of timePT5M, PT10M
xs:anyURIa URIhttps://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2119
xs:NCNamean XML name without a colonreq-7
xs:ID, xs:IDREFa name unique in the document, and a reference to oneterm-flag
xs:languagea language tagen-GB

vane.xsd uses several of them directly: the year of a date is an xs:gYear, the version of rfc an xs:integer, the target of a reference an xs:anyURI.

Each type has a lexical space, the texts that are allowed, and a value space, the values they stand for. 21, 021 and +21 are three texts for one xs:positiveInteger. That matters when values are compared, as XPath compares typed values, not their texts.

Restricting a type

Most simple types you write are restrictions: a built-in type, with facets that narrow down its values. These are the first simple types of vane.xsd:

  <!-- Simple types -->

  <xs:simpleType name="anchor">
    <xs:restriction base="xs:NCName"/>
  </xs:simpleType>

  <xs:simpleType name="draft-name">
    <xs:restriction base="xs:string">
      <xs:pattern value="draft-[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*-[0-9]{2}"/>
    </xs:restriction>
  </xs:simpleType>

  <xs:simpleType name="keyword">
    <xs:annotation>
      <xs:documentation>The requirement levels of BCP 14 (RFC 2119, RFC 8174).</xs:documentation>
    </xs:annotation>
    <xs:restriction base="xs:string">
      <xs:enumeration value="MUST"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="MUST NOT"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="REQUIRED"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="SHALL"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="SHALL NOT"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="SHOULD"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="SHOULD NOT"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="RECOMMENDED"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="NOT RECOMMENDED"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="MAY"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="OPTIONAL"/>
    </xs:restriction>
  </xs:simpleType>

  <xs:simpleType name="month">
    <xs:restriction base="xs:string">
      <xs:enumeration value="January"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="February"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="March"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="April"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="May"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="June"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="July"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="August"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="September"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="October"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="November"/>
      <xs:enumeration value="December"/>
    </xs:restriction>
  </xs:simpleType>

  <xs:simpleType name="day">
    <xs:restriction base="xs:positiveInteger">
      <xs:maxInclusive value="31"/>
    </xs:restriction>
  </xs:simpleType>

The facets in them, and the others XSD has:

  • pattern is a regular expression that the whole text must match. The syntax is the one of XPath's matches, without ^ and $: a pattern always matches the whole value. draft-[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*-[0-9]{2} is draft-, words of small letters and digits joined by hyphens, and a two-digit version.
  • enumeration lists the allowed values, one facet for each value. A keyword is one of the eleven key words of BCP 14, and a month one of the twelve names xml2rfc writes.
  • minInclusive, maxInclusive, minExclusive and maxExclusive limit ordered values: numbers, dates, durations. A day is a positive integer up to 31.
  • minLength, maxLength and length limit the length: the number of characters of a string, or the number of items of a list.
  • totalDigits and fractionDigits limit the digits of decimals.
  • whiteSpace says what happens to spaces: preserve keeps them, replace turns tabs and line ends into spaces, and collapse also removes leading, trailing and double spaces. xs:token is xs:string with whiteSpace set to collapse.

anchor restricts xs:NCName with no facets at all. That is still worth a name: the schema says what an anchor is once, and every attribute that holds one says type="anchor".

xs:annotation and xs:documentation hold text for people. They change nothing about validation, but tools can read them; the state machine's documentation in Documenting the Machine in XHTML does.

A draft with a mistake for three of the types:

$ sed -e 's/vane-protocol-01"/vane-protocol-1"/' \
      -e 's/month="October" day="21"/month="Oct" day="32"/' vane.xml \
  | sxml validate --schema=vane.xsd -
-:8:6: cvc-pattern-valid: attribute 'docName' has the value 'draft-example-vane-protocol-1', which is not valid for type 'draft-name': the value matches no pattern facet (XSD 1.1 Part 2, 4.3.4.4); the pattern facet is 'draft-[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*-[0-9]{2}'
-:20:23: cvc-enumeration-valid: attribute 'month' has the value 'Oct', which is not valid for type 'month': the value is not one of the enumeration facets (XSD 1.1 Part 2, 4.3.5.4); the enumeration facets are 'January', 'February', 'March', 'April', 'May', 'June', 'July', 'August', ...
-:20:35: cvc-maxInclusive-valid: attribute 'day' has the value '32', which is not valid for type 'day': the value is above the maxInclusive facet (XSD 1.1 Part 2, 4.3.7.4); the maxInclusive facet is '31'
-:7:1: cvc-assertion: element 'rfc' breaks the assertion 'not(@docName) or                        @docName = front/ser...' of an anonymous type derived from 'xs:anyType'

Each message names the facet that failed and the facet's value. When the text isn't even a value of the base type, as 26 isn't an xs:gYear in the chapter's first example, the message is cvc-datatype-valid.1.2.1 instead. The last message is a consequence of the first edit: the seriesInfo still says -01, so the two names no longer agree.

A restriction can restrict a type of your own, and the facets add up: a restriction of day with maxInclusive 29 allows 1 to 29. It can only narrow, never widen: a maxInclusive of 40 on a type whose maximum is 31 is an error in the schema.

$ echo '<xs:schema xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema">
  <xs:simpleType name="day">
    <xs:restriction base="xs:positiveInteger"><xs:maxInclusive value="31"/></xs:restriction>
  </xs:simpleType>
  <xs:simpleType name="long-day">
    <xs:restriction base="day"><xs:maxInclusive value="40"/></xs:restriction>
  </xs:simpleType>
</xs:schema>' | sxml validate --schema=- vane.xml
-:6:32: maxInclusive-valid-restriction: a maxInclusive facet must lie within the base type's bounds (XSD 1.1 Part 2, 4.3.7.4)

Lists

A list type holds several values in one text, separated by spaces. levels.xsd adds two types to the draft's, for a summary that names the key words a draft uses and the day of its next meeting:

levels.xsd:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- Lists and unions over the simple types of vane.xsd. A summary of a
     draft names the key words it uses and the day of its next meeting:
       <summary levels="MUST SHOULD MAY" meeting="21"/> -->
<xs:schema xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema">

  <xs:include schemaLocation="vane.xsd"/>

  <!-- A list: key words separated by spaces, at most four of them. -->
  <xs:simpleType name="levels">
    <xs:restriction>
      <xs:simpleType>
        <xs:list itemType="keyword"/>
      </xs:simpleType>
      <xs:maxLength value="4"/>
    </xs:restriction>
  </xs:simpleType>

  <!-- A union: a day of the month, or the word "open". -->
  <xs:simpleType name="meeting-day">
    <xs:union memberTypes="day">
      <xs:simpleType>
        <xs:restriction base="xs:token">
          <xs:enumeration value="open"/>
        </xs:restriction>
      </xs:simpleType>
    </xs:union>
  </xs:simpleType>

  <xs:element name="summary">
    <xs:complexType>
      <xs:attribute name="levels" type="levels" use="required"/>
      <xs:attribute name="meeting" type="meeting-day"/>
    </xs:complexType>
  </xs:element>
</xs:schema>

xs:include brings in the components of vane.xsd, so keyword and day can be used here; Namespaces and Larger Schemas says more about combining schema documents.

levels is a list of keyword, so MUST SHOULD MAY is three values, each a keyword. The list type is written inside a restriction, which adds a facet: on a list, length, minLength and maxLength count the items, so a summary names at most four levels.

$ echo '<summary levels="MUST SHOULD MAY" meeting="21"/>' | sxml validate --schema=levels.xsd -
$ echo '<summary levels="MUST SHOULD MAY MUST OPTIONAL"/>' | sxml validate --schema=levels.xsd -
-:1:10: cvc-maxLength-valid: attribute 'levels' has the value 'MUST SHOULD MAY MUST OPTIONAL', which is not valid for type 'levels': the value is longer than the maxLength facet (XSD 1.1 Part 2, 4.3.3.4); the maxLength facet is '4'

The items of a list are separated by whitespace, always. Two of the key words have a space inside, so a list of keywords can't hold them: MUST NOT is the two items MUST and NOT, and NOT is not a keyword:

$ echo '<summary levels="MUST NOT"/>' | sxml validate --schema=levels.xsd -
-:1:10: cvc-enumeration-valid: attribute 'levels' has the value 'MUST NOT', which is not valid for type 'levels': the value is not one of the enumeration facets (XSD 1.1 Part 2, 4.3.5.4)

A list type is the right choice for names and numbers, which never contain spaces. Lists are handy in attributes, where you can't repeat an element. XSD's own xs:IDREFS and xs:NMTOKENS are lists.

Unions

A union type allows the values of any of its member types. A meeting-day is a day, or the word open. The member types are tried in order, and the first that accepts the text gives the value its type. 32 is not a day, and soon is not open, so neither is a meeting-day:

$ echo '<summary levels="MAY" meeting="open"/>' | sxml validate --schema=levels.xsd -
$ echo '<summary levels="MAY" meeting="32"/>' | sxml validate --schema=levels.xsd -
-:1:23: cvc-datatype-valid.1.2.1: attribute 'meeting' has the value '32', which is not valid for type 'meeting-day'

The members can be named, with memberTypes="day", or written inside the xs:union, as the token is in levels.xsd, or both.

What validation does to values

A validated element or attribute has the value its type says, not the text it was written with. import schema gives a query the schema's declarations and validate validates a node and returns a typed copy (Typed Data and Schema-Aware Queries explains both). Then the values show what the schema did:

$ sxml xquery --method=adaptive --expression='
    import schema default element namespace "" at "levels.xsd";
    for $summary in (<summary levels=" MUST  MAY " meeting="07"/>,
                     <summary levels="MAY" meeting="open"/>)
    let $valid := validate { $summary }
    return (count(data($valid/@levels)), data($valid/@meeting),
            type-of(data($valid/@meeting)))'
2
7
"Q{}day"
1
"open"
"xs:token"

The levels are two values, because their type is a list, and the extra spaces are gone. 07 is the number 7, and its type is day, the member of the union that accepted it; open is a token. Q{}day is the type day in no namespace, written as an expanded name.

The same works on the draft. Its year is a year, so it compares with xs:gYear("2010"), and its day is a number:

$ sxml xquery --method=adaptive --context-item=vane.xml --expression='
    import schema default element namespace "" at "vane.xsd";
    let $draft := validate { / }
    return (
      data($draft/rfc/front/date/@day) + 1,
      $draft//reference[front/date/@year lt xs:gYear("2010")]/@anchor/string()
    )'
22
"RFC2119"
"RFC5234"

Whitespace is part of the value too. keyword restricts xs:string, whose whiteSpace is preserve, so a line break inside a bcp14, as an editor might make when it wraps a long line, makes the key word invalid (the message writes the line break as a space, so that each message stays on one line):

$ sed 's/<bcp14>MUST NOT</<bcp14>MUST\n        NOT</' vane.xml | sxml validate --schema=vane.xsd -
-:94:37: cvc-enumeration-valid: element 'bcp14' has the value 'MUST         NOT', which is not valid for type 'keyword': the value is not one of the enumeration facets (XSD 1.1 Part 2, 4.3.5.4); the enumeration facets are 'MUST', 'MUST NOT', 'REQUIRED', 'SHALL', 'SHALL NOT', 'SHOULD', 'SHOULD NOT', 'RECOMMENDED', ...

Had keyword restricted xs:token, the line break and the spaces would have collapsed to one space, and the text would be MUST NOT. Choose xs:token for words and names that people type, and xs:string when every space counts.

Facets that don't fit

Not every facet applies to every type: fractionDigits makes sense for decimals, not for strings, and a minimum above the maximum allows nothing. Such mistakes are errors in the schema, and sxml reports them before it reads any document:

$ echo '<xs:schema xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema">
  <xs:simpleType name="anchor">
    <xs:restriction base="xs:NCName">
      <xs:fractionDigits value="2"/>
    </xs:restriction>
  </xs:simpleType>
</xs:schema>' | sxml validate --schema=- vane.xml
-:4:7: cos-applicable-facets: the facet does not apply to the base type's variety and primitive type (XSD 1.1 Part 2, 4.1.5)

XSD 1.1 adds two facets: assertion, an XPath condition on the value, and explicitTimezone, which requires or forbids a timezone on dates and times. XSD 1.1 Features shows both.

Complex Types and Content Models

A complex type describes an element that has attributes, children, or both. Its content model says which children it may have, how many, and in which order. This section reads the rest of vane.xsd from the top, and finds every kind of content XSD has in the draft.

Elements and their declarations

xs:element declares an element: its name and its type. An element declared directly in xs:schema is global: it can be the document element, and other declarations can refer to it with ref. The others are local: they exist only inside the content model where they are declared. In vane.xsd, rfc is the only global element, and every other element is local.

A type can be named, with xs:complexType name="section" at the top level, and used by name, type="section"; or anonymous, written inside the element declaration, as for rfc and middle. Name a type when it's used in more than one place, or when you want to refer to it from XQuery or XSLT. vane.xsd names most of its types: front is used by the draft and by every reference, text by every paragraph, dt and dd, and section by sections at every depth.

Local declarations can give the same name different types in different places. t in a section has the type text; name in a section is a plain string; and front declares its own title, which is not the title of anything else.

Sequences, choices and all

Here are the front matter and the section:

  <!-- Sections -->

  <xs:complexType name="section">
    <xs:sequence>
      <xs:element name="name" type="xs:string"/>
      <xs:choice minOccurs="0" maxOccurs="unbounded">
        <xs:element name="t" type="text"/>
        <xs:element name="dl" type="definition-list"/>
        <xs:element name="sourcecode" type="sourcecode"/>
      </xs:choice>
      <xs:element name="section" type="section" minOccurs="0" maxOccurs="unbounded"/>
    </xs:sequence>
    <xs:attribute name="anchor" type="anchor" use="required"/>
  </xs:complexType>

  <xs:complexType name="front">
    <xs:sequence>
      <xs:element name="title" type="title"/>
      <xs:element name="seriesInfo" type="series-info" minOccurs="0" maxOccurs="unbounded"/>
      <xs:element name="author" type="author" maxOccurs="unbounded"/>
      <xs:element name="date" type="date"/>
      <xs:element name="area" type="xs:string" minOccurs="0" maxOccurs="unbounded"/>
      <xs:element name="keyword" type="xs:string" minOccurs="0" maxOccurs="unbounded"/>
      <xs:element name="abstract" minOccurs="0">
        <xs:complexType>
          <xs:sequence>
            <xs:element name="t" type="text" maxOccurs="unbounded"/>
          </xs:sequence>
        </xs:complexType>
      </xs:element>
    </xs:sequence>
  </xs:complexType>

Three model groups combine the children:

  • xs:sequence: the children in this order. The front matter has a title, then the series information, the authors, the date, and the rest.
  • xs:choice: exactly one of the alternatives, each time the choice occurs. After its name, a section has any number of blocks, each a paragraph, a definition list or source code, in any order; then its subsections. Groups nest freely, so a choice inside a sequence is common.
  • xs:all: each child at most once, in any order. vane.xsd has none, but xml2rfc's address is a good use: an email, a phone number and a web address, in whatever order the author wrote them.

minOccurs and maxOccurs on an element or a group say how often it may occur. Both are 1 by default; minOccurs="0" makes it optional, and maxOccurs="unbounded" removes the upper limit. A draft has one or more authors and zero or more keywords; on the section's choice, the two attributes let the choice repeat.

xsd-author.xsd describes an author with a fuller address:

xsd-author.xsd:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- An author with more of xml2rfc's address: an xs:all, whose children
     may come in any order, and an attribute group shared by two types. -->
<xs:schema xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema">

  <!-- The names of a person, as xml2rfc writes them. -->
  <xs:attributeGroup name="names">
    <xs:attribute name="fullname" type="xs:string" use="required"/>
    <xs:attribute name="initials" type="xs:string"/>
    <xs:attribute name="surname" type="xs:string" use="required"/>
  </xs:attributeGroup>

  <xs:complexType name="address">
    <xs:all>
      <xs:element name="email" type="xs:string"/>
      <xs:element name="phone" type="xs:string" minOccurs="0"/>
      <xs:element name="uri" type="xs:anyURI" minOccurs="0"/>
    </xs:all>
  </xs:complexType>

  <xs:element name="author">
    <xs:complexType>
      <xs:sequence>
        <xs:element name="organization" type="xs:string" minOccurs="0"/>
        <xs:element name="address" type="address" minOccurs="0"/>
      </xs:sequence>
      <xs:attributeGroup ref="names"/>
    </xs:complexType>
  </xs:element>

  <!-- A contact of the working group: the same names, no address. -->
  <xs:element name="contact">
    <xs:complexType>
      <xs:attributeGroup ref="names"/>
      <xs:attribute name="role" type="xs:token" default="chair"/>
    </xs:complexType>
  </xs:element>
</xs:schema>

The address may list its children in any order, but each only once:

$ echo '<author fullname="Ada Byron" surname="Byron"><address><uri>https://example.com/</uri><email>ada@example.com</email></address></author>' | sxml validate --schema=xsd-author.xsd -
$ echo '<author fullname="Ada Byron" surname="Byron"><address><email>ada@example.com</email><phone>1</phone><phone>2</phone></address></author>' | sxml validate --schema=xsd-author.xsd -
-:1:101: cvc-complex-type.2.4: element 'phone' is not allowed here; expected 'uri'

Attributes

xs:attribute declares an attribute of a complex type, always with a simple type. Attributes are optional unless use="required": every section must have an anchor, while a paragraph may have one. A default value is added when the attribute is missing; a fixed value is added too, and an attribute that is there must have exactly that value. The version of rfc is fixed at 3.

The default is part of the validated document. A contact of xsd-author.xsd that doesn't say its role has the role chair after validation, and a draft that doesn't say its version has version 3, an integer:

$ sxml xquery --method=adaptive --expression='
    import schema default element namespace "" at "xsd-author.xsd";
    (validate { <contact fullname="Grace Hopper" surname="Hopper"/> })/@role/string()'
"chair"
$ sxml xquery --method=adaptive --expression='
    import schema default element namespace "" at "vane.xsd";
    let $draft := validate {
      <rfc>
        <front><title>T</title><author fullname="A B" surname="B"/><date year="2026"/></front>
        <middle><section anchor="intro"><name>Introduction</name></section></middle>
      </rfc>
    }
    return ($draft/@version/string(), type-of(data($draft/@version)))'
"3"
"xs:integer"

Four kinds of content

The content of a complex type is one of four kinds, and the draft has all four:

  • Element-only: children, and no text except whitespace between them. That's front, section and rfc.
  • Mixed: children with text between them, with mixed="true". That's text, the type of every paragraph, which allows the inline elements anywhere in its text, as often as you like.
  • Simple: text of a simple type, plus attributes, with xs:simpleContent. A title is a string with an abbrev attribute; a sourcecode is a string with a type and a name.
  • Empty: no content at all, only attributes. A complex type with no model group is empty, as date and seriesInfo are.

Here are the mixed and the simple types:

  <!-- Text: paragraphs and the inline elements in them -->

  <xs:group name="inline">
    <xs:choice>
      <xs:element name="xref" type="xref"/>
      <xs:element name="bcp14" type="keyword"/>
      <xs:element name="em" type="xs:string"/>
      <xs:element name="strong" type="xs:string"/>
      <xs:element name="tt" type="xs:string"/>
      <xs:element name="cref" type="cref"/>
    </xs:choice>
  </xs:group>

  <xs:complexType name="xref" mixed="true">
    <xs:attribute name="target" type="anchor" use="required"/>
  </xs:complexType>

  <xs:complexType name="cref" mixed="true">
    <xs:attribute name="anchor" type="anchor"/>
    <xs:attribute name="source" type="xs:string"/>
  </xs:complexType>

  <xs:complexType name="text" mixed="true">
    <xs:group ref="inline" minOccurs="0" maxOccurs="unbounded"/>
    <xs:attribute name="anchor" type="anchor"/>
  </xs:complexType>

  <xs:complexType name="definition-list">
    <xs:sequence maxOccurs="unbounded">
      <xs:element name="dt" type="text"/>
      <xs:element name="dd" type="text"/>
    </xs:sequence>
  </xs:complexType>

  <xs:complexType name="sourcecode">
    <xs:simpleContent>
      <xs:extension base="xs:string">
        <xs:attribute name="type" type="xs:token"/>
        <xs:attribute name="name" type="xs:string"/>
      </xs:extension>
    </xs:simpleContent>
  </xs:complexType>

xref and cref are mixed types without a model group: text, but no child elements. That's how xml2rfc writes them: <xref target="term-flag">flag</xref> has the text a reader sees, and <xref target="RFC2119"/> has none, so the renderer writes the reference's name.

Mistakes in content

This draft breaks a rule of each kind:

bad-content.xml:

<rfc version="2">
  <front>
    <author fullname="Ada Byron" surname="Byron"/>
    <title>Vane in Brief</title>
    <date year="2026">October</date>
    See the mailing list.
  </front>
  <middle>
    <section>
      <name>Introduction</name>
      <t keyword="MUST">A flag <bcp14>MUST</bcp14> start stable.</t>
      <name>Again</name>
    </section>
  </middle>
</rfc>

$ sxml validate --schema=vane.xsd bad-content.xml
bad-content.xml:1:6: cvc-au: attribute 'version' has the value '2', not its fixed value '3'
bad-content.xml:3:5: cvc-complex-type.2.4: element 'author' is not allowed here; expected 'title'
bad-content.xml:4:5: cvc-complex-type.2.4: element 'title' is not allowed here; expected 'author' or 'date'
bad-content.xml:5:23: cvc-complex-type.2.1: the text 'October' is not allowed: element 'date' has empty content
bad-content.xml:5:37: cvc-complex-type.2.3: the text '     See the mailing list.   ' is not allowed: element 'front' has element-only content
bad-content.xml:9:5: cvc-complex-type.4: element 'section' lacks the required attribute 'anchor'
bad-content.xml:11:10: cvc-complex-type.3.2.2: attribute 'keyword' is not allowed on element 't'
bad-content.xml:12:7: cvc-complex-type.2.4: element 'name' is not allowed here; expected 't', 'dl', 'sourcecode' or 'section'

Read them in order:

  • The version is 2, not the fixed 3.
  • The author comes before the title. sxml takes the title as missing, goes on after the author, and then finds the title too late.
  • The date has text, but its type is empty: the month belongs in the month attribute.
  • The front matter has text between its elements; only whitespace is allowed there.
  • The section has no anchor, which is required.
  • The paragraph has an attribute that text doesn't declare. Unlike elements in some other schema languages, attributes must be declared too.
  • The section has a second name, after a paragraph, where only blocks and subsections may come.

cvc-complex-type.2.4 is the message you'll see most. It says which element came where it isn't allowed, and lists the elements that the content model would accept at that point, which usually shows you the fix.

Reusing parts of content models

When several types share attributes or children, name the shared part once. xs:group names a model group, and xs:attributeGroup a set of attributes:

  • vane.xsd names the inline elements inline, and text refers to the group with <xs:group ref="inline" .../>. A schema for more of xml2rfc would refer to it from the other places that allow inline text, such as list items and table cells.
  • xsd-author.xsd names the attributes of a person names, and both author and contact refer to them.
$ echo '<contact surname="Hopper"/>' | sxml validate --schema=xsd-author.xsd -
-:1:1: cvc-complex-type.4: element 'contact' lacks the required attribute 'fullname'

A reference to a group is the same as writing its content in that place. Groups share parts; the next section shows how types share more, by deriving one type from another.

Deriving Types

Simple types are derived by restriction, as Simple Types and Facets showed. Complex types can be derived too, in two ways: extension adds content to a type, and restriction narrows it. A derived type can be used wherever its base type is expected, which gives XSD something like the subclasses of object-oriented languages.

Extension

vane.xsd already has two extensions, of a simple type. A title is an xs:string with an abbrev attribute, and a sourcecode is an xs:string with a type and a name:

  <xs:complexType name="title">
    <xs:simpleContent>
      <xs:extension base="xs:string">
        <xs:attribute name="abbrev" type="xs:string"/>
      </xs:extension>
    </xs:simpleContent>
  </xs:complexType>

xs:simpleContent with xs:extension adds attributes to a simple type, and the result is a complex type with simple content.

An editor who works on the draft keeps a worksheet: the paragraphs to look at, some source code, and the day the next draft is due. Its schema, xsd-derivation.xsd, includes vane.xsd and derives new types from the draft's:

xsd-derivation.xsd:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- An editor's worksheet for the draft: blocks of the draft to work on,
     and the day the next draft is due. It derives types from vane.xsd's
     and makes the blocks a substitution group. -->
<xs:schema xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema">

  <xs:include schemaLocation="vane.xsd"/>

  <!-- Restriction: a requirement is a paragraph whose anchor is required. -->
  <xs:complexType name="requirement" mixed="true">
    <xs:complexContent>
      <xs:restriction base="text">
        <xs:group ref="inline" minOccurs="0" maxOccurs="unbounded"/>
        <xs:attribute name="anchor" type="anchor" use="required"/>
      </xs:restriction>
    </xs:complexContent>
  </xs:complexType>

  <!-- Extension: a changed requirement also says since which draft. -->
  <xs:complexType name="changed-requirement" mixed="true" final="#all">
    <xs:complexContent>
      <xs:extension base="requirement">
        <xs:attribute name="since" type="draft-name" use="required"/>
      </xs:extension>
    </xs:complexContent>
  </xs:complexType>

  <!-- A substitution group: t, dl and sourcecode can stand in for block. -->
  <xs:element name="block" abstract="true"/>
  <xs:element name="t" type="text" substitutionGroup="block"/>
  <xs:element name="dl" type="definition-list" substitutionGroup="block"/>
  <xs:element name="sourcecode" type="sourcecode" substitutionGroup="block"/>

  <xs:element name="worksheet">
    <xs:complexType>
      <xs:sequence>
        <xs:element ref="block" maxOccurs="unbounded"/>
        <xs:element name="due" type="xs:date" nillable="true"/>
      </xs:sequence>
    </xs:complexType>
  </xs:element>
</xs:schema>

changed-requirement extends requirement with a since attribute that names the draft that changed it. An extension's content is the base type's content followed by its own, and its attributes are the base type's and its own. Here only an attribute is added, so a changed requirement has the mixed content of every paragraph.

Restriction

A restriction of a complex type allows a subset of what its base type allows. It writes out the whole content again, narrowed. requirement is a text whose anchor is required: every requirement is a valid paragraph, but not every paragraph is a requirement. sxml checks, when it compiles the schema, that a restriction really narrows. Making the anchor optional again in a restriction of requirement is an error:

$ echo '<xs:schema xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema">
  <xs:include schemaLocation="xsd-derivation.xsd"/>
  <xs:complexType name="loose-requirement" mixed="true">
    <xs:complexContent>
      <xs:restriction base="requirement">
        <xs:group ref="inline" minOccurs="0" maxOccurs="unbounded"/>
        <xs:attribute name="anchor" type="anchor"/>
      </xs:restriction>
    </xs:complexContent>
  </xs:complexType>
</xs:schema>' | sxml validate --schema=- xsd-worksheet.xml
-:3:3: derivation-ok-restriction.3: The attributes of a restriction are not allowed by its base

Choosing the type in the document: xsi:type

The worksheet declares its paragraphs as t with the type text. In the document, the attribute xsi:type says that a paragraph has a type derived from text. xsi is the namespace http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance, which XSD reserves for attributes that talk to the validator:

xsd-worksheet.xml:

<worksheet xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance">
  <t xsi:type="requirement" anchor="req-3">A rolling-out flag
  <bcp14>SHOULD</bcp14> return to the state "stable" ten minutes after
  its rollout step began.</t>
  <t xsi:type="changed-requirement" anchor="req-7"
     since="draft-example-vane-protocol-01">After three failed checks in
  a row, a service <bcp14>MUST</bcp14> put the flag in a pause.</t>
  <t>Check the pause section against the state machine.</t>
  <sourcecode type="abnf">percentage = 1*3DIGIT</sourcecode>
  <due xsi:nil="true"/>
</worksheet>

$ sxml validate --schema=xsd-derivation.xsd xsd-worksheet.xml

Each t is validated by the type its xsi:type names, or by text when it has none. These mistakes show the rules:

bad-worksheet.xml:

<worksheet xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance">
  <t xsi:type="requirement">A flag <bcp14>MUST</bcp14> start stable.</t>
  <t xsi:type="changed-requirement" anchor="req-8">A pause
  <bcp14>SHOULD</bcp14> last five minutes.</t>
  <t xsi:type="xs:string" xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema">Plain.</t>
  <block/>
  <figure>A drawing of the states.</figure>
  <due/>
</worksheet>

$ sxml validate --schema=xsd-derivation.xsd bad-worksheet.xml
bad-worksheet.xml:2:3: cvc-complex-type.4: element 't' lacks the required attribute 'anchor'
bad-worksheet.xml:3:3: cvc-complex-type.4: element 't' lacks the required attribute 'since'
bad-worksheet.xml:5:6: cvc-elt.4.3: xsi:type gives element 't' type 'xs:string', which is not validly derived from its declared type, type 'text'
bad-worksheet.xml:6:3: cvc-elt.2: element 'block' has an abstract declaration
bad-worksheet.xml:7:3: cvc-complex-type.2.4: element 'figure' is not allowed here; expected 'block' or 'due'
bad-worksheet.xml:8:3: cvc-datatype-valid.1.2.1: element 'due' has the value '', which is not valid for type 'xs:date'
  • The first paragraph says it is a requirement, but has no anchor.
  • The second is a changed requirement without its since.
  • The third names a type that isn't derived from text at all. sxml ignores that xsi:type, and validates the paragraph as text.

The last three are about the substitution group and xsi:nil, below.

Types derived from the declared type are what make queries over mixed content easy. With the schema's types, element(*, requirement) matches every element whose type is requirement or derived from it, so the changed requirement counts too:

$ sxml xquery --method=adaptive --context-item=xsd-worksheet.xml --expression='
    import schema default element namespace "" at "xsd-derivation.xsd";
    (validate { / })//t[. instance of element(*, requirement)]/@anchor/string()'
"req-3"
"req-7"

A type can be abstract too. abstract="true" on a complex type means that no element may have that type itself, only a type derived from it; it is a type that exists to be derived from. Made abstract, requirement can no longer be named in xsi:type, while changed-requirement still can:

$ sed 's/<xs:complexType name="requirement" mixed="true">/<xs:complexType name="requirement" mixed="true" abstract="true">/' \
    xsd-derivation.xsd > abstract.xsd
$ sxml validate --schema=abstract.xsd xsd-worksheet.xml
xsd-worksheet.xml:2:3: cvc-type.2: the type of element 't' is abstract: type 'requirement'

Substitution groups

xsi:type keeps one element name and varies the type. A substitution group varies the element name instead: a global element declares that it can stand in for another, the head of the group, wherever the head is allowed. In the worksheet, t, dl and sourcecode are members of the group whose head is block, and the worksheet's content model names only block.

block is abstract="true", so it can't appear itself; only its members can. That was the fourth mistake above. The fifth, a figure, is no member of the group, and the message names the head, block, which stands for every member. A member's type must be the head's type or derived from it; block has no type, which means xs:anyType, so any type will do.

In XQuery and XSLT, schema-element(block) matches the head and all its members:

$ sxml xquery --method=adaptive --context-item=xsd-worksheet.xml --expression='
    import schema default element namespace "" at "xsd-derivation.xsd";
    (validate { / })/worksheet/*[. instance of schema-element(block)] ! name()'
"t"
"t"
"t"
"sourcecode"

In vane.xsd, a section's blocks are a choice of three local elements. A substitution group is the open alternative: another schema that includes this one can add a member, a table say, and every content model that allows a block allows it too, without a change.

Nothing, explicitly

An element that is required but has no value can be declared nillable="true". The document then says xsi:nil="true", and the element must be empty: the worksheet's due is there, but no day is set yet. That's different from an empty element, which is an empty string, and an empty string is not a date: the sixth mistake.

In XPath, nilled tells a nilled element from others:

$ sxml xquery --method=adaptive --context-item=xsd-worksheet.xml --expression='
    import schema default element namespace "" at "xsd-derivation.xsd";
    (validate { / })//due ! nilled(.)'
true()

Controlling derivation

A schema can forbid what others may do with its types. final on a type forbids deriving from it (final="extension", "restriction" or "#all"), and block on a type or element forbids using derived types in documents, through xsi:type or substitution. changed-requirement is final, so a schema that extends it is in error:

$ echo '<xs:schema xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema">
  <xs:include schemaLocation="xsd-derivation.xsd"/>
  <xs:complexType name="reviewed-requirement" mixed="true">
    <xs:complexContent>
      <xs:extension base="changed-requirement">
        <xs:attribute name="reviewer" type="xs:string"/>
      </xs:extension>
    </xs:complexContent>
  </xs:complexType>
</xs:schema>' | sxml validate --schema=- xsd-worksheet.xml
-:3:3: cos-ct-extends.1.1: The base type's final forbids extension

Use them for types whose meaning would break if someone extended them, or for elements that must have exactly their declared type.

Namespaces and Larger Schemas

The draft's vocabulary has no namespace. Most real vocabularies have one: XHTML, SVG, Atom, and SCXML, the W3C's language for state machines. This section, and the rest of the chapter, works in the scxml directory, on the Vane feature flag written as an SCXML machine, flag.scxml. Project: Self-Describing State Machines explains the machine itself; here it is a document with three namespaces in it:

  • SCXML's, http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml, for the states and transitions;
  • urn:example:vane, with the prefix vane, for the annotations that describe the machine's events and data;
  • XHTML's, http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml, for the documentation of each state and event.

Here is its start and one state:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<scxml xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml"
       xmlns:vane="urn:example:vane"
       version="1.0" name="feature_flag" initial="stable" datamodel="ecmascript">

  <vane:events>

  <state id="stable" vane:implements="req-2">
    <div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">
      <p>The flag keeps its percentage. It waits for a rollout.</p>
    </div>
    <transition event="rollout.request" target="checking"/>
    <transition event="status.request" vane:implements="req-6">
      <send event="status.response"/>
    </transition>
  </state>

Two schemas describe it: scxml.xsd for SCXML, and vane-data.xsd for the annotations. XHTML has no schema here, and the machine is valid all the same:

$ sxml validate --schema=scxml.xsd flag.scxml; echo "exit status $?"
exit status 0

This section shows how a schema describes a namespace, how two schemas for two namespaces work together, and how a schema leaves room for namespaces it doesn't know.

A target namespace

targetNamespace on xs:schema puts every global declaration and named type of the schema into that namespace. Here is the top of scxml.xsd:

<xs:schema xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"
           xmlns:vc="http://www.w3.org/2007/XMLSchema-versioning"
           xmlns:sc="http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml"
           targetNamespace="http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml"
           elementFormDefault="qualified"
           vc:minVersion="1.1">

Inside the schema, references to its own components are QNames in the target namespace. scxml.xsd binds the prefix sc to it, so a reference to its own group or type is written with the prefix:

  <xs:complexType name="executable-block">
    <xs:group ref="sc:executable" minOccurs="0" maxOccurs="unbounded"/>
  </xs:complexType>

The other way is to make the target namespace the schema's default namespace, with xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml"; then ref="executable" finds it. Either way, a reference without the right namespace names nothing, and the schema doesn't compile. Built-in types keep their xs: prefix.

elementFormDefault="qualified" puts the local elements, such as state and transition, into the target namespace as well. Without it, only global elements are in the namespace, and local elements are in no namespace, which surprises almost everyone; most schemas say qualified. Attributes are different: unprefixed attributes such as id and event are in no namespace, and attributeFormDefault stays at its default, unqualified.

Namespace mistakes

The same machine without its namespace has an element that the schema doesn't know at all:

$ sed 's| xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml"||' flag.scxml | sxml validate --schema=scxml.xsd -
-:2:1: cvc-elt.1: no global declaration governs element 'scxml'

When cvc-elt.1 says no declaration governs an element that you can see in the schema, check its namespace first.

A namespace declaration that is missing lower down moves elements into the wrong namespace. Without its xmlns, the first state's div is in the default namespace of its parent, SCXML's, and SCXML has no div:

$ sed '0,/<div xmlns="http:\/\/www.w3.org\/1999\/xhtml">/s//<div>/' flag.scxml \
  | sxml validate --schema=scxml.xsd -
-:44:5: cvc-complex-type.2.4: element 'div' is not allowed here; expected 'onentry', 'onexit', 'transition', 'state', 'final', 'datamodel' or an element of another namespace

An element's namespace comes from the namespace declarations in scope where it is written, never from what it means.

Import

A schema can be split into several documents.

  • xs:include brings in a schema document with the same target namespace (or none, in which case its components take the including schema's namespace). The draft's levels.xsd includes vane.xsd this way.
  • xs:import makes the components of another namespace available. The vane annotations have their own schema, vane-data.xsd, with the target namespace urn:example:vane, and scxml.xsd imports it:
  <xs:import namespace="urn:example:vane" schemaLocation="vane-data.xsd"/>

vane-data.xsd declares the annotation attributes as global attributes, so that they can be used on elements of other namespaces:

  <xs:attribute name="type" type="xs:QName"/>
  <xs:attribute name="payload" type="xs:QName"/>
  <!-- The anchors of the requirements a state or transition carries out. -->
  <xs:attribute name="implements">
    <xs:simpleType>
      <xs:list itemType="xs:NCName"/>
    </xs:simpleType>
  </xs:attribute>

schemaLocation is relative to the document that contains it. It's only a hint on xs:import: the components can also come from another schema document given on the command line.

Wildcards and lax processing

Nothing in scxml.xsd mentions XHTML or the vane attributes by name. Instead, almost every type has wildcards:

<xs:any namespace="##other" processContents="lax"/>
<xs:anyAttribute namespace="##other" processContents="lax"/>

xs:any allows an element, and xs:anyAttribute an attribute, of the namespaces it names. ##other means every namespace except the target namespace (and except no namespace); others are ##any, ##local, ##targetNamespace, or a list of namespace names. processContents says what happens to what the wildcard lets in:

  • strict: it must have a declaration, and be valid by it;
  • lax: it is validated when the schema has a declaration for it, and let through when not;
  • skip: it is not validated at all.

So the vane attributes, which vane-data.xsd declares, are validated, and the XHTML, which no schema declares, is let through. A machine with an anchor that is not a name, a type given without its prefix, and an XHTML element that XHTML doesn't have, shows the difference:

$ sed -e 's/vane:implements="req-5 req-8"/vane:implements="req-5 8"/' \
      -e 's/vane:type="vane:seconds"/vane:type="seconds"/' \
      -e 's|<p>The flag is archived.|<p><blink>The flag</blink> is archived.|' flag.scxml \
  | sxml validate --schema=scxml.xsd -
-:80:22: cvc-datatype-valid.1.2.1: attribute 'vane:implements' has the value 'req-5 8', which is not valid for an anonymous type derived from 'xs:anySimpleType'

Only the anchor is reported. 8 is not an xs:NCName, so it can't be an item of the list. seconds is a valid xs:QName, the name seconds in the default namespace, SCXML's; that it names no type is a mistake the schema can't see, and Checking What the Schema Cannot finds it. blink is not checked at all.

Lax processing has a price: when a declaration is missing, nothing is validated and nothing is said. Without the schemaLocation of the import, scxml.xsd doesn't find vane-data.xsd, and the broken anchor goes through:

$ sed 's| schemaLocation="vane-data.xsd"||' scxml.xsd > scxml-alone.xsd
$ sed 's/vane:implements="req-5 req-8"/vane:implements="req-5 8"/' flag.scxml > broken.scxml
$ sxml validate --schema=scxml-alone.xsd broken.scxml; echo "exit status $?"
exit status 0
$ sxml validate --schema=scxml-alone.xsd --schema=vane-data.xsd broken.scxml
broken.scxml:80:22: cvc-datatype-valid.1.2.1: attribute 'vane:implements' has the value 'req-5 8', which is not valid for an anonymous type derived from 'xs:anySimpleType'

Every --schema adds documents to one schema, which is how you combine vocabularies that don't import each other.

Schema hints in documents

Documents often name their schema with xsi:schemaLocation (pairs of a namespace and a location) or xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation (a location for names in no namespace). Here is the broken machine with such a hint on its document element:

$ sed 's|<scxml xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml"|& xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml scxml.xsd"|' broken.scxml > hinted.scxml
$ head -2 hinted.scxml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<scxml xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml scxml.xsd"

By default sxml validate doesn't follow these hints: a document doesn't get to choose the schema it's checked against, so you name the schema with --schema. Without one, there is nothing to validate against:

$ sxml validate hinted.scxml
sxml validate: missing option '--schema' (or give --use-schema-location)
Usage: sxml validate [--schema=SCHEMA]... [--use-schema-location] [--mode=MODE] [--format=FORMAT] FILE...
Try 'sxml validate --help'.

--use-schema-location asks for the hints to be followed. The hinted documents are local files, relative to the document that names them, and they join the --schema documents, if you give any, in one schema for that document:

$ sxml validate --use-schema-location hinted.scxml
hinted.scxml:80:22: cvc-datatype-valid.1.2.1: attribute 'vane:implements' has the value 'req-5 8', which is not valid for an anonymous type derived from 'xs:anySimpleType'
$ sxml validate --use-schema-location --schema=scxml.xsd hinted.scxml
hinted.scxml:80:22: cvc-datatype-valid.1.2.1: attribute 'vane:implements' has the value 'req-5 8', which is not valid for an anonymous type derived from 'xs:anySimpleType'

The hinted copy is the broken machine, so both runs find its anchor; the second takes SCXML's schema from --schema. A hint only adds a namespace the schema doesn't have yet: with --schema=scxml.xsd, the hint for SCXML's namespace is ignored, so a document can't swap the schema you chose for one of its own. A hinted file that doesn't exist isn't an error by itself (XSD 1.1 Part 1, 4.3.2); the elements it would have declared are then simply undeclared.

Namespaces in queries

In XQuery, import schema binds a prefix to the schema's namespace, or makes it the default element namespace. Then element names and type names work as in the schema. The imported vane-data.xsd comes along with scxml.xsd, so its declarations are known; declare namespace only binds the prefix:

$ sxml xquery --method=adaptive --context-item=flag.scxml --expression='
    import schema namespace sc = "http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml" at "scxml.xsd";
    declare namespace vane = "urn:example:vane";
    let $machine := validate { / }
    return (
      count($machine//sc:state[. instance of element(*, sc:state)]),
      $machine//sc:state ! `{@id}: {count(data(@vane:implements))}`
    )'
5
"stable: 1"
"checking: 1"
"rolling-out: 1"
"paused: 2"
"archived: 0"

data(@vane:implements) is a sequence of names, because the attribute's type is a list. Without a prefix, a name in a path means no namespace, and finds nothing in this document:

$ sxml xquery --context-item=flag.scxml --expression='count(//state)'
0

Keys and References

Types check each value on its own. Some rules are about values together: no two states have the same id, every transition goes to a state that exists, no event is declared twice. XSD's identity constraints express them: xs:unique, xs:key and xs:keyref.

The machine's keys

The end of scxml.xsd declares three constraints on the scxml element:

    <!-- Every state has its own id, and every target and initial state is
         one of them. -->
    <xs:key name="state-id">
      <xs:selector xpath=".//sc:state | .//sc:final"/>
      <xs:field xpath="@id"/>
    </xs:key>
    <xs:keyref name="transition-target" refer="sc:state-id">
      <xs:selector xpath=".//sc:transition"/>
      <xs:field xpath="@target"/>
    </xs:keyref>
    <xs:keyref name="initial-state" refer="sc:state-id">
      <xs:selector xpath=". | .//sc:state"/>
      <xs:field xpath="@initial"/>
    </xs:keyref>
  </xs:element>

and vane-data.xsd declares one on the event declarations:

  <xs:element name="events">
    <xs:complexType>
      <xs:sequence>
        <xs:element name="event" maxOccurs="unbounded">
          <xs:complexType>
            <xs:sequence>
              <xs:any namespace="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" processContents="lax"
                      minOccurs="0" maxOccurs="unbounded"/>
            </xs:sequence>
            <xs:attribute name="name" type="xs:token" use="required"/>
            <xs:attribute ref="vane:payload"/>
          </xs:complexType>
        </xs:element>
      </xs:sequence>
    </xs:complexType>
    <xs:unique name="event-name">
      <xs:selector xpath="vane:event"/>
      <xs:field xpath="@name"/>
    </xs:unique>
  </xs:element>

An identity constraint has three parts:

  • where it is declared: on the element whose content it covers. The rule holds within each such element. The state ids are unique in the whole machine, because the key is declared on scxml; the event names are unique within each vane:events.
  • a selector, a path from that element to the elements the rule is about: every state and final at any depth, every transition, or each vane:event;
  • one or more fields, paths from each selected element to the values that make its key sequence, here @id, @target, @initial or @name.

The three kinds differ in what they require:

  • xs:unique: no two selected elements have the same key sequence. Elements that lack a field are left out.
  • xs:key: the same, and every selected element must have every field. Every state has an id.
  • xs:keyref: the key sequence of each selected element must be one of a key's (or a unique's) sequences. That's a foreign key, as in a database: a target is a state id. A transition without a target, as status.request in the stable state, is left out; so are the states without an initial.

Checking a machine

This small machine has a mistake for each of the machine's rules:

bad-target.scxml:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- A small machine with mistakes in its state ids and targets. -->
<scxml xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml"
       version="1.0" name="small_flag" initial="off">
  <state id="stable">
    <transition event="check.passed" target="rolling"/>
  </state>
  <state id="rolling-out">
    <transition event="kill.request" target="stable"/>
  </state>
  <state id="stable" initial="steady">
    <state id="steady"/>
  </state>
</scxml>

$ sxml validate --schema=scxml.xsd bad-target.scxml
bad-target.scxml:11:3: cvc-identity-constraint.4.2.2: element 'Q{http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml}state': its key sequence is that of an earlier member (key 'Q{http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml}state-id')
bad-target.scxml:6:5: cvc-identity-constraint.4.3: element 'Q{http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml}transition': its key sequence is no key sequence of the referenced key (keyref 'Q{http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml}transition-target')
bad-target.scxml:9:5: cvc-identity-constraint.4.3: element 'Q{http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml}transition': its key sequence is no key sequence of the referenced key (keyref 'Q{http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml}transition-target')
bad-target.scxml:3:1: cvc-identity-constraint.4.3: element 'Q{http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml}scxml': its key sequence is no key sequence of the referenced key (keyref 'Q{http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml}initial-state')
  • The third state has the id of the first, stable.
  • The first transition goes to rolling, which is no state's id: the state is rolling-out.
  • The second goes to stable, which is an id, but twice: a keyref can't refer to a key value that is not unique, so it is reported too. Fix the duplicate first, and this one goes away.
  • The machine's initial names off, which doesn't exist. The nested initial="steady" is fine.

The elements and the constraints are written as expanded names, Q{namespace}local, because the document writes them without a prefix; an element with a prefix, such as vane:event below, is written with it.

Each message names the constraint, so you can find it in the schema. They are reported in groups, by constraint, at the end of the element that the constraint is declared on: only then are all the values known.

A field's value must also be valid for its type, or it is no key value at all. A state id is an xs:NCName, so an id with spaces in it is a mistake of the attribute, and then of the key: the state has no id that the key could hold, which xs:key doesn't allow, and the transition from checking to paused now names no state:

$ sed 's/<state id="paused"/<state id="paused for now"/' flag.scxml \
  | sxml validate --schema=scxml.xsd -
-:80:10: cvc-datatype-valid.1.2.1: attribute 'id' has the value 'paused for now', which is not valid for type 'xs:NCName'
-:80:3: cvc-identity-constraint.4.2.1: element 'Q{http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml}state': a key field has no value (key 'Q{http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml}state-id')
-:63:5: cvc-identity-constraint.4.3: element 'Q{http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml}transition': its key sequence is no key sequence of the referenced key (keyref 'Q{http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml}transition-target')

The first message is the one to fix; the other two follow from it. (In xs:unique, a field without a valid value leaves the element out, as a missing field does; Reading Validation Errors shows that on the draft's anchors.)

The event declarations have their own rule:

duplicate-event.scxml:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- A machine that declares one of its events twice. -->
<scxml xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml"
       xmlns:vane="urn:example:vane"
       version="1.0" name="small_flag" initial="stable">
  <vane:events>
    <vane:event name="kill.request"/>
    <vane:event name="rollout.request" vane:payload="vane:rollout"/>
    <vane:event name="kill.request"/>
  </vane:events>
  <state id="stable">
    <transition event="rollout.request" target="rolling-out"/>
  </state>
  <state id="rolling-out">
    <transition event="kill.request" target="stable"/>
  </state>
</scxml>

$ sxml validate --schema=scxml.xsd duplicate-event.scxml
duplicate-event.scxml:9:5: cvc-identity-constraint.4.1: element 'vane:event': its key sequence is that of an earlier member (unique 'Q{urn:example:vane}event-name')

Values are compared as typed values, not as text. An event name is an xs:token, whose spaces collapse, so name=" kill.request" would be a duplicate too; and when a field's type is xs:integer, 7 and 007 are the same key.

Paths in constraints

The paths of selector and field are a small subset of XPath: child steps, .// at the start, . for the element itself, @ for attributes, *, and | to combine paths. There are no predicates and no functions. . | .//sc:state in initial-state selects the machine and every state, the elements that may have an initial.

Names with a namespace need a prefix that the schema binds, as scxml.xsd binds sc. Without it, .//transition means transitions in no namespace, and in a machine, where every transition is in SCXML's namespace, the keyref silently selects nothing. Only the two other mistakes are left:

$ sed 's|xpath=".//sc:transition"|xpath=".//transition"|' scxml.xsd > loose.xsd
$ sxml validate --schema=loose.xsd bad-target.scxml
bad-target.scxml:11:3: cvc-identity-constraint.4.2.2: element 'Q{http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml}state': its key sequence is that of an earlier member (key 'Q{http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml}state-id')
bad-target.scxml:3:1: cvc-identity-constraint.4.3: element 'Q{http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml}scxml': its key sequence is no key sequence of the referenced key (keyref 'Q{http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml}initial-state')

In XSD 1.1, xpathDefaultNamespace="##targetNamespace" on xs:schema (or on a selector or field) makes unprefixed names in the paths mean the target namespace, which avoids the mistake.

The value of refer is a QName too: the keyrefs say refer="sc:state-id", because the key is a component of the target namespace like any other.

Keys or IDs?

xs:ID and xs:IDREF are simple types with a similar purpose: an ID is unique in the whole document, and an IDREF must be one of the document's IDs. They are older and simpler, but blunt: one namespace of ids for the whole document, only names (no numbers or dates), and only one field. The Recommendation's own schema for SCXML gives state ids the type xs:ID. Use keys when the rule belongs to a part of the document, or when the key is a number, a date or several values.

Choosing between xs:key and xs:unique is choosing whether the field is required. The draft's schema, vane.xsd, makes its anchors unique with an xs:unique, because most paragraphs have no anchor: only requirements do. With an xs:key in its place, every selected element must have one, and the draft has six paragraphs without (vane.xml here is a link to the draft in the spec directory, and vane.xsd to its schema):

$ sed 's/<xs:unique name="anchor">/<xs:key name="anchor">/; s|</xs:unique>|</xs:key>|' vane.xsd \
  | sxml validate --schema=- vane.xml 2>&1 | head -3
vane.xml:25:7: cvc-identity-constraint.4.2.1: element 't': a key field has no value (key 'anchor')
vane.xml:35:7: cvc-identity-constraint.4.2.1: element 't': a key field has no value (key 'anchor')
vane.xml:42:9: cvc-identity-constraint.4.2.1: element 't': a key field has no value (key 'anchor')

A keyref may refer to a unique as well as to a key, which is what the draft's xref-target does.

XSD 1.1 Features

XSD 1.1 keeps everything of XSD 1.0 and adds what users had missed most: rules written in XPath, types chosen by attribute values, content models that are open to extensions, and a clean way to change a schema without copying it. sxml implements XSD 1.1, and validates XSD 1.0 schemas with the same engine. The machine's schemas already use some of it, and vane-1.1.xsd, a stricter version of the annotations' schema, uses the rest:

vane-1.1.xsd:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- XSD 1.1 on the vane annotations: vane-data.xsd, overridden and
     extended. Give it to the validator together with scxml.xsd: its
     override then stands for vane-data.xsd, which scxml.xsd imports. -->
<xs:schema xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"
           xmlns:vc="http://www.w3.org/2007/XMLSchema-versioning"
           xmlns:vane="urn:example:vane"
           targetNamespace="urn:example:vane"
           elementFormDefault="qualified"
           defaultAttributes="vane:traced"
           vc:minVersion="1.1">

  <xs:override schemaLocation="vane-data.xsd">
    <!-- An event's type depends on whether it carries a payload. -->
    <xs:element name="events">
      <xs:complexType>
        <xs:sequence>
          <xs:element name="event" type="vane:event" maxOccurs="unbounded">
            <xs:alternative test="@vane:payload" type="vane:event-with-payload"/>
          </xs:element>
        </xs:sequence>
      </xs:complexType>
      <xs:unique name="event-name">
        <xs:selector xpath="vane:event"/>
        <xs:field xpath="@name"/>
      </xs:unique>
    </xs:element>

    <!-- A status may end with elements of other namespaces, so that a
         vendor can add its own fields. -->
    <xs:element name="status">
      <xs:complexType>
        <xs:openContent mode="suffix">
          <xs:any namespace="##other" processContents="lax"/>
        </xs:openContent>
        <xs:sequence>
          <xs:element name="flag" type="vane:flag-key"/>
          <xs:element name="state" type="vane:state"/>
          <xs:element name="failed-checks" type="vane:failure-count"/>
          <xs:element name="retry-after" type="vane:seconds" minOccurs="0"/>
        </xs:sequence>
        <xs:assert test="exists(vane:retry-after) = (vane:state = 'paused')"/>
      </xs:complexType>
    </xs:element>
  </xs:override>

  <!-- A delay as SCXML writes it, such as "600s" or "250ms", of at most
       an hour: the pattern checks the form, the assertion the size. -->
  <xs:simpleType name="delay">
    <xs:restriction base="xs:string">
      <xs:pattern value="[0-9]+(s|ms)"/>
      <xs:assertion test="xs:integer(replace($value, '[a-z]+$', ''))
                          le (if (ends-with($value, 'ms')) then 3600000 else 3600)"/>
    </xs:restriction>
  </xs:simpleType>

  <!-- A moment in a log: a date and time that says its timezone. -->
  <xs:simpleType name="moment">
    <xs:restriction base="xs:dateTime">
      <xs:explicitTimezone value="required"/>
    </xs:restriction>
  </xs:simpleType>

  <!-- Every complex type of this document gets these attributes. -->
  <xs:attributeGroup name="traced">
    <xs:attribute ref="vane:implements"/>
  </xs:attributeGroup>

  <!-- An event without a payload: the XHTML description is optional. -->
  <xs:complexType name="event">
    <xs:sequence>
      <xs:any namespace="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" processContents="lax"
              minOccurs="0" maxOccurs="unbounded"/>
    </xs:sequence>
    <xs:attribute name="name" type="xs:token" use="required"/>
    <xs:attribute ref="vane:payload"/>
  </xs:complexType>

  <!-- An event with a payload must say in XHTML what it carries. -->
  <xs:complexType name="event-with-payload">
    <xs:complexContent>
      <xs:restriction base="vane:event">
        <xs:sequence>
          <xs:any namespace="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" processContents="lax"
                  minOccurs="1" maxOccurs="unbounded"/>
        </xs:sequence>
        <xs:attribute name="name" type="xs:token" use="required"/>
        <xs:attribute ref="vane:payload" use="required"/>
      </xs:restriction>
    </xs:complexContent>
  </xs:complexType>
</xs:schema>

It is used together with scxml.xsd. The machine is valid by it too:

$ sxml validate --schema=vane-1.1.xsd --schema=scxml.xsd flag.scxml; echo "exit status $?"
exit status 0

Assertions on values

The assertion facet restricts a simple type by an XPath condition, in which $value is the value being checked. SCXML writes the delay of a send as a number and a unit, 600s or 250ms. A pattern can check the form, and an assertion the size: delay allows at most an hour.

The second new facet, explicitTimezone, says whether dates and times must have a timezone (required), must not have one (prohibited), or may (optional, the default). A moment in a log is only one when its timezone is known.

vane-data.xsd declares an element vane:value whose type is xs:anySimpleType, any simple value at all, so that a value can be checked against any of the schema's types with xsi:type:

$ for delay in 600s 250ms 2h 4000s; do \
    echo "<vane:value xmlns:vane='urn:example:vane' xmlns:xsi='http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance' xsi:type='vane:delay'>$delay</vane:value>" \
      | sxml validate --schema=vane-1.1.xsd -; \
  done
-:1:1: cvc-pattern-valid: element 'vane:value' has the value '2h', which is not valid for type 'vane:delay': the value matches no pattern facet (XSD 1.1 Part 2, 4.3.4.4); the pattern facet is '[0-9]+(s|ms)'
-:1:1: cvc-assertions-valid: the value '4000s' breaks an assertion of type 'vane:delay'
$ echo "<vane:value xmlns:vane='urn:example:vane' xmlns:xsi='http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance' xsi:type='vane:moment'>2026-10-21T09:15:00</vane:value>" \
  | sxml validate --schema=vane-1.1.xsd -
-:1:1: cvc-explicitTimezone-valid: element 'vane:value' has the value '2026-10-21T09:15:00', which is not valid for type 'vane:moment': the value's timezone is not what the explicitTimezone facet requires (XSD 1.1 Part 2, 4.3.14.4); the explicitTimezone facet is 'required'

Hours are not a unit SCXML has, and 4000 seconds is more than an hour. The moment has no timezone.

Assertions on elements

xs:assert in a complex type is a condition on the whole element, as the draft's docName rule in Validating with XSD showed. The context item is the element, with its children and attributes already validated and typed. The machine's schemas have three:

  • SCXML 1.0, section 3.5, says that a transition has an event, a condition or a target, at least one of them. scxml.xsd says exists(@event | @cond | @target) on the transition type.
  • Section 5.3.1 says that a data element gets its value from an expr, from a src, or from its content, and from at most one of them: count((@expr, @src, *)) le 1.
  • vane-data.xsd says that a status has a retry-after exactly when the flag is paused: exists(vane:retry-after) = (vane:state = 'paused'). The comparison of two booleans says "if and only if".

A machine and a status that break them:

$ sed -e 's|<data id="pauseSeconds" expr="300"|& src="durations.json"|' \
      -e 's|<transition event="flag.evaluated">|<transition>|' flag.scxml \
  | sxml validate --schema=scxml.xsd -
-:40:5: cvc-assertion: element 'Q{http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml}data' breaks the assertion 'count((@expr, @src, *)) le 1' of an anonymous type derived from 'xs:anyType'
-:75:5: cvc-assertion: element 'Q{http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml}transition' breaks the assertion 'exists(@event | @cond | @target)' of type 'Q{http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml}transition'
$ echo '<status xmlns="urn:example:vane"><flag>new-checkout</flag><state>stable</state><failed-checks>0</failed-checks><retry-after>300</retry-after></status>' \
  | sxml validate --schema=vane-data.xsd -
-:1:1: cvc-assertion: element 'Q{urn:example:vane}status' breaks the assertion 'exists(vane:retry-after) = (vane:state = 'paused')' of an anonymous type derived from 'xs:anyType'

No structure could say any of the three. An assertion is reported at the end of its element, when all its content is known.

Conditional type assignment

xs:alternative chooses an element's type by a condition on its attributes. The first alternative whose test is true gives the type; one without a test is the fallback. The declared type is used when no alternative applies, and each alternative's type must be derived from it.

In vane-1.1.xsd, an event is a vane:event, whose XHTML description is optional; an event with a vane:payload gets the type vane:event-with-payload instead, a restriction that requires the description: an event that carries data must say what it is. Without its paragraph, status.response breaks the rule:

$ sed 's|<p xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">The service answers with the state.</p>||' flag.scxml \
  | sxml validate --schema=vane-1.1.xsd --schema=scxml.xsd -
-:22:5: cvc-complex-type.2.4: the content of element 'vane:event' is incomplete; expected an element of the wildcard's namespaces

The tests can only look at attributes, not children: the type must be known before the children are read. An alternative whose type is xs:error, a type that no element can be valid against, is how a schema says "not this one at all".

Open content

xs:openContent lets elements that a content model doesn't name appear among the ones it does. With mode="interleave", they may appear anywhere; with mode="suffix", only at the end. The wildcard inside says which elements. The status of vane-1.1.xsd is open at the end for any element of another namespace, so a team that runs the service can add its own fields, such as the error rate its checks measured:

$ echo '<status xmlns="urn:example:vane" xmlns:acme="urn:example:acme"><flag>new-checkout</flag><state>paused</state><failed-checks>3</failed-checks><retry-after>300</retry-after><acme:error-rate>0.07</acme:error-rate></status>' \
  | sxml validate --schema=vane-1.1.xsd -; echo "exit status $?"
exit status 0
$ echo '<status xmlns="urn:example:vane" xmlns:acme="urn:example:acme"><flag>new-checkout</flag><acme:error-rate>0.07</acme:error-rate><state>paused</state><failed-checks>3</failed-checks><retry-after>300</retry-after></status>' \
  | sxml validate --schema=vane-1.1.xsd -
-:1:89: cvc-complex-type.2.4: element 'acme:error-rate' is not allowed here; expected 'state'
-:1:128: cvc-complex-type.2.4: element 'state' is not allowed here; expected an element of another namespace
-:1:149: cvc-complex-type.2.4: element 'failed-checks' is not allowed here; expected an element of another namespace
-:1:181: cvc-complex-type.2.4: element 'retry-after' is not allowed here; expected an element of another namespace

In the middle, the error rate is not allowed. sxml takes it as the start of the suffix, so the fields after it are reported too: once the suffix has begun, only elements of other namespaces may follow.

xs:defaultOpenContent, at the top of a schema, gives every complex type of the schema the same open content.

Default attributes

defaultAttributes on xs:schema names an attribute group that every complex type of the schema document gets, unless it says defaultAttributesApply="false". In vane-1.1.xsd, the group traced holds vane:implements, so an event may now say which requirements it implements, which vane-data.xsd doesn't allow:

$ sed 's|<vane:event name="check.passed">|<vane:event name="check.passed" vane:implements="req-4">|' flag.scxml > traced.scxml
$ sxml validate --schema=scxml.xsd traced.scxml
traced.scxml:10:37: cvc-complex-type.3.2.2: attribute 'vane:implements' is not allowed on element 'vane:event'
$ sxml validate --schema=vane-1.1.xsd --schema=scxml.xsd traced.scxml; echo "exit status $?"
exit status 0

Changing a schema: xs:override

vane-1.1.xsd doesn't copy vane-data.xsd: it names it in xs:override, and replaces two of its components, the events and status elements, keeping the rest. Every schema document that includes or imports the overridden one sees the replacements, so scxml.xsd's import of vane-data.xsd now finds the new events.

scxml.xsd itself is simplified in one place: its comment says that a transition has at most one target. SCXML allows a list, target="motor light", to enter several states at once. This machine has one:

two-targets.scxml:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- A transition with two targets: SCXML allows a list of states. -->
<scxml xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml"
       version="1.0" name="test_rig" initial="idle">
  <state id="idle">
    <transition event="test.start" target="motor light"/>
  </state>
  <state id="motor">
    <transition event="test.stop" target="idle"/>
  </state>
  <state id="light"/>
</scxml>

scxml-targets.xsd overrides the transition type, with a list type for the target. That is not enough: a keyref compares a field's whole value with each key, and the list motor light is no state's id. The keyref can't check each item of a list, so the override replaces the scxml element too, and an assertion takes the keyref's place:

scxml-targets.xsd:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- SCXML's full rule for targets: a transition may name several
     states, as a list. scxml.xsd overridden: the transition type and the
