archived is in the top layer and stable in the next; checking is below stable, and rolling-out and paused share the bottom layer. The layers between them hold the labels of the transitions, each beside its arrow. The transitions that stay are loops:

$ grep -A3 'id="edge-stable-stable"' flag.svg
  <g class="edge" id="edge-stable-stable">
    <path d="M 282 136 L 298 136 L 298 152 L 282 152" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>
    <text x="304" y="148">status.request</text>
  </g>

Drawing a change

machine-diagram.xq takes an optional parameter, before: the file of an earlier version of the machine. States and edges that the earlier version doesn't have get the class added, and the ones only the earlier version has get removed. draw.xqm copies the classes to the SVG groups, and its style draws added parts in green and removed parts dashed in red. The fixed machine against the seed:

$ sxml xquery --context-item=flag-fixed.scxml --param=before=flag.scxml machine-diagram.xq \
  | sxml xquery --context-item=- --output=changes.svg --expression='
      import module namespace draw = "urn:example:draw" at "draw.xqm";
      declare option output:indent "yes";
      draw:svg(/diagram)'
$ sxml xpath --context-item=changes.svg '//*:g[contains-token(@class, "added")] ! `{@id}: {*:text}`'
"edge-stable-archived: flag.archived"
"edge-paused-archived: flag.archived"

The two new transitions on flag.archived are the change, and they move archived to the bottom: something now leads to it, from stable and from paused, so it goes in the layer below them, and its own transition to stable runs up. The new declaration of flag.evaluated and the new vane:implements change no state or transition, so the drawing doesn't show them; the page of Documenting the Machine in XHTML does.

The same mechanism, a diagram description with classes drawn by one module, draws the diff of call chains in Comparing Two Versions and the diff of traces in Rendering the Diff.

Parsing Text with Invisible XML

A great deal of data is text with a structure that only a person can see: a log line, a date written in words, a configuration file, a small language of your own. Invisible XML (iXML) makes that structure visible. You describe the text with a grammar, and the grammar turns every text it describes into an XML document, which the XPath, XQuery and XSLT of the earlier parts can query and transform. The examples of this part are in docs/book/examples/ixml.

A first grammar

This grammar describes a date such as 2026-10-20:

date.ixml:

date: year, -"-", month, -"-", day.
year: digit, digit, digit, digit.
month: digit, digit.
day: digit, digit.
-digit: ["0"-"9"].

Each rule names a part of the text and says what it is made of, in order, separated by commas: a date is a year, a hyphen, a month, a hyphen and a day. A quoted string matches itself, and ["0"-"9"] matches one character in a range. The first rule describes the whole text.

The function invisible-xml compiles a grammar into a parser, which is itself a function: give it a text, and it returns a document.

$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'invisible-xml(unparsed-text("date.ixml"))("2026-10-20")'
<date><year>2026</year><month>10</month><day>20</day></date>

Every rule became an element, except digit: the - before its name hides it, so its characters go straight into the element around it. The hyphens between the parts are hidden too, by the - before each "-". Without the marks, every digit would be an element of its own and the hyphens would be text.

Compile once, parse many times

Compiling a grammar takes more work than parsing one short text with it. Keep the parser in a variable and call it for every text:

$ sxml xpath 'let $parse := invisible-xml(unparsed-text("date.ixml")) for $text in ("2026-10-20", "1999-12-31") return $parse($text)/date/year/string()'
"2026"
"1999"

The result of the parser is a document node, so $parse($text)/date is its document element, and every path, function and FLWOR expression works on it.

Running a grammar from the command line

The sxml command has no command of its own for Invisible XML: the xquery command runs it, with the grammar and the input as parameters. This query, kept in a file, works for any grammar and any input:

ixml.xq:

(: Parses the file $input with the Invisible XML grammar in the file
   $grammar and writes the XML, indented. :)
declare option output:indent "yes";
declare variable $grammar external;
declare variable $input external;
invisible-xml(unparsed-text($grammar))(unparsed-text($input))

$ sxml xquery --param=grammar=date.ixml --param=input=today.txt ixml.xq
<failed xmlns:ixml="http://invisiblexml.org/NS" ixml:state="failed">
  <line>1</line>
  <column>11</column>
  <position>11</position>
  <unexpected>#a</unexpected>
</failed>

The parse failed. today.txt holds the date and a line feed, as text files do, and the grammar says nothing about a line feed: after the day, at column 11, it expected the end of the text and found #a, the line feed. A failed parse is not an error. The parser returns a document whose element is failed, with the attribute ixml:state="failed", and says where the parse stopped; When a Parse Fails has more on reading it.

The grammar can allow the line feed. dates.ixml in the next chapter's tasks reads a date on each line; here it reads dates.txt:

$ sxml xquery --param=grammar=dates.ixml --param=input=dates.txt ixml.xq
<dates>
  <date>
    <year>2026</year>
    <month>10</month>
    <day>20</day>
  </date>
  <date>
    <day>20</day>
    <month>10</month>
    <year>2026</year>
  </date>
  <date>
    <month>07</month>
    <day>04</day>
    <year>1976</year>
  </date>
  <date>
    <day>01</day>
    <month>05</month>
    <year>1886</year>
  </date>
</dates>

To keep the result, add --output=FILE; to use it at once, put the parse in a query of its own, as the tasks in this part do.

Errors or documents

By default a text that does not match gives the failed document, so a query can look at it and go on. With the option fail-on-error, the parser raises the error FOIX0002 instead:

$ sxml xpath 'invisible-xml(unparsed-text("date.ixml"), {"fail-on-error": true()})("2026-1-20")'
expression:1:1: err:FOIX0002: The input does not match the grammar, and fail-on-error is true (F&O 4.0, fn:invisible-xml)

A grammar that is not a grammar is always an error, FOIX0001; the errors chapter shows the common ones.

A grammar is XML too

Called without a grammar, invisible-xml returns the parser of iXML grammars themselves. Its result is the grammar in its XML form, which the specification defines and which invisible-xml accepts as well:

$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'invisible-xml()("greeting: ""hello"".")'
<ixml><rule name="greeting"><alt><literal string="hello"/></alt></rule></ixml>
$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'invisible-xml(invisible-xml()("greeting: ""hello"".")/ixml)("hello")'
<greeting>hello</greeting>

A program can therefore read a grammar, change it with XQuery or XSLT, and compile the changed grammar: add a rule, rename an element, or build a grammar from a table.

In this part

  • Writing Grammars: rules, characters, repetition, marks, attributes, insertions, renaming, and what an ambiguous grammar does.
  • Real Tasks: log files, semicolon-separated values, dates in many forms, a small programming language, and Markdown-like text.
  • When a Parse Fails: the failed document, grammar errors, and how to fix a grammar.
  • Invisible XML Performance: how large an input can be, and which grammars parse in time proportional to the input.

sxml implements the Invisible XML Specification 1.0 with its errata and the renaming of the Community Group's draft of version 1.1, and fn:invisible-xml of F&O 4.0. It passes every test of the iXML community test suite that it runs (Appendix B).

Writing Grammars

A grammar is a list of rules. This chapter goes through everything a rule can say, with a small grammar for each feature. All the grammars are files in docs/book/examples/ixml.

Rules and alternatives

A rule is a name, a colon (or =), one or more alternatives and a full stop. Alternatives are separated by ; (or |), and the parts of an alternative by commas:

greeting.ixml:

greeting: hello, -", ", name, -"!".
hello: "Hello"; "Hi".
name: letter+.
-letter: ["A"-"Z"; "a"-"z"].

$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'invisible-xml(unparsed-text("greeting.ixml"))("Hello, World!")'
<greeting><hello>Hello</hello><name>World</name></greeting>
$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'invisible-xml(unparsed-text("greeting.ixml"))("Hi, Ada!")'
<greeting><hello>Hi</hello><name>Ada</name></greeting>

Spaces and line breaks between the parts of a rule do not matter, and text in braces, {like this}, is a comment. An alternative may be empty: sign: "-"; . is a minus sign or nothing.

Characters

The smallest parts of a grammar match single characters:

NotationMatches
"abc" or 'abc'the characters a, b and c, in that order; "" inside "..." is one quote
#a, #20ACthe one character with that hexadecimal code point: line feed, the euro sign
["a"-"z"; "_"; #9]one character of a set: here a letter from a to z, an underscore or a tab
~["0"-"9"]one character that is not in the set
[L], [Nd], [Lu; Ll]one character of a Unicode general category: any letter, a decimal digit, an upper- or lowercase letter

fields.ixml reads a word in any script, a number with an optional fraction, and a quoted text, separated by tabs:

fields.ixml:

{A word, a number and a quoted text, separated by tabs.}
fields: word, -#9, number, -#9, quoted.
word: [L]+.
number: ["0"-"9"]+, (".", ["0"-"9"]+)?.
quoted: -'"', ~['"']*, -'"'.

$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'invisible-xml(unparsed-text("fields.ixml"))(unparsed-text("fields.txt"))'
<fields><word>Zürich</word><number>42.5</number><quoted>two words</quoted></fields>

sxml's categories are those of Unicode 16.0, the version its regular expressions use.

Repetition and options

After any part:

  • ? makes it optional;
  • * repeats it zero or more times, + one or more times;
  • **sep and ++sep repeat it with sep between the repetitions, so item++"," is one or more items separated by commas.

Parentheses group parts into one: ("+"; "-")? is an optional sign.

list.ixml:

list: -"[", s, item**(-",", s), s, -"]".
item: ["0"-"9"]+.
-s: -" "*.

$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'invisible-xml(unparsed-text("list.ixml"))("[1, 22,333 ]")'
<list><item>1</item><item>22</item><item>333</item></list>
$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'invisible-xml(unparsed-text("list.ixml"))("[]")'
<list/>

Elements, attributes and hidden parts

A mark before a name says what the part becomes in the XML:

  • ^ (the default): an element;
  • @: an attribute, which goes on the nearest element around it;
  • -: nothing of its own; its content goes into the element around it.

A mark on a rule applies wherever the rule is used. A mark where a name is used applies there only and wins over the rule's. Strings and character sets take - too, which drops their characters, as the hyphens of the date did.

person.ixml:

person: name, -", ", age, -", ", city.
name: first, -" ", last.
@first: [L]+.
@last: [L]+.
@age: ["0"-"9"]+.
-city: [L]+.

$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'invisible-xml(unparsed-text("person.ixml"))("Ada Lovelace, 36, London")'
<person age="36"><name first="Ada" last="Lovelace"/>London</person>

first and last are attributes of name, the element they are in; age is an attribute of person. city is hidden, so its text is part of person's content. An attribute's value is all the text inside it: marks inside an attribute only drop characters.

Insertions

+"text" adds text to the XML that is not in the input. An insertion matches nothing, so it can go anywhere in an alternative:

temperature.ixml:

temperature: number, unit.
number: ["0"-"9"]+.
unit: -"C", +"celsius"; -"F", +"fahrenheit".

$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'invisible-xml(unparsed-text("temperature.ixml"))("21C")'
<temperature><number>21</number><unit>celsius</unit></temperature>

The input says C; the XML says celsius. Insertions are how a grammar fills in what the text leaves out, such as the leading zero of a month in the dates task.

Renaming

A rule describes one form of text, and its name is the element's name. Sometimes one form appears in two roles: the two numbers of a range are both numbers, but one is the low end and one the high end. > gives a part another name in the XML:

range.ixml:

ixml version "1.1".
range: number>low, -"..", number>high.
number: ["0"-"9"]+.

$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'invisible-xml(unparsed-text("range.ixml"))("1..10")'
<range><low>1</low><high>10</high></range>

> can also follow a rule's name, to rename it everywhere. Renaming is part of version 1.1 of the specification, so the grammar starts with ixml version "1.1".; sxml reads the rest of a 1.0 grammar the same way.

Ambiguous grammars

A grammar is ambiguous when it describes a text in more than one way. This grammar reads a name as a first and a last part, but either part may contain spaces:

name.ixml:

name: first, -" ", last.
first: [L; " "]+.
last: [L; " "]+.

$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'invisible-xml(unparsed-text("name.ixml"))("Mary Ann Smith")'
<name xmlns:ixml="http://invisiblexml.org/NS" ixml:state="ambiguous"><first>Mary</first><last>Ann Smith</last></name>

"Mary" and "Ann Smith" is one way to read the text; "Mary Ann" and "Smith" is another. An ambiguous parse is not an error: the parser returns one of the ways and marks the document element with ixml:state="ambiguous". Which way it picks is not specified, so a query must not depend on it. The attribute is in the namespace http://invisiblexml.org/NS, so a query tests it as @Q{http://invisiblexml.org/NS}state or @*:state.

Ambiguity is almost always a mistake in the grammar. Ask where a part can end: here, at any space. The fix is to say which part may contain spaces. If the last name is one word, the reading is unique:

$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'invisible-xml(replace(unparsed-text("name.ixml"), "last: \[L; "" ""\]\+", "last: [L]+"))("Mary Ann Smith")'
<name><first>Mary Ann</first><last>Smith</last></name>

(The expression changes the grammar's text before compiling it, a quick way to try a fix.) Three more causes of ambiguity are common: two repetitions next to each other that can both take the same character ("x"*, "x"*); an optional part next to a repetition that can stand for it; and a separator that a field may also contain. The tasks and errors chapters show each.

The prolog

A grammar may start with ixml version "1.0". or ixml version "1.1".. sxml reads both versions. For any other version it parses with its own and marks the result with ixml:state="version-mismatch", as the specification asks.

Real Tasks

This chapter solves six everyday problems with a grammar each: a log file, semicolon-separated values, dates written in several ways, a small programming language, Markdown-like text, and the grammar inside a specification. Every solution has two parts, a grammar that turns the text into XML and a query that uses the XML.

Log files

log.ixml:

log: line++-#a, -#a?.
line: date, -" ", time, -" ", level, -" ", message.
@date: digit, digit, digit, digit, "-", digit, digit, "-", digit, digit.
@time: digit, digit, ":", digit, digit, ":", digit, digit.
@level: "INFO"; "WARN"; "ERROR".
message: ~[#a]*.
-digit: ["0"-"9"].

A log is lines separated by line feeds, with an optional line feed at the end (-#a?). The date, time and level become attributes of their line, and message takes everything up to the end of the line, ~[#a]*. The grammar describes this log:

app.log:

2026-10-20 09:15:02 INFO server started
2026-10-20 09:17:45 WARN disk 91% full
2026-10-20 09:21:13 ERROR disk full
2026-10-20 09:21:14 INFO cleanup started
2026-10-20 09:24:50 INFO cleanup done
2026-10-20 10:02:31 ERROR connection refused

Once the log is a document, grouping and filtering are ordinary XQuery:

levels.xq:

(: Counts the lines of each level in app.log and lists the errors. :)
let $parse := invisible-xml(unparsed-text("log.ixml"))
let $log := $parse(unparsed-text("app.log"))
return string-join((
  for $line in $log//line
  group by $level := $line/@level
  order by count($line) descending, $level
  return `{$level}: {count($line)}`,
  $log//line[@level = "ERROR"] ! `{@time} {message}`
), "&#10;")

$ sxml xquery --method=text levels.xq
INFO: 3
ERROR: 2
WARN: 1
09:21:13 disk full
10:02:31 connection refused

Real logs are rarely this tidy. Two habits keep the grammar useful: make the part you care about precise (the date, the level) and let the rest be "anything up to the end of the line", and test the grammar on the oddest lines first.

Semicolon-separated values

For plain CSV, parse-csv (JSON, CSV, HTML and Invisible XML) is quicker. A grammar earns its place when the format is a variant that a CSV parser does not know. This one separates fields with semicolons and lets a quoted field hold semicolons and doubled quotes:

prices.ixml:

{Semicolon-separated values: a header line, then rows. A field in
 double quotes may hold semicolons; "" in it is one quote.}
table: header, -#a, (row, -#a)+.
header: field++-";".
row: field++-";".
field: quoted; plain.
-plain: ~[";"; '"'; #a]*.
-quoted: -'"', (~['"']; -'"', '"')*, -'"'.

prices.txt:

item;price;note
Coffee;3.50;"hot; large"
Tea;2.10;
"Juice ""fresh""";4.20;cold

$ sxml xquery --param=grammar=prices.ixml --param=input=prices.txt ixml.xq
<table>
  <header>
    <field>item</field>
    <field>price</field>
    <field>note</field>
  </header>
  <row>
    <field>Coffee</field>
    <field>3.50</field>
    <field>hot; large</field>
  </row>
  <row>
    <field>Tea</field>
    <field>2.10</field>
    <field/>
  </row>
  <row>
    <field>Juice "fresh"</field>
    <field>4.20</field>
    <field>cold</field>
  </row>
</table>

Note the first rule: every row ends with a line feed, (row, -#a)+. A first try, row++-#a, -#a?, reads the last line feed in two ways, as the end of the file or as a separator before a row with one empty field, and the result is ambiguous. Saying exactly where each line feed belongs removes the doubt.

From the table to JSON is one query, with the header naming the fields:

prices-json.xq:

(: Turns prices.txt into JSON: one object per row, keyed by the header. :)
declare option output:method "json";
declare option output:indent "yes";
let $table := invisible-xml(unparsed-text("prices.ixml"))(unparsed-text("prices.txt"))
let $names := $table//header/field ! string()
return array {
  for $row in $table//row
  return map:merge(
    for $field at $position in $row/field
    return map:entry($names[$position],
      if ($field castable as xs:decimal) then xs:decimal($field) else string($field)))
}

$ sxml xquery prices-json.xq
[
  {
    "item": "Coffee",
    "price": 3.5,
    "note": "hot; large"
  },
  {
    "item": "Tea",
    "price": 2.1,
    "note": ""
  },
  {
    "item": "Juice \"fresh\"",
    "price": 4.2,
    "note": "cold"
  }
]

Dates

People write dates in many ways. One grammar can read several forms and give them all the same XML, so the query after it sees one form only:

dates.ixml:

ixml version "1.1".
{Dates in three forms, one per line, all made into year, month and day.}
dates: (date, -#a)+.
date: iso; written; american.
-iso: year, -"-", month, -"-", day.
-written: day, -" ", month-name, -" ", year.
-american: month, -"/", day, -"/", year.
year: digit, digit, digit, digit.
month: digit, digit; +"0", digit.
day: digit, digit; +"0", digit.
month-name>month:
    -"January", +"01"; -"February", +"02"; -"March", +"03";
    -"April", +"04"; -"May", +"05"; -"June", +"06";
    -"July", +"07"; -"August", +"08"; -"September", +"09";
    -"October", +"10"; -"November", +"11"; -"December", +"12".
-digit: ["0"-"9"].

dates.txt:

2026-10-20
20 October 2026
7/4/1976
1 May 1886

Three features do the work. The three forms are hidden alternatives of date, so each gives year, month and day directly. The month names are hidden strings with an insertion of the month's number, and >month renames month-name to month, so a written month and a numbered one are the same element. And +"0", digit pads a one-digit day or month. The result is in the first chapter; here a query sorts the dates:

sort-dates.xq:

(: Reads dates.txt as xs:date values and lists them in order. :)
let $dates := invisible-xml(unparsed-text("dates.ixml"))(unparsed-text("dates.txt"))
for $date in $dates//date
let $value := xs:date(`{$date/year}-{$date/month}-{$date/day}`)
order by $value
return format-date($value, "[D] [MNn] [Y], a [FNn]")

$ sxml xquery --method=adaptive sort-dates.xq
"1 May 1886, a Saturday"
"4 July 1976, a Sunday"
"20 October 2026, a Tuesday"
"20 October 2026, a Tuesday"

The first and second lines of dates.txt were the same day in two forms.

A small programming language

A grammar can describe a language with statements, names and expressions. In this one, let names a value, print prints one, and * and / bind tighter than + and -:

calc.ixml:

ixml version "1.1".
{A small language: statements end with ";", "let" names a value,
 "print" prints one. Products bind tighter than sums.}
program: s, (statement, s, -";", s)*.
-statement: let; print.
let: -"let", S, @name, s, -"=", s, expression.
print: -"print", S, expression.
-expression: sum; -term.
sum: expression, s, @add>op, s, term.
-term: product; -factor.
product: term, s, @multiply>op, s, factor.
-factor: number; variable; -"(", s, expression, s, -")".
number: ["0"-"9"]+.
variable: @name.
@name: ["a"-"z"]+.
add: ["+-"].
multiply: ["*/"].
-s: -[" "; #a]*.
-S: -[" "; #a]+.

Precedence comes from the shape of the rules: a sum adds terms, a term is a product or a factor, and a product multiplies factors, so 1 + 2 * 3 can only be read with the product inside the sum. Because sum begins with expression and product with term, both are left-recursive, and 8 - 2 - 1 groups as (8 - 2) - 1. @add>op and @multiply>op make both kinds of operator an attribute op. s is optional space and S required space.

area.calc:

let width = 6;
let height = 7;
print width * height;
print (width + height) * 2;

$ sxml xquery --param=grammar=calc.ixml --param=input=area.calc ixml.xq
<program>
  <let name="width">
    <number>6</number>
  </let>
  <let name="height">
    <number>7</number>
  </let>
  <print>
    <product op="*">
      <variable name="width"/>
      <variable name="height"/>
    </product>
  </print>
  <print>
    <product op="*">
      <sum op="+">
        <variable name="width"/>
        <variable name="height"/>
      </sum>
      <number>2</number>
    </product>
  </print>
</program>

The XML is the program's syntax tree, and an interpreter is a recursive function over it:

run.xq:

(: Runs a program of the small language of calc.ixml, in the file $file:
   each print statement gives one integer. :)
declare variable $file external;

declare function local:value($node as element(), $names as map(*)) as xs:integer {
  typeswitch ($node)
    case element(number) return xs:integer($node)
    case element(variable) return $names(string($node/@name))
    default return
      let $left := local:value($node/*[1], $names)
      let $right := local:value($node/*[2], $names)
      return switch (string($node/@op))
        case "+" return $left + $right
        case "-" return $left - $right
        case "*" return $left * $right
        default return $left idiv $right
};

declare function local:run($statements as element()*, $names as map(*)) as xs:integer* {
  if (empty($statements)) then () else
  let $statement := head($statements)
  return
    if ($statement instance of element(let)) then
      local:run(tail($statements),
        map:put($names, string($statement/@name), local:value($statement/*, $names)))
    else (
      local:value($statement/*, $names),
      local:run(tail($statements), $names)
    )
};

let $program := invisible-xml(unparsed-text("calc.ixml"))(unparsed-text($file))
return local:run($program/program/*, {})

$ sxml xquery --method=adaptive --param=file=area.calc run.xq
42
26

The same tree could be checked for names used before they are set, pretty-printed, or translated into another language with XSLT.

Markdown-like text

The last grammar reads a little of Markdown: headings, lists and paragraphs separated by blank lines, with emphasis and code inside. Its names are HTML's, so the XML it makes is HTML:

markdown.ixml:

ixml version "1.1".
{A little Markdown: headings, lists and paragraphs, separated by blank
 lines, with *emphasis* and `code` inside. The names are HTML's.}
document>body: block++(-#a, -#a+), -#a*.
-block: h1; h2; ul; p.
h1: -"# ", inline.
h2: -"## ", inline.
ul: li++-#a.
li: -"- ", inline.
p: line++(-#a, +" ").
-line: ~["#-*`"; #a], inline?.
-inline: (char; em; code)+.
-char: ~["*`"; #a].
em: -"*", ~["*"; #a]+, -"*".
code: -"`", ~["`"; #a]+, -"`".

notes.md:

# Release notes

Version 2 reads *Invisible XML* grammars
and parses `CSV` files.

## Changes

- faster parsing
- better *error* messages

$ sxml xquery --param=grammar=markdown.ixml --param=input=notes.md ixml.xq
<body>
  <h1>Release notes</h1>
  <p>Version 2 reads <em>Invisible XML</em> grammars and parses <code>CSV</code> files.</p>
  <h2>Changes</h2>
  <ul>
    <li>faster parsing</li>
    <li>better <em>error</em> messages</li>
  </ul>
</body>

Two details make this grammar unambiguous. The characters of a line are single hidden characters, -char, so a run of them is one text node and there is only one way to split it. And a paragraph line may not start with # or -, so a heading or a list item can never also be read as a paragraph. The line feed inside a paragraph becomes a space with -#a, +" ".

The grammar in a specification

Specifications define their syntax in ABNF (RFC 5234), and the grammar sits in the document as text. The Vane draft (Transforming with XSLT and the chapters before it use it) has the syntax of its messages in a sourcecode element; vane.xml here is a link to the draft:

$ sxml xpath --context-item=vane.xml --method=text '//sourcecode[@type = "abnf"]'

message        = rollout-update / kill-update / status-request
rollout-update = "ROLLOUT" SP flag-key SP percentage CRLF
kill-update    = "KILL" SP flag-key CRLF
status-request = "STATUS" SP flag-key CRLF
flag-key       = 1*32(ALPHA / DIGIT / "-")
percentage     = 1*3DIGIT

To a program, those lines are one string. A small grammar for ABNF rules turns them into XML: rule names, alternatives separated by /, sequences of elements, repetitions such as 1*32 and 1*3, quoted strings and groups in parentheses:

abnf.ixml:

ixml version "1.1".
{The rules of ABNF (RFC 5234): one rule on each line, a name, "=" and
 alternatives separated by "/", each a sequence of elements, each
 element with an optional repetition.}
rules: -#a*, rule++(-#a+), -#a*.
rule: @name, s, -"=", s, alternatives.
-alternatives: alternative++(s, -"/", s).
alternative: element++S.
-element: repeat; -item.
repeat: (@min, -"*", @max?; -"*", @max; @min), -item.
-item: ref; string; group.
ref: @name.
string: -'"', ~['"']*, -'"'.
group: -"(", s, alternatives, s, -")".
@name: ["A"-"Z"; "a"-"z"], ["A"-"Z"; "a"-"z"; "0"-"9"; "-"]*.
@min: ["0"-"9"]+.
@max: ["0"-"9"]+.
-s: -" "*.
-S: -" "+.

rule++(-#a+) is one or more rules separated by line feeds, and element++S one or more elements separated by spaces. A repetition has a minimum, a maximum or both around the *, or just a number, which ABNF reads as an exact count. XPath extracts the text, and the grammar parses it:

$ sxml xquery --context-item=vane.xml --expression='declare option output:indent "yes"; invisible-xml(unparsed-text("abnf.ixml"))(string(//sourcecode[@type = "abnf"]))/rules/rule[@name = ("flag-key", "percentage")]'
<rule name="flag-key">
  <alternative>
    <repeat min="1" max="32">
      <group>
        <alternative>
          <ref name="ALPHA"/>
        </alternative>
        <alternative>
          <ref name="DIGIT"/>
        </alternative>
        <alternative>
          <string>-</string>
        </alternative>
      </group>
    </repeat>
  </alternative>
</rule>
<rule name="percentage">
  <alternative>
    <repeat min="1" max="3">
      <ref name="DIGIT"/>
    </repeat>
  </alternative>
</rule>

Once the grammar is XML, questions about it are paths. Which rules does each rule use, and which names does the draft use without defining them?

$ sxml xquery --context-item=vane.xml --method=adaptive --expression='
    let $rules := invisible-xml(unparsed-text("abnf.ixml"))(string(//sourcecode[@type = "abnf"]))//rule
    return (
      for $rule in $rules
      return `{$rule/@name} uses {string-join(distinct-values($rule//ref/@name), ", ")}`,
      `undefined: {string-join(distinct-values($rules//ref/@name[not(. = $rules/@name)]), ", ")}`
    )'
"message uses rollout-update, kill-update, status-request"
"rollout-update uses SP, flag-key, percentage, CRLF"
"kill-update uses SP, flag-key, CRLF"
"status-request uses SP, flag-key, CRLF"
"flag-key uses ALPHA, DIGIT"
"percentage uses DIGIT"
"undefined: SP, CRLF, ALPHA, DIGIT"

The four undefined names are the core rules of RFC 5234 (Appendix B.1), which every ABNF grammar may use, so the draft is complete. A misspelled rule name, flag_key for flag-key, would show up in the same list, and a broken rule fails to parse with the line and column of the mistake:

$ sxml xpath 'invisible-xml(unparsed-text("abnf.ixml"))("limit = percentage / ")'
<failed xmlns:ixml="http://invisiblexml.org/NS" ixml:state="failed"><line>1</line><column>22</column><position>22</position><end-of-input/><expected>"("</expected><expected>"*"</expected><expected>#20</expected><expected>'"'</expected><expected>["0"-"9"]</expected><expected>["A"-"Z"; "a"-"z"]</expected></failed>

When a Parse Fails

Two things can go wrong: the input does not match the grammar, or the grammar itself is wrong. The first gives a document that says where the parse stopped; the second is an error, FOIX0001, that says what is wrong with the grammar and where. This chapter shows how to read both and how to fix the grammar.

Reading a failed parse

date.ixml wants two digits for the month:

$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'invisible-xml(unparsed-text("date.ixml"))("2026-1-20")'
<failed xmlns:ixml="http://invisiblexml.org/NS" ixml:state="failed"><line>1</line><column>7</column><position>7</position><unexpected>"-"</unexpected><expected>["0"-"9"]</expected></failed>

The failed element says:

  • line and column: where the parse stopped, counting from 1, and position, the same place counted in characters from the start of the input;
  • unexpected: the character found there, written as the grammar would write it, or end-of-input when the input ended too soon;
  • expected: each character set that the grammar could have read at that place, once each, in the grammar's notation and in code-point order.

The parse reads as far as any reading of the input can go, so the place it stops is the first character that no reading can take. The mistake is often a little before it. Here the parser read 2026-1 as the start of a month and stopped at the hyphen, where it wanted the month's second digit.

A missing quote is a common case. The third line of this file opens a quoted field and never closes it:

bad-prices.txt:

item;price;note
Coffee;3.50;"hot; large"
Tea;2.10;"strong

$ sxml xquery --param=grammar=prices.ixml --param=input=bad-prices.txt ixml.xq
<failed xmlns:ixml="http://invisiblexml.org/NS" ixml:state="failed">
  <line>4</line>
  <column>1</column>
  <position>59</position>
  <end-of-input/>
  <expected>'"'</expected>
  <expected>~['"']</expected>
</failed>

The parse reached the end of the input inside the quoted field, which may hold line feeds, and still wanted a quote, or more of the field: ~['"'] is any character but a quote. The failure is reported at the end, but the cause is the quote on line 3.

Failures in a query

The failed document is a document like any other, so a query can test for it, exists($result/failed) or $result/*/@*:state = "failed", and read its parts:

$ sxml xpath 'invisible-xml(unparsed-text("date.ixml"))("2026-1-20")/failed/(line, column) ! string()'
"1"
"7"

With fail-on-error, a failed parse raises FOIX0002, which try and catch handle like any other error. This query reports every line of a file that is not a date, and goes on after each:

check-dates.xq:

(: Reads each line of the file $file as a date and reports the lines that
   are not dates, instead of stopping at the first. :)
declare variable $file external;
let $parse := invisible-xml(unparsed-text("date.ixml"), {"fail-on-error": true()})
return string-join(
  for $line at $number in unparsed-text-lines($file)
  return try {
    $parse($line) ! ()
  } catch err:FOIX0002 {
    `line {$number}: {$line} is not a date`
  },
  "&#10;")

$ sxml xquery --method=text --param=file=some-dates.txt check-dates.xq
line 2: 2026-1-20 is not a date
line 4: yesterday is not a date

Mistakes in grammars

A grammar that does not follow the rules of iXML raises FOIX0001 when invisible-xml compiles it, and the description says what is wrong.

A missing full stop is the most common mistake. Here line 3 does not end with one:

unfinished.ixml:

date: year, -"-", month, -"-", day.
year: digit, digit, digit, digit.
month: digit, digit
day: digit, digit.
-digit: ["0"-"9"].

$ sxml xpath 'invisible-xml(unparsed-text("unfinished.ixml"))'
expression:1:1: err:FOIX0001: The grammar does not match the ixml grammar at line 4, column 1, at "d" (F&O 4.0, fn:invisible-xml)

The grammar is read like any input, so the place is where reading stopped, as in a failed document: line 3 could go on (digit, digit could be followed by , more or by ;), and only day on line 4 shows that it did not. Look just before the place for the missing ., , or quote.

A name used but not defined, usually a typing mistake, is the error S02 of the specification:

typo.ixml:

date: year, -"-", month, -"-", day.
year: digit, digit, digit, digit.
month: digit, digit.
day: digti, digit.
-digit: ["0"-"9"].

$ sxml xpath 'invisible-xml(unparsed-text("typo.ixml"))'
expression:1:1: err:FOIX0001: iXML S02: the grammar uses the nonterminal digti, which no rule defines

Two rules for one name is S03. One rule with two alternatives says the same, and that is what the author meant:

dup.ixml:

date: year, -"-", month, -"-", day.
year: digit, digit, digit, digit.
month: digit, digit.
day: digit, digit.
date: day, -".", month, -".", year.
-digit: ["0"-"9"].

$ sxml xpath 'invisible-xml(unparsed-text("dup.ixml"))'
expression:1:1: err:FOIX0001: iXML S03: the grammar has more than one rule for date

The other grammar errors are about characters:

ErrorCauseExample
S07a hexadecimal character beyond the Unicode range#110000
S08a hexadecimal character that is a noncharacter or a surrogate#FFFF, #D800
S09a range whose first character comes after its last["z"-"a"]
S10a class that is not a Unicode general category[Xx]

Grammars that make bad XML

Some grammars are correct but make XML that cannot exist for some inputs, for example an element with two attributes of one name. The parse succeeds, but no document can hold its result, so the parser raises FOIX0002 whatever fail-on-error says:

twice.ixml:

entry: @key, -"=", @key.
key: ["a"-"z"]+.

$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'invisible-xml(unparsed-text("twice.ixml"))("a=b")'
expression:1:1: err:FOIX0002: iXML D02: the parse puts two attributes named key on the element entry

Rename one of them (@key>value, version 1.1) or make the second an element. The specification's other errors of this kind:

ErrorCause
D03a name that is not an XML name, such as one from renaming
D04a character that XML does not allow, such as one an insertion +#1 adds
D05an attribute as the root of the document: the first rule is marked @
D06not exactly one element at the top: the first rule is hidden and gives text, or several elements
D07an attribute named xmlns

Ambiguity

An ambiguous grammar is not an error, but it is a warning sign: the document says ixml:state="ambiguous", and the parser has picked one reading of several (Writing Grammars). To find the cause, shorten the input until the attribute goes away: the last part you removed holds the ambiguity. Then look for a place where two parts of the grammar can both take the same characters: two repetitions side by side, an optional part beside a repetition, a separator that a field may also contain, or a line feed that two rules both want, as in the first try of the semicolon grammar.

A checklist

When a grammar does not do what you expect:

  1. Start from the smallest input that shows the problem.
  2. Remove the - marks for a moment: every hidden rule and string then shows in the XML, and you see how the input was read.
  3. Check the ends: the start of the first rule and the end of the input, which often has a line feed the grammar does not mention.
  4. For an ambiguous result, find the two readings, then say in the grammar which one you mean.
  5. Compile the grammar once and keep the parser: errors in the grammar show at once, before any input is read.

Invisible XML Performance

An iXML grammar can describe any context-free language, and a parser for all of them must be able to keep many readings of the input open at once. That is more work than a parser made for one fixed language, such as sxml's XML parser, does. This chapter says how much work, which grammars sxml parses in time proportional to the input, and how to write grammars that stay fast on inputs of many megabytes.

What to expect

The times below are processor seconds of a release build on one core of an ordinary Linux machine, for the whole sxml command: starting, reading the input, parsing, and building the XML tree. Memory is the most memory the process held, about 10 MB of it the program itself; per MB is how much more each further megabyte of input takes, the memory the parse and its XML really cost. The benchmark suite tests/bench/run-ixml-bench.py measures them, and its --check option fails when a number is worse than this chapter says (--large adds the 100 MB log).

GrammarInputTimeMemoryPer MB
the log of Real Tasks1 MB, 16,000 linesunder 0.2 sunder 60 MBunder 20 MB
semicolon-separated values1 MB, 34,000 rowsunder 0.4 sunder 100 MBunder 60 MB
the small programming language1 MB, 43,000 statementsunder 0.6 sunder 150 MBunder 100 MB
Markdown-like text1 MB, 8,700 sectionsunder 0.4 sunder 120 MBunder 80 MB
a right-recursive list1 MB, 159,000 numbersunder 0.4 sunder 80 MBunder 40 MB
brackets nested 100,000 deep200 KBunder 0.2 sunder 100 MB
a grammar of 5,800 rules, compiled200 KBunder 0.5 sunder 200 MB
the ambiguous sum below2,000 charactersunder 2 sunder 200 MB
the log10 MB, 160,000 linesunder 1.5 sunder 250 MBunder 20 MB
the log100 MB, 1,600,000 linesunder 15 sunder 2,000 MBunder 20 MB

For every grammar in the table but the ambiguous sum, four times the input takes about four times as long and four times the memory: the parser is linear on them. A large input costs what its XML costs and little more. The XML tree of the log, an element and three attributes for each line and the messages as text, takes about 9 bytes for each character of the log; the parse adds about one more, and lets go of all of it before the query goes on.

A 1 MB log, made by a query:

make-log.xq:

(: Writes a log of $lines lines in the format of log.ixml. :)
declare variable $lines external;
string-join(
  for $number in 1 to xs:integer($lines)
  let $time := xs:time("00:00:00") + xs:dayTimeDuration("PT1S") * ($number mod 86400)
  let $level := ("INFO", "WARN", "ERROR")[$number mod 3 + 1]
  return `2026-10-20 {$time} {$level} message {$number}`,
  "&#10;"
)

$ sxml xquery --method=text --param=lines=25000 --output=big.log make-log.xq
$ sxml xpath 'string-length(unparsed-text("big.log"))'
972227
$ sxml xquery --method=text --param=file=big.log count-levels.xq
ERROR 8333
INFO 8333
WARN 8334

count-levels.xq is the grouping query of the log task, reading the file that $file names.

Which grammars are linear

sxml parses with Earley's algorithm, which reads the input once, from left to right, and keeps a set of items for each position: the rules that a reading could be in the middle of there. The work is the number of items, and five refinements keep it in proportion to the input and small:

  • One character of lookahead. An item is kept only when the next character can continue it, so the parser does not follow readings that the next character already rules out. A rule that could end anywhere, such as ~[#a]*, ends only where the next character can follow it.
  • Leo's items for right recursion. A rule that ends with itself, such as rest: ",", number, rest?, would otherwise complete once for every level of the recursion at every place the list could end; sxml completes the whole chain at once.
  • Compiled character classes. Each character of the input is looked up once in a table that says which of the grammar's character sets it belongs to.
  • Groups written out. A group or an option, such as (char; em) or inline?, and a hidden rule of one character set, such as -digit, is replaced where it is used, so the parser does not complete a rule of its own for every character. The XML is the same.
  • Regular rules read at once. A rule such as @date: digit, digit, ... or message: ~[#a]* needs no nesting: it is made of characters, character sets, repetitions and other such rules, without recursion, so its language is regular. When its XML is nothing but its text, as for a hidden rule, an attribute, or an element with only text inside, sxml compiles it once, with the grammar, into an automaton. The parser runs the automaton over the input in one step instead of making items for every character, and completes the rule at each place it can end where the next character can follow it. The XML is the same, and so is an ambiguity inside such a rule: the automaton counts the ways it reaches each end.

With these, the parser is linear on every grammar that has one reading for each input and can tell, at each place, how to go on with a bounded look ahead: the LR-regular grammars of parsing theory (Joop Leo, 1991). They include left recursion, right recursion, nesting, repetition and every grammar of Real Tasks. A right-recursive list of 200,000 numbers:

numbers.ixml:

numbers: number, rest?, -#a?.
-rest: -",", number, rest?.
number: ["0"-"9"]+.

$ sxml xpath --method=text --output=numbers.txt 'string-join(1 to 200000, ",")'
$ sxml xpath 'count(invisible-xml(unparsed-text("numbers.ixml"))(unparsed-text("numbers.txt"))//number)'
200000

Brackets nested 100,000 deep:

$ sxml xpath 'count(invisible-xml("nest: -""("", nest?, -"")"".")(string-join(((1 to 100000) ! "(", (1 to 100000) ! ")")))//nest)'
100000

Large inputs

The parser needs memory for its items and for the parse tree it reads out of them. A rule read at once makes no items inside it and one node for all its text; characters and hidden rules that the XML leaves out make no nodes, and neighbouring characters share one. So the memory follows the rules the parser cannot read at once, and is small when a grammar's text is in rules that it can: the log needs some 15 items and 9 nodes for each line of about 60 characters. All of it is released when the XML is built.

A log of 10 MB:

$ sxml xquery --method=text --param=lines=250000 --output=bigger.log make-log.xq
$ sxml xpath 'string-length(unparsed-text("bigger.log"))'
9972228
$ sxml xquery --method=text --param=file=bigger.log count-levels.xq
ERROR 83333
INFO 83333
WARN 83334

Ambiguous grammars

A grammar with many readings costs more. This one says nothing about how a sum groups, so a sum of n numbers has as many readings as there are ways to put in brackets, which grows faster than any power of n:

sum.ixml:

sum: sum, -"+", sum; number.
number: ["0"-"9"]+.

$ sxml xpath 'let $sum := invisible-xml(unparsed-text("sum.ixml"))(string-join(1 to 300, "+")) return (count($sum//number), string($sum/sum/@*:state))'
300
"ambiguous"

sxml never lists the readings. It keeps one for each item, so the items grow with the square of the input and the time with its cube: 2,000 characters take one to two seconds, eight times as long as 1,000. The cure is the cure of Writing Grammars: say how the parts group, here sum: sum, -"+", number; number., and the grammar is linear again.

Steps and limits

Every item the parser makes, every node of the parse tree, and every run of an automaton, with one more for every 16 characters it reads, counts as one step of the evaluation, so the step limit that stops a runaway query stops a runaway parse too. A linear grammar makes a few items for each character that no automaton reads, so the default limit of 108 steps allows inputs of many megabytes: the log of 100 MB parses within it. A host that embeds sxml can set a higher limit (Chapter "Embedding sxml in C").

Compared with tree-sitter

Source Code as XML parses code with tree-sitter, the parser generator behind the syntax highlighting of many editors. The two take different routes to a parse. A tree-sitter grammar is a JavaScript program that a generator turns, ahead of time, into a table of an LR parser in C, compiled into the program that uses it; sxml comes with a few. An iXML grammar is text that sxml compiles while the query runs, and the parser follows every reading the grammar allows. So tree-sitter takes only the grammars its generator accepts, and needs a build step for a new one; iXML takes any context-free grammar, at run time, ambiguous ones too. Faced with a mistake in the input, tree-sitter recovers, marks the place with an ERROR node and goes on, as an editor needs; an iXML parse fails, with the place where it failed (When a Parse Fails).

The trees differ as well. The same JSON both ways:

json.ixml:

json: -s, value, -s.
-value: object; array; string; number; true; false; null.
object: -"{", -s, (member, (-s, -",", -s, member)*)?, -s, -"}".
member: @name, -s, -":", -s, value.
array: -"[", -s, (value, (-s, -",", -s, value)*)?, -s, -"]".
@name: -'"', ~['"\']*, -'"'.
string: -'"', ~['"\']*, -'"'.
number: "-"?, ["0"-"9"]+, (".", ["0"-"9"]+)?, (["eE"], ["+-"]?, ["0"-"9"]+)?.
true: -"true".
false: -"false".
null: -"null".
-s: -[" "; #9; #a; #d]*.

$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'invisible-xml(unparsed-text("json.ixml"))(unparsed-text("flag.json"))'
<json><object><member name="flag"><string>dark-mode</string></member><member name="rollout"><number>25</number></member><member name="owners"><array><string>web</string></array></member></object></json>
$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("flag.json"), "json", { "highlights": false() })'
<document xmlns:sxml="urn:sxml"><object>{<pair><string field="key">"<string_content>flag</string_content>"</string>: <string field="value">"<string_content>dark-mode</string_content>"</string></pair>, <pair><string field="key">"<string_content>rollout</string_content>"</string>: <number field="value">25</number></pair>, <pair><string field="key">"<string_content>owners</string_content>"</string>: <array field="value">[<string>"<string_content>web</string_content>"</string>]</array></pair>}</object>
</document>

The grammar says what the XML is: hidden rules and strings leave the punctuation out, and the names become attributes. Tree-sitter's tree keeps every character of the text, the punctuation as text between the elements, and names its elements after the grammar's rules.

In time the two are close. The same benchmark suite parses 1 MB of JSON and the Markdown input of the table above both ways, and JSON with fn:json-to-xml too, sxml's hand-written JSON parser. The numbers are for the whole command, as above:

InputParserTimeMemoryElements
1 MB of JSONjson.ixmlunder 0.3 sunder 80 MB103,000
sxml:parse-code, tree-sitterunder 0.35 sunder 90 MB208,000
fn:json-to-xmlunder 0.25 sunder 60 MB62,000
1 MB of Markdown-like textmarkdown.ixmlunder 0.4 sunder 120 MB70,000
sxml:parse-code, tree-sitterunder 1.6 sunder 160 MB252,000

Of tree-sitter's time on the JSON, about 0.11 s is its parse alone: a small C program that runs tree-sitter's library on the same file, with no XML, takes that long. The rest is the XML tree, which has twice as many elements as the iXML grammar makes. A parser made for one language in advance, fn:json-to-xml, is faster than both, but not by much.

Markdown is two grammars in tree-sitter, one for the blocks and one for the text inside them, and its grammar for the blocks keeps several readings open where Markdown is unclear; it parses all of CommonMark, where markdown.ixml knows the few constructs of Real Tasks. The inline grammar is parsed anew for every paragraph, as a layer of its own (Code inside code). Both grow linearly with the input.

Writing fast grammars

  1. Avoid ambiguity. It is the one thing that makes a parse more than linear, and it is a mistake in the grammar anyway.
  2. Hide what you do not need. Hidden rules and strings make no elements, so the tree is smaller and the query after the parse is faster.
  3. Use character sets for runs of characters. [L]+ is one set read many times; letter+ with letter: "a"; "b"; ... is one rule with many alternatives at every character.
  4. Keep text in rules of its own. A rule whose XML is just its text is read at once when it is regular (see above). A mark or an insertion inside it, or a hidden character among visible ones, such as the -'"' of a quoted field, makes it an ordinary rule again: leave such parts to the rule around it, as -quoted: -'"', text, -'"' with -text: ~['"']* does.
  5. Compile once. Keep the parser in a variable and call it for every input (Compile once).

JSON, CSV and HTML

Not all data comes as XML. The XDM 4.0 data model that sxml's languages share has room for other formats: JSON becomes maps and arrays, CSV becomes rows of strings, and HTML becomes a tree of elements. Once data is in the model, everything in the previous chapters works on it. The examples use the trace files of Project: Comparing Traces Before and After a Change, in docs/book/examples/traces.

JSON

json-doc reads a JSON file into maps and arrays (parse-json does the same with a string). Then the lookup operator ? navigates it. An OTLP file is an object whose resourceSpans is an array; each member has scopeSpans, an array again, whose members have spans:

$ sxml xpath 'json-doc("before.json")?resourceSpans?1?resource?attributes?1?value?stringValue'
"storefront"
$ sxml xpath 'json-doc("before.json")?resourceSpans?*?scopeSpans?*?spans?* => count()'
14
$ sxml xpath 'json-doc("before.json")?resourceSpans?*?scopeSpans?*?spans?*[?kind = 3]?name'
"GET /api/getFlags"
"SELECT flags"
"SELECT flags"
"UPDATE flags"
"GET"
"POST /api/killFlag"

?1 is the first member of an array, and ?* is every member, so ?resourceSpans?*?scopeSpans?*?spans?* is every span of every scope of every resource. [?kind = 3] keeps the client spans, and ?name gets their names: the backend SDK's call of the service, the service's queries to PostgreSQL and Redis (the Redis span is named after its command, GET), and the console's call. A key that is not a name, such as Duration (ms), is looked up with a string in parentheses: ?("Duration (ms)").

JSON numbers become doubles, and JSON's null becomes the empty sequence:

$ sxml xpath 'json-doc("before.json")?resourceSpans?1?scopeSpans?1?spans?1?kind'
3.0e0

A double has 53 bits for its digits, about sixteen decimal digits. That is why OTLP writes the 64-bit integers, times in nanoseconds and intValue attributes, as strings: a JSON reader that turns numbers into doubles would lose their last digits. Two times one nanosecond apart are the same double, but xs:integer reads the strings exactly:

$ sxml xpath 'parse-json("1792573200000000001") = parse-json("1792573200000000000")'
true()
$ sxml xpath 'xs:integer("1792573200000000001") - xs:integer("1792573200000000000")'
1

When you read JSON that writes such numbers as numbers anyway, ask parse-json or json-doc for decimals with the option number-format. A decimal keeps every digit; "adaptive" makes a decimal of a number written without an exponent and a double of one written with it:

$ sxml xpath 'parse-json("1792573200000000001", { "number-format": "decimal" }) - parse-json("1792573200000000000", { "number-format": "decimal" })'
1
$ sxml xpath 'parse-json("[1792573200000000001, 2.5e0]", { "number-format": "adaptive" })?* ! (. instance of xs:decimal)'
true()
false()

To write JSON, build maps and arrays and use the json output method. The Trace Diff writes its result that way, and select.xq there writes a whole OTLP file.

JSON as XML

Sometimes it's more convenient to treat JSON as XML, for example to search it with paths or transform it with XSLT templates. json-to-xml turns JSON into an XML vocabulary of map, array, string, number, boolean and null elements, with the keys in key attributes, and xml-to-json turns that vocabulary back into JSON text. Here is the span with a given id, wherever it is in the file:

$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'json-to-xml(unparsed-text("before.json"))//*:map[*:string[@key = "spanId"] = "fb73f92d181aced2"]'
<map xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/xpath-functions"><string key="traceId">48114dcf6840d1bd46460c4b1ce0d09d</string><string key="spanId">fb73f92d181aced2</string><string key="parentSpanId">448683a55e6803a1</string><string key="name">SELECT flags</string><number key="kind">3</number><string key="startTimeUnixNano">1792573200005000000</string><string key="endTimeUnixNano">1792573200044000000</string><array key="attributes"><map><string key="key">db.system.name</string><map key="value"><string key="stringValue">postgresql</string></map></map><map><string key="key">db.operation.name</string><map key="value"><string key="stringValue">SELECT</string></map></map><map><string key="key">db.collection.name</string><map key="value"><string key="stringValue">flags</string></map></map><map><string key="key">db.query.text</string><map key="value"><string key="stringValue">SELECT key, name, state, percentage, rules, owners FROM flags</string></map></map><map><string key="key">server.address</string><map key="value"><string key="stringValue">postgresql</string></map></map><map><string key="key">server.port</string><map key="value"><string key="intValue">5432</string></map></map></array></map>
$ sxml xpath --method=text 'json-to-xml(unparsed-text("before.json"))//*:map[*:string[@key = "spanId"] = "fb73f92d181aced2"]/*:array => xml-to-json()'
[{"key":"db.system.name","value":{"stringValue":"postgresql"}},{"key":"db.operation.name","value":{"stringValue":"SELECT"}},{"key":"db.collection.name","value":{"stringValue":"flags"}},{"key":"db.query.text","value":{"stringValue":"SELECT key, name, state, percentage, rules, owners FROM flags"}},{"key":"server.address","value":{"stringValue":"postgresql"}},{"key":"server.port","value":{"intValue":"5432"}}]

CSV

The csv output method writes each array as a row, quoting the fields that need it. A query can so write the spans for a spreadsheet:

spans-csv.xq:

(: The spans of a trace file as CSV, one row per span, for a spreadsheet. :)
import module namespace trace = "urn:example:trace" at "trace.xqm";
declare option output:method "csv";

declare variable $file external := "before.json";

["route", "service", "name", "kind", "start", "duration"],
for $span in trace:load($file)//span
return [
  string($span/ancestor::trace/@route),
  string($span/@service), string($span/@name), string($span/@kind),
  xs:decimal($span/@start), xs:decimal($span/@duration)
]

$ sxml xquery spans-csv.xq
route,service,name,kind,start,duration
GET /api/getFlags,storefront,GET /api/getFlags,client,0,50
GET /api/getFlags,vane,GET /api/getFlags,server,1,48
GET /api/getFlags,vane,flags.listFlags,internal,2,46
GET /api/getFlags,vane,registry.getFlags,internal,3,43
GET /api/getFlags,vane,SELECT flags,client,5,39
POST /api/killFlag,vane-console,POST /api/killFlag,client,0,34
POST /api/killFlag,vane,POST /api/killFlag,server,1,32
POST /api/killFlag,vane,flags.killFlag,internal,2,30
POST /api/killFlag,vane,cache.getFlag,internal,3,3
POST /api/killFlag,vane,GET,client,4,1
POST /api/killFlag,vane,registry.getFlag,internal,7,9
POST /api/killFlag,vane,SELECT flags,client,8,7
POST /api/killFlag,vane,registry.setPercentage,internal,17,13
POST /api/killFlag,vane,UPDATE flags,client,18,11

The other way round, a tracing tool's user interface often exports a trace as CSV. spans.csv is such an export of the new version's GET /api/getFlags, the backend SDK downloading the flags:

spans.csv (the start):

Trace ID,Span ID,Parent ID,Service,Operation,Start Time,Duration (ms),Statement
95cfc9416dff30ee3edeae4b2c53e1c4,6a06eb67c8c7b1df,,storefront,GET /api/getFlags,2026-10-21 09:00:00.000,110,
95cfc9416dff30ee3edeae4b2c53e1c4,4784b113aa8e01c1,6a06eb67c8c7b1df,vane,GET /api/getFlags,2026-10-21 09:00:00.001,108,
95cfc9416dff30ee3edeae4b2c53e1c4,c078a6c13fbbb2b7,4784b113aa8e01c1,vane,flags.listFlags,2026-10-21 09:00:00.002,104,
95cfc9416dff30ee3edeae4b2c53e1c4,4a09e0dc364b4ceb,c078a6c13fbbb2b7,vane,registry.getFlagKeys,2026-10-21 09:00:00.003,12,
95cfc9416dff30ee3edeae4b2c53e1c4,59be2e375b69cde3,4a09e0dc364b4ceb,vane,SELECT flags,2026-10-21 09:00:00.005,8,SELECT key FROM flags
95cfc9416dff30ee3edeae4b2c53e1c4,3916e2d3c40454dd,c078a6c13fbbb2b7,vane,registry.getFlag,2026-10-21 09:00:00.016,20,
95cfc9416dff30ee3edeae4b2c53e1c4,68edbeb8d88faf5c,3916e2d3c40454dd,vane,SELECT flags,2026-10-21 09:00:00.018,16,"SELECT key, name, state, percentage, rules, owners FROM flags WHERE key = $1"

parse-csv reads CSV text. With "header": true(), the first row names the columns. The result is a record with the column names, a map from each name to its position, the rows, each an array of strings, and a function get that takes a row number and a column name:

$ sxml xpath 'parse-csv(unparsed-text("spans.csv"), { "header": true() })?columns'
"Trace ID"
"Span ID"
"Parent ID"
"Service"
"Operation"
"Start Time"
"Duration (ms)"
"Statement"
$ sxml xpath 'parse-csv(unparsed-text("spans.csv"), { "header": true() })?rows[7]'
["95cfc9416dff30ee3edeae4b2c53e1c4","68edbeb8d88faf5c","3916e2d3c40454dd","vane","SELECT flags","2026-10-21 09:00:00.018","16","SELECT key, name, state, percentage, rules, owners FROM flags WHERE key = $1"]
$ sxml xpath 'parse-csv(unparsed-text("spans.csv"), { "header": true() })?get(7, "Statement")'
"SELECT key, name, state, percentage, rules, owners FROM flags WHERE key = $1"

The statement has commas in it, so the file quotes it, and parse-csv takes the quotes away. A query can read CSV, compute, and write CSV again:

durations.xq:

(: Time per service and operation, from a CSV export of one trace,
   written as CSV. :)
declare option output:method "csv";

let $spans := parse-csv(unparsed-text("spans.csv"), { "header": true() })
let $column := $spans?column-index
return (
  ["service", "operation", "calls", "total ms"],
  for $row in $spans?rows
  group by $service := $row($column?Service),
           $operation := $row($column?Operation)
  order by $service, $operation
  return [
    $service,
    $operation,
    count($row),
    sum($row ! xs:decimal(.($column?("Duration (ms)"))))
  ]
)

$ sxml xquery durations.xq
service,operation,calls,total ms
storefront,GET /api/getFlags,1,110
vane,GET /api/getFlags,1,108
vane,SELECT flags,5,72
vane,flags.listFlags,1,104
vane,registry.getFlag,4,80
vane,registry.getFlagKeys,1,12

The five queries take 72 of the 104 milliseconds of flags.listFlags. order by compares strings by their code points, so SELECT flags, in capitals, comes before the function names in lower case.

$row($column?Service) looks up the position of the Service column and then that member of the row, so the query keeps working if the columns are reordered; a column name with spaces needs a string, $column?("Duration (ms)"). csv-to-xml turns CSV into XML instead, with row and field elements:

$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'csv-to-xml(unparsed-text("spans.csv"), { "header": true() })//*:row[1]'
<row xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/xpath-functions"><field column="Trace ID">95cfc9416dff30ee3edeae4b2c53e1c4</field><field column="Span ID">6a06eb67c8c7b1df</field><field column="Parent ID"/><field column="Service">storefront</field><field column="Operation">GET /api/getFlags</field><field column="Start Time">2026-10-21 09:00:00.000</field><field column="Duration (ms)">110</field><field column="Statement"/></row>

HTML

Real HTML is rarely well-formed XML: end tags are left out, attributes have no quotes, and browsers fix it all up by rules that the HTML standard spells out. html-doc and parse-html parse HTML by exactly those rules, into elements in the XHTML namespace. This is the status page of Vane, the service, its console, and the two databases the service uses:

status.html:

<!doctype html>
<title>Vane status</title>
<h1>Components</h1>
<table id=components>
  <tr><th>Component<th>Version<th>Status
  <tr><td>vane<td>2.4.0<td class=ok>up
  <tr><td>vane-console<td>1.8.0<td class=ok>up
  <tr><td>postgresql<td>16.4<td class=ok>up
  <tr><td>redis<td>7.4.1<td class=slow>slow
</table>
<p>Updated at <time datetime=2026-10-21T09:05:00Z>09:05</time>, <b>4 of 4</b> components answering.

$ sxml xpath 'html-doc("status.html")/*:html/*:head/*:title/string()'
"Vane status"
$ sxml xpath 'html-doc("status.html")//*:tr[*:td] ! { string(*:td[1]): normalize-space(*:td[3]) } => map:merge()'
{"vane":"up","vane-console":"up","postgresql":"up","redis":"slow"}
$ sxml xpath 'html-doc("status.html")//*:td[@class = "slow"]/preceding-sibling::*:td[1]/string()'
"7.4.1"
$ sxml xpath 'xs:dateTime(html-doc("status.html")//*:time/@datetime)'
xs:dateTime("2026-10-21T09:05:00Z")

Because the elements are in the XHTML namespace, a plain td would not match them; *:td matches td in any namespace. In XQuery, you can write declare default element namespace "http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"; instead and use plain names. The parser found the head, the tbody and every missing end tag, as a browser would. A cell without an end tag runs to the next tag, so the last cell of each row holds the line break after it, and normalize-space removes it.

$ sxml xpath 'parse-html("<p>One<p>Two")//*:p => count()'
2

To write HTML, use the html output method, which knows which elements have no end tag and how to write <!DOCTYPE html>; Rendering the Diff writes a report with it.

Other text

Text that has a grammar but no standard parser, a log format or the syntax of a configuration file, can become XML too: Invisible XML turns a grammar into a parser. Parsing Text with Invisible XML shows how.

Source Code as XML

Program source code has a grammar too, and for many languages the grammar is already written: tree-sitter grammars power the syntax highlighting and code navigation of many editors. sxml includes the tree-sitter grammars of JSON, JavaScript (with JSX), TypeScript, TSX, Python, C, CSS, HTML, Go and Markdown, and sxml:parse-code turns code in any of them into an XML document. Other tree-sitter grammars can be added when sxml runs (see Supplying your own language). Then XPath, XQuery and XSLT can answer questions about the code: where a function is called, which functions a module exports, which comments say TODO. The examples are in docs/book/examples/source-code.

Parsing code

greet.js:

// Says hello.
function greet(name) {
  return "Hello, " + name;
}

sxml:parse-code takes the code as a string and the name of its language, and returns a document:

$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("greet.js"), "javascript")'
<program xmlns:sxml="urn:sxml"><comment highlight="comment">// Says hello.</comment>
<function_declaration><sxml:token highlight="keyword">function</sxml:token> <identifier field="name" highlight="function">greet</identifier><formal_parameters field="parameters"><sxml:token highlight="punctuation.bracket">(</sxml:token><identifier highlight="variable.parameter">name</identifier><sxml:token highlight="punctuation.bracket">)</sxml:token></formal_parameters> <statement_block field="body"><sxml:token highlight="punctuation.bracket">{</sxml:token>
  <return_statement><sxml:token highlight="keyword">return</sxml:token> <binary_expression><string field="left" highlight="string">"<string_fragment>Hello, </string_fragment>"</string> <sxml:token field="operator" highlight="operator">+</sxml:token> <identifier field="right" highlight="variable.parameter">name</identifier></binary_expression><sxml:token highlight="punctuation.delimiter">;</sxml:token></return_statement>
<sxml:token highlight="punctuation.bracket">}</sxml:token></statement_block></function_declaration>
</program>

The document follows the grammar's syntax tree:

  • Each named node of the tree is an element whose name is the node's kind: function_declaration, identifier, return_statement. The names are the grammar's own; tree-sitter's playground and each grammar's node-types.json list them.
  • When the grammar gives a node a field name, as in name, parameters and body, the element has a field attribute.
  • Tokens, the keywords and punctuation, are text, and so are the spaces and line breaks between nodes, so the string value of the document is the source code, exactly:
$ sxml xpath 'string(sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("greet.js"), "javascript")) = unparsed-text("greet.js")'
true()
  • The highlight attribute is what the language's highlighting query (the queries/highlights.scm of its grammar) says about the node: keyword, function, string, comment, variable.parameter and so on. Where the grammar has a locals query (queries/locals.scm), a name that refers to a parameter or variable gets the highlight of its definition: the name in return "Hello, " + name is a variable.parameter, like the parameter it names. A token that has a highlight or a field becomes an sxml:token element, so that it can carry the attribute; with the option { "highlights": false() } most tokens stay plain text.

The prefix sxml is bound to the namespace urn:sxml in the sxml command's XPath and XQuery; a stylesheet declares it. The elements of the tree itself are in no namespace.

The third argument takes options:

OptionDefaultMeaning
highlightstrue()Run the language's highlighting query and write highlight attributes
positionsfalse()Write line and column attributes (where each element starts, from 1, columns counted in characters) and end-line and end-column (where it ends)
injectionstrue()Parse code inside code (a Markdown code block, an HTML script element) with its own language; see Code inside code

sxml:code-languages() lists the languages:

$ sxml xpath 'sxml:code-languages()'
"c"
"css"
"go"
"html"
"javascript"
"json"
"markdown"
"markdown_inline"
"python"
"tsx"
"typescript"

Which functions does a module export?

cart.js:

import { formatPrice } from "./money.js";

const TAX_RATE = 0.2;

export function total(items) {
  // TODO: apply discounts
  return items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price * item.quantity, 0);
}

export function totalWithTax(items) {
  return total(items) * (1 + TAX_RATE);
}

function describe(item) {
  // TODO: localize the currency
  return `${item.name}: ${formatPrice(item.price)}`;
}

export const summary = (items) => items.map(describe).join("\n");

An exported function is a function_declaration, or a const with an arrow function, inside an export_statement. The name is the child whose field is name:

$ sxml xpath 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("cart.js"), "javascript")//export_statement//*[@field = "name"][1] ! string()'
"total"
"totalWithTax"
"summary"

The same with the functions that are not exported, and how many parameters each has:

$ sxml xpath 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("cart.js"), "javascript")/program/function_declaration ! `{identifier} takes {count(formal_parameters/identifier)}`'
"describe takes 1"

TODO comments and where they are

With the option positions, each element knows its line. A comment knows the function it is in through the ancestor axis:

$ sxml xpath 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("cart.js"), "javascript", { "positions": true() })//comment[contains(., "TODO")] ! `line {@line}, in {ancestor::function_declaration/identifier}: {substring-after(., "TODO: ")}`'
"line 6, in total: apply discounts"
"line 15, in describe: localize the currency"

Python works the same way. report.py:

import csv


def load(path):
    """Reads the rows of a CSV file."""
    with open(path, newline="") as source:
        return list(csv.DictReader(source))


def total(rows):
    # TODO: skip rows without an amount
    return sum(float(row["amount"]) for row in rows)


class Report:
    """A report on the rows of one file."""

    def __init__(self, path):
        self.rows = load(path)

    def render(self):
        return f"{len(self.rows)} rows, {total(self.rows):.2f} in all"

$ sxml xpath 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("report.py"), "python", { "positions": true() })//comment ! `{@line}: {ancestor::function_definition/identifier[@field = "name"]}: {.}`'
"11: total: # TODO: skip rows without an amount"

A function whose body does not start with a string has no docstring:

$ sxml xpath 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("report.py"), "python")//function_definition[not(block/*[1][self::string])]/identifier[@field = "name"] ! string()'
"total"
"__init__"
"render"

Checking a style rule

sxml's own C code has two rules that a query can check: a function has at most three parameters, and names are spelled out. buffer.c:

#include <stddef.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Appends one byte; returns 0 when the buffer is full. */
static int buffer_append(char *bytes, size_t *byte_count, size_t capacity, char byte) {
    if (*byte_count == capacity) {
        return 0;
    }
    bytes[*byte_count] = byte;
    *byte_count += 1;
    return 1;
}

size_t buffer_copy(char *target, const char *source, size_t len) {
    memcpy(target, source, len);
    return len;
}

void buffer_clear(char *buf, size_t capacity) {
    memset(buf, 0, capacity);
}

$ sxml xpath 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("buffer.c"), "c", { "positions": true() })//function_declarator[count(parameter_list/parameter_declaration) > 3] ! `{@line}: {*[@field = "declarator"]} has {count(parameter_list/parameter_declaration)} parameters`'
"5: buffer_append has 4 parameters"
$ sxml xpath 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("buffer.c"), "c", { "positions": true() })//parameter_declaration//identifier[. = ("buf", "len", "ptr", "tmp")] ! `{@line}:{@column}: {.} is not spelled out`'
"14:61: len is not spelled out"
"19:25: buf is not spelled out"

Counting JSX elements

Gallery.jsx:

import { Photo } from "./Photo.jsx";
import { Footer } from "./Footer.jsx";

export function Gallery({ photos }) {
  return (
    <section className="gallery">
      <h2>Photos</h2>
      {photos.map((photo) => (
        <Photo key={photo.id} src={photo.url} />
      ))}
      <Footer />
    </section>
  );
}

JSX is part of the JavaScript grammar. An element with content is a jsx_element, one that closes itself a jsx_self_closing_element:

$ sxml xpath 'count(sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("Gallery.jsx"), "javascript")//(jsx_element | jsx_self_closing_element))'
4

The highlighting query tells HTML tags from components: it marks a lowercase name as tag and a capitalized one as constructor. So the components the file uses are:

$ sxml xpath 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("Gallery.jsx"), "javascript")//(jsx_opening_element | jsx_self_closing_element)/identifier[@highlight = "constructor"] => distinct-values()'
"Photo"
"Footer"

A refactoring report

Before renaming a function, find every call of it. money.js:

export function formatPrice(amount) {
  return amount.toFixed(2) + " EUR";
}

export function formatTotal(amounts) {
  return formatPrice(amounts.reduce((sum, amount) => sum + amount, 0));
}

calls.xq:

(: Every call of the function $name in the JavaScript files, with its line. :)
declare option output:method "text";
declare option output:item-separator "&#10;";

declare variable $name external := "formatPrice";

for $file in ("cart.js", "money.js")
let $code := sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text($file), "javascript", { "positions": true() })
for $call in $code//call_expression[*[@field = "function"] = $name]
return `{$file}:{$call/@line}: {$call}`

$ sxml xquery calls.xq
cart.js:16: formatPrice(item.price)
money.js:6: formatPrice(amounts.reduce((sum, amount) => sum + amount, 0))

TypeScript and TSX

shapes.ts:

// Shapes and their areas.
export interface Circle {
  kind: "circle";
  radius: number;
}

export interface Rectangle {
  kind: "rectangle";
  width: number;
  height: number;
}

export type Shape = Circle | Rectangle;

export function area(shape: Shape): number {
  switch (shape.kind) {
    case "circle":
      return Math.PI * shape.radius ** 2;
    case "rectangle":
      return shape.width * shape.height;
  }
}

export function describe(shape: Shape, digits?: number): string {
  return `${shape.kind}: ${area(shape).toFixed(digits ?? 2)}`;
}

The TypeScript grammar has the nodes of JavaScript and the types on top of them. The properties of each interface:

$ sxml xpath 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("shapes.ts"), "typescript")//interface_declaration ! `{type_identifier}: {string-join(.//property_signature/property_identifier, ", ")}`'
"Circle: kind, radius"
"Rectangle: kind, width, height"

The signature of each exported function, with the types written as in the source:

$ sxml xpath 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("shapes.ts"), "typescript")//export_statement/function_declaration ! `{identifier}({string-join(formal_parameters/(required_parameter | optional_parameter), ", ")}){*[@field = "return_type"]}`'
"area(shape: Shape): number"
"describe(shape: Shape, digits?: number): string"

TSX is TypeScript with JSX, and has a grammar of its own, tsx. Profile.tsx:

type Props = { name: string; avatar?: string; bio?: string };

export function Profile({ name, avatar, bio }: Props) {
  return (
    <div className="profile">
      <Avatar src={avatar} size={48} />
      <h2>{name}</h2>
      {bio && <Markdown text={bio} />}
    </div>
  );
}

The components the file uses, and the properties that are optional:

$ sxml xpath 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("Profile.tsx"), "tsx")//(jsx_opening_element | jsx_self_closing_element)/identifier[@highlight = "constructor"] ! string()'
"Avatar"
"Markdown"
$ sxml xpath 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("Profile.tsx"), "tsx")//property_signature[contains(., "?")]/property_identifier ! string()'
"avatar"
"bio"

Markdown

Markdown has two grammars: markdown for the blocks (headings, paragraphs, lists, code blocks) and markdown_inline for what is inside a paragraph or a heading (emphasis, links, code spans). notes.md:

# Release notes

## Fixed

- Nested lists no longer lose their *last* item
  ([issue 12](https://example.com/issues/12)).
- `parse` keeps comments; see [the guide](guide.md).

## Example

```python
def greet(name):
    return "Hello, " + name
```

```javascript
console.log(greet("world"));
```

The headings and their levels:

$ sxml xpath 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("notes.md"), "markdown")//atx_heading ! `{string-length(*[1])}: {normalize-space(inline)}`'
"1: Release notes"
"2: Fixed"
"2: Example"

sxml:parse-code parses the text of each block with the inline grammar (see the next section), so the links are there too:

$ sxml xpath 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("notes.md"), "markdown")//inline_link ! `{link_text}: {link_destination}`'
"issue 12: https://example.com/issues/12"
"the guide: guide.md"

Code inside code

A Markdown code block holds code in another language, and so does an HTML script element. The grammar's injections query (queries/injections.scm) says which nodes hold code and in which language: the info string after the fence, javascript for a script element, the inline grammar for Markdown's paragraphs. sxml:parse-code parses each such node with that language, when it knows the language, and puts the tree inside the node's element. The tree's document element names its language in a language attribute:

$ sxml xpath --method=xml 'sxml:parse-code("Some *text*.", "markdown")'
<document xmlns:sxml="urn:sxml"><section><paragraph><inline><inline language="markdown_inline">Some <emphasis highlight="text.emphasis"><emphasis_delimiter highlight="punctuation.delimiter">*</emphasis_delimiter>text<emphasis_delimiter highlight="punctuation.delimiter">*</emphasis_delimiter></emphasis>.</inline></inline></paragraph></section></document>

So the Python function in the release notes is a function_definition like any other:

$ sxml xpath 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("notes.md"), "markdown")//*[@language = "python"]//function_definition/identifier ! string()'
"greet"
$ sxml xpath 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("notes.md"), "markdown")//fenced_code_block ! `{info_string}: {code_fence_content/*[@language]/name()}`'
"python: module"
"javascript: program"

and the script and style sheet of an HTML page are JavaScript and CSS, highlighted as such. page.html:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <style>
      .total { font-weight: bold; }
    </style>
  </head>
  <body>
    <p class="total" id="total"></p>
    <script>
      const prices = [3, 4.5];
      document.getElementById("total").textContent = prices.reduce((sum, price) => sum + price);
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

$ sxml xpath 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("page.html"), "html")//*[@language] ! `{@language}: {count(.//*[@highlight])} highlighted`'
"css: 7 highlighted"
"javascript: 33 highlighted"
$ sxml xpath 'sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text("page.html"), "html")//*[@language = "javascript"]//*[@highlight = "function.method"] ! string()'
"getElementById"
"reduce"

The text is still the source text: the string value of the document is the page, and the option { "injections": false() } leaves the code inside code as text.

Highlighted HTML with XSLT

Because the highlighting query has already named each part of the code, turning code into highlighted HTML takes one template rule: every element with a highlight attribute becomes a span whose class is the highlight, and the built-in rules copy the text of everything else.

highlight.xsl:

<xsl:stylesheet version="4.0"
    xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform"
    xmlns:sxml="urn:sxml"
    exclude-result-prefixes="sxml">
  <xsl:param name="file" required="yes"/>
  <xsl:param name="language" select="'javascript'"/>
  <xsl:output method="html" html-version="5"/>

  <xsl:template name="xsl:initial-template">
    <pre class="code">
      <xsl:apply-templates select="sxml:parse-code(unparsed-text($file), $language)"/>
    </pre>
  </xsl:template>

  <!-- Every node a highlights query captured becomes a span. -->
  <xsl:template match="*[@highlight]">
    <span class="{translate(@highlight, '.', ' ')}">
      <xsl:apply-templates/>
    </span>
  </xsl:template>
</xsl:stylesheet>

$ sxml transform --param=file=greet.js highlight.xsl
<pre class="code"><span class="comment">// Says hello.</span>
<span class="keyword">function</span> <span class="function">greet</span><span class="punctuation bracket">(</span><span class="variable parameter">name</span><span class="punctuation bracket">)</span> <span class="punctuation bracket">{</span>
  <span class="keyword">return</span> <span class="string">"Hello, "</span> <span class="operator">+</span> <span class="variable parameter">name</span><span class="punctuation delimiter">;</span>
<span class="punctuation bracket">}</span>
</pre>

A style sheet with rules such as .keyword { color: purple } and .string { color: green } does the rest. The language parameter selects another grammar: --param=language=python.

Code with syntax errors

tree-sitter does not stop at a syntax error. It parses what it can and marks the rest: an ERROR element holds text it could not place, and an element with missing="true" stands for a token it expected but did not find (an sxml:token with the token's kind when the token is punctuation).
